Operating Systems.title: Towards Fully-fledged GPU Multitasking via Proactive Memory Scheduling
Operating Systems.summary: Limited HBM capacity has become the primary bottleneck for hosting a growing number of increasingly larger-scale GPU tasks. While demand paging extends capacity via host DRAM, it can incur order-of-magnitude slowdowns due to the massive working sets of GPU workloads. However, we observe that GPU memory accesses are inherently predictable from kernel launch arguments, prior executions, and the asynchronous execution nature. Leveraging this opportunity, we propose MSched, an OS-level scheduler that extends GPU context switching to include proactive working set preparation. This approach coalesces fragmented, eventual, and expensive page faults into a single efficient migration. MSched combines parameterized templates with page fault feedback to accurately predict working sets, and co-designs the task scheduler and memory manager to resolve global access order and enforce near-optimal page replacement. Across scientific, deep learning, and LLM workloads, MSched outperforms demand paging by up to 186.69x and whole-process swapping by up to 8.63x. MSched is open-source and has been integrated into https://github.com/XpuOS/nvxsched.

Operating Systems.title: Device-Life Boundary Indicators and the Classification of Restored Versus Native Records on Android
Operating Systems.summary: A phone that shows calls, messages and photographs from years ago may have been set up recently and carried them over from an earlier handset, so its screen dates do not date the device's own life. Which traces fix where that life begins, how well they agree and how much of what is visible predates it is unmeasured. We read 14 Android full file system extractions (12 Samsung; Android 10 to 16), seven bug reports and 33 iOS extractions (a probe). Every Android device recorded a first boot, but the first evidence of user setup came a median of 98 days later (0 to 563). Of the 13 devices with messages, 7 held some dated before the first boot, a majority of them on 5; 24% of the apps outside the system image were installed as restored. Against the creator field that a migration tool leaves on messages, a boundary at user setup recalled all but 1 of 46,968 such messages, the first-boot boundary 94 to 100%. On synthetic fixtures, the labelling error followed the boundary error. A date on a record dates the device only once the record is shown to have been created on it.
Operating Systems.comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Lab Technical Report LAB-TR-0028, SectraTEK Lab; preprint, not peer reviewed. Corresponding author: Daniel Kwaku Ntiamoah Addai

Operating Systems.title: Retention Horizons of Volatile Stores in iOS and Android Extractions
Operating Systems.summary: Whether an extraction can answer a question about a given day depends on how far back each store reaches, yet public statements rest on single test devices. We measured the retention horizon, the time from a store's oldest retained record to acquisition, for eight iOS and seven Android stores on 48 full file system extractions and seven bug reports, keeping devices whose clock agreed with the acquisition time (26 Apple devices, 13 Android phones). Horizons ranged from minutes to years and followed the mechanism that bounds each store. The unified log Persist stream reached a median of 2.5 days; interactionC reached 166 to 170 days on 18 of 25 devices. Android stores stayed within their source-code limits (usage statistics 10.2 days, DropBox 3.1, notifications 1.5); bug-report logs reached 3.1 hours at most. The oldest record misled three times: one knowledgeC stream reached back two years, the others a median of 29 days; interactionC read without its write-ahead log showed older records on 18 of 25 devices; and four of seven bug reports began with stray lines up to 16.6 days old above a body of 3.1 hours or less. A horizon belongs to a store, a release and a device.
Operating Systems.comment: 17 pages, 3 figures. Lab Technical Report LAB-TR-0021, SectraTEK Lab; preprint, not peer reviewed. Corresponding author: Daniel Kwaku Ntiamoah Addai. Also archived at Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24023417

Operating Systems.title: The Storage View Of KV Cache: Characterizing Cache Behavior Across LLM Workloads
Operating Systems.summary:
Modern LLM serving increasingly extends KV caches beyond GPU memory into host DRAM, SSDs, and remote storage, yet these stores remain largely governed by workload-agnostic policies such as LRU and fixed TTLs. We ask what execution context is needed by storage to make retention, reclamation, and placement decisions across heterogeneous workloads.
  We characterize KV-cache reuse, lifetime, and footprint at block granularity across 11 production and public traces spanning chat, API serving, RAG, coding agents, tool-using agents, and multi-lineage workflows. We examine reuse sources, recurrence timing and frequency, useful lifetimes, and storage consumption. Across workloads, KV state takes two recurring forms. Single-session state is reused within one execution: its footprint grows as sessions deepen and accumulates across concurrent sessions; it can remain useful through long idle periods but loses value at session completion. Multi-session state recurs across sessions of the same workload, outlives individual sessions, and spans hot prefixes and a large infrequent tail.
  While prior systems often exploit application-, agent-, or workflow-specific knowledge, our results suggest that three generic signals (a workload identifier, a session identifier, and session completion) expose much of the structure needed for KV-storage management. Trace-driven comparisons show that workload-specific recurrence estimates retain up to 22% more within-session hits and reduce dead state by up to 40%; a session completion signal eliminates the fundamental idle-time reclamation tradeoff for single-session state; and session-aware reuse classification identifies shared state 4-700x more selectively than request-level access counts. These results motivate a small cross-layer interface for workload-aware KV storage without application-specific semantics.

Hardware Architecture.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
Hardware Architecture.summary: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.

Hardware Architecture.title: Atik: A Shared-Mesh Transformer Accelerator for RISC-V
Hardware Architecture.summary: Transformer inference repeatedly invokes dense matrix multiplication and attention, including its data-dependent softmax normalization. We present Atik, an open-source RoCC accelerator for RocketChip that executes matrix multiplication and dense attention through one shared fixed-point MAC mesh. Atik accepts and returns BF16 tensors, uses a streaming online-softmax schedule that never materializes the full score matrix, and is invoked through a small descriptor-based ABI. We evaluate three meshes cycle-by-cycle on FireSim and report standalone Sky130 physical-design area. Across 137 logged FireSim test records, all tests pass their benchmark tolerance with zero reported output mismatches. Relative to the same scalar Rocket BF16 reference, the 8x8 configuration reaches 31.5x peak matmul speedup and 225.8x peak attention speedup. Hybrid projections for the single-layer workload-derived C models, using directly measured accelerator-kernel cycles, give aggregate speedups of 44.2x, 77.1x, and 32.3x for ViT, TinyBERT, and GPT-2 prefill, respectively; these are not full-model hardware replays.

Hardware Architecture.title: Memory as a Temporal Resource: Lifetime Contracts for Multi-Retention Systems
Hardware Architecture.summary: Computers move and rewrite data whose useful lifetimes range from inner-loop iterations to years, yet memory systems usually hide retention as a fixed physical property. We argue that required lifetime should become a first-class resource across algorithms, programming systems, controllers, and devices. Building on prior lifetime-aware placement, we propose an event-based validity contract that links application completion events to retention-class selection and renewal of protection. Applications would be enabled to express semantic contracts such as ``until this tile completes'' and the system will map data to homogeneous arrays engineered for ephemeral, epoch, or durable retention and preserve correctness through margins, ECC, refresh, migration, or recomputation. We present a trace-based simulator and FPGA prototype that exercises class migration.

Hardware Architecture.title: Robust & Scalable Website Fingerprinting via Minimal DRAM Traffic
Hardware Architecture.summary: Website fingerprinting attacks infer websites visited by users and threaten their privacy. These attacks are classified as on-path, which monitor network traffic, and co-located, which exploit shared system resources. Existing co-located attacks, such as sweep-counting and loop-counting, achieve over 90% accuracy but suffer significant performance degradation on many-core systems. Loop-counting accuracy drops from 93% on 8 cores to 50% on 24 cores, while sweep-counting accuracy decreases from 84% to 45% across multiple Core Complex Dies (CCDs). To address these limitations, we propose memory-chasing, a scalable website fingerprinting attack that exploits DRAM traffic interference through pointer-chasing traversals with minimal interference. By counting DRAM accesses over fixed intervals, the attack generates distinctive traces for website classification. Evaluated on the top 50 websites, memory-chasing achieves 96% accuracy on a 24-core system, 86% across multiple CCDs, 80% across multiple sockets, and 97% in an open-world setting. Extensive evaluation across hardware configurations, browsers, operating systems, isolation mechanisms, system noise, and countermeasures demonstrates its robustness and scalability.

Hardware Architecture.title: TwinHash: Two-Sided Object Identity Management for Time- and Energy-Efficient Agentic Workflows
Hardware Architecture.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) services interleave large language model (LLM) generation with external tool execution, and increasingly rely on search-based workflows that repeatedly revisit shared reasoning states and computations. These patterns create substantial redundancy across tool outputs, LLM responses, and key-value (KV) prefixes, yet existing serving systems primarily optimize shared prompt prefixes, while naive input-keyed caching is unsafe when identical requests produce different outputs. We present TwinHash, a unified object management architecture that assigns each object an input-side hash key to recognize repeated requests and an output-side content fingerprint to validate and locate stored state, complemented by type-specific reuse guards that preserve correctness and response diversity. A software object identity table maintains reusable objects across requests and trajectories, while a hardware object placement table tracks their residency across hierarchical memory tiers so that evicted state can be retrieved rather than recomputed. Across seven agent frameworks and five benchmark suites, reuse follows workflow structure more than benchmark identity. TwinHash serves up to 81% of tool outputs wherever deterministic tool reads recur, and up to 92% of LLM responses in search-based frameworks. Retrieving an evicted KV-prefix from DRAM reduces TTFT by up to 5.6x on Qwen3-32B, with greater gains projected for larger dense models. Under search-based frameworks, TwinHash reduces end-to-end wall-clock time by up to 87% and measured task energy by up to 81% over a prefix-cached baseline, while a per-key serving cap controls the quality-reuse trade-off in adaptive search. These results demonstrate that unified identity, safety, and placement management can convert structural redundancy in emerging agentic workflows into substantial serving-efficiency gains.

Hardware Architecture.title: Embedded Arena: Iterative Optimization via Hardware Feedback
Hardware Architecture.summary: As AI moves into the physical world, from robots to environmental sensors to medical wearables, it increasingly relies on local inference to meet latency, communication, or privacy constraints. Optimizing models for heterogeneous edge hardware such as microcontrollers (MCUs) requires simultaneously satisfying hard physical constraints on memory, power, and temperature while preserving accuracy, a multidimensional optimization that is today performed manually by experts. We ask whether an LLM agent can autonomously navigate this complex, multi-turn pipeline guided by real hardware feedback, and introduce a hardware-in-the-loop agent arena in which the agent iteratively refines both model and firmware by compiling, flashing, and measuring on real hardware, enabling closed-loop optimization. Frontier models, including Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, fail entirely without hardware feedback (0% deployment success), whereas our hardware-in-the-loop formulation achieves the first successful deployment within three iterations and can surpass human expert results within seven. This agentic co-optimization achieves 250x compression for vision models with <3.3% accuracy loss and 400x for audio with <6% Feature Error Rate loss, enabling battery-free operation on a commercial MCU via solar harvesting. We demonstrate practical impact in two real-world systems: an elk-detection camera trap (96.7% accuracy) and a phonetic-transcription wearable (8.37% FER) for child development research.

Hardware Architecture.title: The World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA): Hardware-Algorithm Co-Design for Embedded AI in Robotics
Hardware Architecture.summary: Embedded AI is moving from perception to prediction. Robots now use world models$\unicode{x2014}$learned simulators that predict the outcome of candidate actions in a compressed latent space before any is executed. Every predicted step must be computed on board within a tight power and thermal budget, yet the energy these steps fundamentally require, and how far real hardware sits from it, have not been characterized. We derive lower bounds on the arithmetic operations and the CMOS dynamic energy of a latent state transition from information theory and Boolean circuit complexity. Profiling a DreamerV3-style Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) shows that every rollout operation is memory-bandwidth bound and that a GPU consumes at least $5.9\times10^{10}$ times the CMOS energy floor. Transient 3D thermal simulations show that this inefficiency is also a thermal one, since sustained back-to-back planning heats a millimeter-scale silicon tile to 556 K even behind an ideal copper heat spreader. Guided by this chain from bound to bottleneck, we propose the World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA), a chip architecture for embedded world model planning that combines near-memory computation, real-time entropy estimation, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads. With a design target of 40x lower power, the same tile stays near ambient at 306 K in simulation, pointing toward practical planning on thermally constrained robots.

Hardware Architecture.title: Trilinear Compute-in-Memory Architecture for Energy-Efficient Transformer Acceleration
Hardware Architecture.summary: Self-attention in Transformers generates dynamic operands that force conventional Compute-in-Memory (CIM) accelerators into costly non-volatile memory (NVM) reprogramming cycles, degrading throughput and stressing device endurance. Existing solutions either reduce but retain NVM writes through matrix decomposition or sparsity, or move attention computation to digital CMOS at the expense of NVM density. We present TrilinearCIM, a Double-Gate FeFET (DG-FeFET)-based architecture that uses back-gate modulation to realize a three-operand multiply-accumulate primitive for in-memory attention computation without dynamic ferroelectric reprogramming. Evaluated on BERT-base (GLUE) and ViT-base (ImageNet and CIFAR), TrilinearCIM outperforms conventional CIM on seven of nine GLUE tasks while achieving up to 46.6\% energy reduction and 20.4\% latency improvement over conventional FeFET CIM at 37.3\% area overhead. To our knowledge, this is the first architecture to perform complete Transformer attention computation exclusively in NVM cores without runtime reprogramming.

Hardware Architecture.title: SPMW: A Grid-Based Programming Model for Scalable Accelerator Design
Hardware Architecture.summary: Modern accelerators specialize recurring computation and replicate it across regular hardware structures to achieve high performance. Sustaining this parallelism requires equally deliberate data delivery. Yet design tools often express these structures as sequential programs or flatten them into separate hardware modules and connections. This obscures shared patterns and leads to repeated compiler work. We introduce Single Program, Multiple Connected Work Units (SPMW), a grid-based programming model for scalable accelerator design that makes grid regularity a first-class abstraction. SPMW decouples local work-unit behavior from grid connectivity and data delivery. To our knowledge, SPMW is the first programming model to retain regularity throughout the compilation process, combining behavioral HLS with structural RTL generation for both fixed-function and domain-specific instruction-programmable accelerators. We implement SPMW with a Python frontend and an MLIR-based compiler that synthesizes each distinct kernel configuration once for reuse across independent hardware instances. Preserving regularity also enables parallel compilation and functional simulation to accelerate iterative design feedback. We use SPMW to generate a 32x32 systolic array that reduces GEMM latency and parallel kernel-to-RTL compilation time by 4.36x and 619x relative to AutoSA. Our FFT achieves up to 2.65x lower latency than HP-FFT. Our mini-TPU and our SPMW implementation of the FEATHER accelerator demonstrate complex composition and outperform their RTL baselines. Parallel functional simulation provides up to 18.4x speedup over Vitis HLS C simulation on the mini-TPU workloads. SPMW is also agent-friendly: given the same design specification, all five coding agents produce SPMW designs that satisfy the correctness and latency requirements, with 7.51x lower token usage than for SystemVerilog.

Programming Languages.title: Ensemble Methodology for Reference-Free Confidence Estimation in LLM-based Code Summarization
Programming Languages.summary: This paper describes an approach and use case to estimate the correctness of LLM-generated COBOL summaries without access to human-authored references. The core intuition is that inter-model agreement on semantics is informative about truth, and that an LLM-as-judge can provide higher-fidelity pairwise assessments than traditional string- or embedding-based metrics. We operationalise this intuition with (i) controlled summary generation from diverse models; (ii) a LLM evaluator that compares pairs of summaries and emits structured judgments; and (iii) a calibrated aggregation rule that combines supportive evidence while penalising only corroborated contradictions.

Programming Languages.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
Programming Languages.summary: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

Programming Languages.title: Fuss-free cumulative universes: theory and practice
Programming Languages.summary: Universes are central to dependent type theory, and they are notoriously difficult to handle in a way that is both correct and usable. We propose a new "fuss-free" generalised algebraic presentation for polymorphic cumulative universes that dispenses with the intricate theory of coherent universe coercions in favour of a simpler formulation, which we prove equivalent by means of a normalisation theorem for the former. We study the fuss-free formulation by means of (1) an abstract specification of its bidirectional elaboration algorithm, and (2) a concrete implementation in Haskell. We also describe and implement an extension of the fuss-free universe hierarchy with a judgemental notion of datatype description from which prior notions of cumulative inductive type may be derived.
Programming Languages.comment: Extended version of a paper to appear in POPL 2027

Programming Languages.title: Nothing Is Shared Until You Synchronise: Reinterpreting Java for Data-Race Freedom
Programming Languages.summary:
In mainstream shared-memory languages, programmers use synchronisation mechanisms such as locks to isolate shared data accesses across threads to avoid data races. Yet synchronisation enforces only a temporal ordering, while shared memory still communicates updates between threads at every ordinary read and write. To achieve isolation, programmers therefore need to understand the connection between ordering and communication, and to apply synchronisation correctly and consistently, while compilers and hardware optimise assuming they have. When programmers synchronise incorrectly, they lose isolation, and the semantics of their programs change without notice.
  We propose Sync-as-Share, a memory model built on isolation and communication rather than on the ordering of accesses to shared memory. We start from thread isolation, where each thread reads and writes a private view of memory, and reinterpret programs' existing synchronisation actions to also communicate updates explicitly. As nothing is communicated outside synchronisation actions, data races become impossible by construction. Instead, conflicting updates are detected at synchronisation points. Viewing synchronisation as explicit communication exposes the design decisions of what should be communicated, to whom, and what counts as a conflict. We propose two communication topologies with different trade-offs. We instantiate Sync-as-Share for Java by making the synchronisation actions already defined by its memory model the only points at which threads communicate, so Java programs can adopt Sync-as-Share unmodified. We formalise this instantiation as version-controlled memory, in which synchronisation actions push and pull updates between private views, and mechanise it in Rocq. We show that Java programs that are correctly synchronised under the Java memory model behave identically under shared memory and Sync-as-Share.

Programming Languages.title: The Program Logic of Abstract Interpretation
Programming Languages.summary: Hoare-style program logics and abstract interpretation are two of the principal frameworks for reasoning about programs, and their affinity has long been recognised informally: both derive over-approximate judgements about program behaviour by structural, syntax-directed reasoning. Turning this analogy into a formal correspondence runs into two challenges. First, the disjunction (or join) rule, sound and admissible in Hoare logic, becomes unsound over non-additive abstract semantics. Second, the extrapolation operators that make abstract interpretation effective on unbounded computations, i.e. widening and narrowing, have no analogue in the derivations of existing program logics. We introduce APPL (Abstract Program Property Logic), a Hoare-style program logic that provides a proof-theoretic foundation for abstract interpretation while addressing both challenges. The key technical idea is density: abstract semantics is additive over dense families of logical assertions. This leads to a density-guarded join rule that enables sound disjunctive reasoning over arbitrary abstract domains. We also internalise the application of widening and narrowing through inference rules for iterative commands. As a result, an entire analysis by abstract interpretation can be viewed as a logical derivation in APPL. The logic is sound over any abstract domain and, when the assertion language is expressive enough, it is also relatively complete. Finally, by interpreting nondeterminism through a monoidal operator, APPL provides a single logical framework that uniformly subsumes Hoare logic, incorrectness logic, and Hoare-style logics for hyperproperties, thereby enabling their abstraction. Remarkably, the density-guarded join rule introduced to handle non-additive abstract semantics is also fundamental in guaranteeing completeness for hyperproperties.

Programming Languages.title: A Physically-Realisable Quantum Programming Language with Quantum-Controlled Quantum Channels
Programming Languages.summary:
In contrast to a classical bit, which can only take the value $0$ or $1$, its quantum counterpart---a qubit---can exist in a superposition of $0$ and $1$. This is a superposition of data values, and it is then tempting to superpose programs as well. Indeed, a particular superposition of programs, known as the quantum SWITCH, has attracted considerable attention. A natural way to superpose programs is conditional branching on quantum data, and several studies have pursued this idea. However, there is a well-known semantic difficulty with this approach, and the fundamental question of whether the languages proposed in prior work can be physically realised remains open.
  This paper proposes a physically realisable quantum programming language with quantum branching over quantum channels. We first analyse the semantic difficulty from an implementation perspective and show that the difficulty is caused by arbitrariness in the implementation. We then design a language that is free from this arbitrariness. As expected from its implementation-oriented design, our language is physically realisable. We argue for this from two directions: first, we give a method for compiling programs into quantum circuits; and second, we show that our programs stay within the physically admissible range, namely, that they neither yield probabilities greater than one nor violate causal inequalities. The absence of such violations is established through the inclusion of our language in QC-QC, a notion of realisability studied in physics.

Programming Languages.title: SPMW: A Grid-Based Programming Model for Scalable Accelerator Design
Programming Languages.summary: Modern accelerators specialize recurring computation and replicate it across regular hardware structures to achieve high performance. Sustaining this parallelism requires equally deliberate data delivery. Yet design tools often express these structures as sequential programs or flatten them into separate hardware modules and connections. This obscures shared patterns and leads to repeated compiler work. We introduce Single Program, Multiple Connected Work Units (SPMW), a grid-based programming model for scalable accelerator design that makes grid regularity a first-class abstraction. SPMW decouples local work-unit behavior from grid connectivity and data delivery. To our knowledge, SPMW is the first programming model to retain regularity throughout the compilation process, combining behavioral HLS with structural RTL generation for both fixed-function and domain-specific instruction-programmable accelerators. We implement SPMW with a Python frontend and an MLIR-based compiler that synthesizes each distinct kernel configuration once for reuse across independent hardware instances. Preserving regularity also enables parallel compilation and functional simulation to accelerate iterative design feedback. We use SPMW to generate a 32x32 systolic array that reduces GEMM latency and parallel kernel-to-RTL compilation time by 4.36x and 619x relative to AutoSA. Our FFT achieves up to 2.65x lower latency than HP-FFT. Our mini-TPU and our SPMW implementation of the FEATHER accelerator demonstrate complex composition and outperform their RTL baselines. Parallel functional simulation provides up to 18.4x speedup over Vitis HLS C simulation on the mini-TPU workloads. SPMW is also agent-friendly: given the same design specification, all five coding agents produce SPMW designs that satisfy the correctness and latency requirements, with 7.51x lower token usage than for SystemVerilog.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be computationally hard in this setting, so prior work has explored natural assumptions that make planning easier. Recent work [Golowich et al., 2022] gave quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for observable POMDPs. These are POMDPs whose observation channels satisfy an $\ell_1$-observability condition, but notably, no assumptions are required on the transition dynamics. In a similar vein, for every fixed $ρ>0$, we give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for $ρ$-decodable POMDPs. We show that decodability is implied by both $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. Moreover, we show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal $\ell_1$-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. We also show that the fast filter-forgetting guarantee underlying the approach of [Golowich et al., 2022] does not extend directly from $\ell_1$-observability to constant $\ell_2$-observability. Thus, decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: New Algorithms for Incremental Minimum Spanning Trees and Temporal Graph Applications
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Processing graphs with temporal information (the temporal graphs) has become increasingly important in the real world. In this paper, we study efficient solutions to temporal graph applications using new algorithms for Incremental Minimum Spanning Trees (MST). The first contribution of this work is to formally discuss how a broad set of setting-problem combinations of temporal graph processing can be solved using incremental MST, along with their theoretical guarantees. Despite the importance of the problem, we observe a gap between theory and practice for efficient incremental MST algorithms. While many classic data structures, such as the link-cut tree, provide strong bounds for incremental MST, their performance is limited in practice. Meanwhile, existing practical solutions used in applications do not have any non-trivial theoretical guarantees. Our second and main contribution includes new algorithms for incremental MST that are efficient both in theory and in practice. Our new data structure, the AM-tree, achieves the same theoretical bound as the link-cut tree for temporal graph processing and shows strong performance in practice. In our experiments, the AM-tree has competitive or better performance than existing practical solutions due to theoretical guarantees, and can be significantly faster than the link-cut tree (7.8-11x in updates and 7.7-13.7x in queries).

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The k-Clique hypothesis is dead, for good
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We present an algorithm that solves the $k$-Clique problem for any large enough $k$ and any $n$-vertex graph in $n^{\left(\fracω{3}-c\right)k}$ time, where $ω\geq 2$ is the matrix multiplication exponent and $c>0$ is a positive constant independent of both $ω$ and $k$. This refutes the long-standing $k$-Clique conjecture, regardless of the value of the matrix multiplication constant, even if $ω=2$. In fact, our algorithm solves the more general problem of counting weighted $k$-Cliques.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Privacy Filters are Captured by Residues: A Characterization of Free Natural Filters and the Cost of Adaptivity
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study privacy filters, which enable privacy accounting for differentially private (DP) mechanisms with adaptively chosen privacy characteristics. We show that the worst-case privacy loss of interacting with any privacy filter is characterized by a Bellman equation. We apply this theory to develop residue filters, which unify existing privacy filters. We develop the Gaussian DP (GDP) residue filter, which strictly improves upon the naïve GDP filter. We show that, in the average case, this new filter asymptotically permits as many pure DP queries as in the non-adaptive case and a factor $π/2$ more pure DP queries than the naïve GDP filter. We also show that residue filters capture the natural filter, which promises greater utility by leveraging exact privacy accounting techniques. Earlier privacy filters consider only simple privacy parameters such as Rényi-DP or GDP parameters. Natural filters account for the entire privacy profile of every query, promising more efficient use of a given privacy budget. We show that, contrary to other forms of DP, natural privacy filters are not free in general. We present a characterization of when a family of private queries admits free natural filters for a given budget. In particular, only families of privacy mechanisms that are totally-ordered when composed admit free natural privacy filters with respect to an arbitrary privacy budget. Finally, we show that, while the natural approximate-DP filter can fail in the presence of an adaptive adversary, it cannot fail too badly: the output remains approximate-DP with parameters at most poly-logarithmically worse than the intended privacy parameters.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Simulating Gaussian boson sampling on graphs in polynomial time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We show that a distribution related to Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) on graphs can be sampled classically in polynomial time. Graphical applications of GBS typically sample from this distribution, and thus quantum algorithms do not provide exponential speedup for these applications. We also show that another distribution related to Boson sampling can be sampled classically in polynomial time.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Contention Resolution Against an Adversarial Scheduler
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the classical contention-resolution problem, a set of players share a broadcast channel, and a player succeeds in a given time step if it is the only player to broadcast during that step. Implicit in the classical problem is the assumption that every player is free to act on every step: once a player arrives, it participates until it succeeds.
  We study what happens when that assumption is removed. In our model, an adversarial \emph{scheduler} decides, on each step, which subset of the players gets scheduled to participate in the step. An unscheduled player simply sleeps through the step. We measure a protocol by its \emph{efficiency}: the number of players divided by the expected number of steps in which at least one player was active.
  Our first result says that, so long as the players are given access to a global clock and to shared randomness, they can achieve efficiency $Ω(1/\log n)$. The players are able to achieve this bound without requiring any channel feedback, and even if the adversarial scheduler is adaptive. We also give a matching lower bound of $O(1 / \log n)$, which holds even with channel feedback, and even for an oblivious scheduler.
  Our upper bounds all require the players to have access to a shared global clock and to shared randomness. Our final result says that this type of implicit shared state is necessary. If the players have neither a global clock nor shared randomness, then no protocol can achieve efficiency better than $O(\log n / n)$; and this holds even if the other aspects of the problem are designed to be as favorable for the players as possible (the channel gives ternary feedback and the adversary is oblivious).

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Faster Regular Expression Matching via Two-Dimensional Tabulation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A regular expression specifies a set of strings formed by single characters combined with concatenation, union, and Kleene star operators. Given a regular expression $R$ and a string $Q$, the classic regular expression matching problem is to decide whether $Q$ matches any string specified by $R$. Let $m$ and $n$ be the lengths of $R$ and $Q$, respectively.
  Our main result is a new algorithm that, given a parameter $t \geq m$, solves the problem in \[
  O\left(\frac{nm\,\lg\lg(t/m)}{\lg^2(t/m)}+t+n\right) \] time and $O(t)$ words of space. In particular, for any fixed $0<\eps<1$, when $m\leq n^{1-\eps}$, we solve the problem in $O(nm \lg \lg n/\lg^2 n + m + n)$ time and $O(n)$ space. Compared to the previous best result [Bille and Thorup, ICALP 2009], this improves the leading term by a factor $\sqrt{\lg n}/\lg\lg n$.
  The key new technique is a two-dimensional tabulation specialized to the regular expression.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: From Function Inversion to Preimage Reporting
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Given an arbitrary function $f:[N]\to[M]$, the function inversion problem asks to preprocess $f$ and to be able to, when given some $y\in [M]$, decide whether there exists some $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$ and if so, to report such an $x$. Recently, Fiat-Naor's solution to this problem has seen significant traction in theoretical computer science, and allowed for several conjectures related to meta-complexity and the 3SUM problem to be broken.
  In this paper, we consider the natural extension of the function inversion problem that we call preimage reporting. Here, instead of having to report only one $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$, the whole set $f^{-1}(y)$ must be found.
  We present a new general method to convert any arbitrary function inversion scheme into an efficient corresponding preimage reporting scheme. In particular, if $Δ$ is the maximal indegree of $f$, we show that we can perform preimage reporting using space $S$ in time $T$ for any $T$ and $S$ satisfying $TS^2=N^2 Δ$, matching a variant of a tradeoff obtained by Fiat and Naor for function inversion. This last result implies an improvement over the corresponding function inversion scheme itself, which constitutes the first function inversion scheme whose query time is inversely proportional to $|f^{-1}(y)|$. We derive new simple solutions for the $k$SUM-indexing with reporting and Jumbled indexing with reporting problems.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Parallel Algorithms for Higher-Order Temporal H-Index Computation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Ranking vertices by importance is a fundamental task in network mining. The H-index provides such a ranking by asking how many neighbors are themselves well connected; its higher-order temporal variant recursively applies this idea over time-respecting neighborhoods in temporal networks. Scaling its computation is difficult because the existing streaming algorithm intertwines temporal processing with H-index order, incurring maximum-degree-dependent costs and exposing little parallelism. We show that the temporal dependencies can instead be resolved once: each edge's time-dependent lookup is mapped to a fixed successor position, turning every H-index order into a parallel gather followed by a segmented suffix-H computation. Based on this reformulation, we derive a linear-work suffix-H algorithm, a parallel multicore CPU implementation, degree-adaptive GPU kernels, and a multi-GPU scheme that exchanges only distinct remotely queried states. Experiments on synthetic and real-world temporal graphs show that the reformulation alone is substantially faster than the streaming algorithm, and that GPUs add order-round speedups exceeding an order of magnitude over our multicore implementation on synthetic inputs with up to one billion temporal edges. On a 636M-edge Reddit network, eight GPUs compute 128 orders in 3.6 s of round time, whereas the streaming algorithm does not finish within an hour even at order 8.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: What remains of the planar induced minor conjectures?
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Dallard, Milanič, and Štorgel, and independently Gartland and Lokshtanov, conjectured that for every planar graph $H$, Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring are polynomial-time solvable in $H$-induced-minor-free graphs. As a structural explanation, Gartland and Lokshtanov further conjectured that such graphs admit balanced separators dominated by a constant number of vertices. Bonnet and Chang recently refuted the independent-set part of the algorithmic conjecture, by showing that Maximum Independent Set is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in graphs excluding the $5\times5$ grid as an induced minor.
  We revisit both conjectures. We show that the graphs used by Bonnet and Chang exclude much simpler planar graphs, including several $16$-vertex trees, and we introduce a second, independent family of hard instances. We also prove that $3$-Coloring is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in both settings, thus refuting the algorithmic conjecture in full, even in its quasipolynomial version, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{QP}$. On the structural side, we identify planar graphs $H$ for which the structural conjecture holds, while the algorithmic one fails. Thus, constantly dominated balanced separators cannot by themselves explain the tractability of Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Online Timely Bin Packing Revisited: A Simpler Algorithm with Optimality in Special Cases
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Online Timely Bin Packing is a variant of classical online bin packing in which items arrive over time with sizes and deadlines. Packing an item may be deferred until its deadline, but once a collection of items is packed into a bin, the bin is closed and cannot be used again. The objective is to minimize the total number of bins used. The problem was introduced by Khattar in 2023. In 2025, Aminian proposed Discrete-Greedy, a deterministic online algorithm with a competitive ratio of exactly $2$, which remains the best-known upper bound. Its analysis is particularly simple; however, the algorithm requires maintaining a fractional simulation internally and may leave usable space in some bins unfilled.
  We propose Thrifty-Greedy, a simple deterministic online algorithm that does not require a fractional simulation. We prove that its competitive ratio is exactly $2$, matching the best-known upper bound. At the same time, the algorithm automatically achieves the optimal competitive ratio on two natural classes of inputs: it is $1$-competitive when all items have the same size, and $1.5$-competitive when every item has size in $\{1/3,2/3\}$. In contrast, Discrete-Greedy has a competitive ratio of at least $2$ on both classes.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Fast and Accurate Algorithm for the $p \to q$ Norm of Sparse Non-Negative Matrices
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We present an algorithm that computes the $p \to q$ norm of a non-negative matrix with $s$ nonzero entries to accuracy $\varepsilon$ in time $\widetilde{O}(s^{3/2} \log (1/\varepsilon))$, for any $p \ge q \ge 1$. The fastest algorithm previously designed for this problem has running time $\widetilde{O}(s / \varepsilon)$ (Objois and Vladu, 2026), which is slower when high accuracy solutions are desired.
  Our algorithm employs a surprising application of Laplacian solvers inside an Interior Point Method (IPM). We formulate the problem as a linear optimization problem over a product of power cones, and show that the Newton updates of the IPM can be computed by solving a Laplacian system in a Schur complement after subtracting a rank-2 matrix.
  We also discuss an implementation of our algorithm, showing that it is practical and it outperforms optimized solvers such as MOSEK by factors of up to $20\times$ on a variety of tasks.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Coresets for Capacitated Clustering via Dual Concentration
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study coresets for clustering problems, focusing on the classical $k$-median and $k$-means objectives. A coreset is a small weighted summary of the input data that approximately preserves the clustering cost for every choice of centers. Such summaries are a central tool for scaling clustering algorithms to large datasets.
  In this work, we consider the capacitated setting, where the clustering is subject not only to choosing centers but also to respecting prescribed cluster-size constraints. This model is a natural generalization of standard clustering and has been widely studied, but its coreset complexity is less well understood. For finite metric spaces, we obtain optimal-size coresets; surprisingly, these match the best-known bounds for unconstrained clustering. We also give improved coreset bounds in Euclidean space, notably the first coresets with near-linear dependence in $k$ while being independent of the dimension and input size.
  The main new technical ingredients are concentration bounds for the dual solutions of min-cost flow problems, which allow for both significantly simpler and tighter analyses of the underlying sampling distribution used in the coreset construction.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dual-Number Associative Arrays for One-Pass Provenance and Sensitivity
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Associative arrays and GraphBLAS express sparse computations as matrix operations over a chosen semiring, but the result normally contains only the ordinary value. We define a dual-number extension $D_k(S)=S\ltimes S^k$ that carries this value together with $k$ independent auxiliary channels in the same computation. We prove that the construction is a split square-zero extension of any commutative semiring. Over min-plus, the auxiliary value is the weight of the shortest walk constrained to use the corresponding edge, excluding the weight of that edge. This gives an exact shortest-path membership test for that edge, although ties return the union of the edges on all optimal paths. We implement the min-plus construction using sparse \texttt{python-graphblas} operations, with a fixpoint test that checks the value and auxiliary components together. We validate the implementation across 18,692 checks, including 2,825 tied target pairs. On random graphs with 100,000 vertices and 32 seed edges, the dual method is $3.39\times$ faster than the sequential algorithm but $1.50\times$ slower than a min-plus-specific batched method. This difference is largely explained by the dual method requiring $1.55\times$ as many sweeps. Thus, the main contribution is a general algebraic approach with competitive sparse performance, rather than information that specialized min-plus algorithms cannot already compute.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Additive $Ω(\log^* OPT)$ Gap for Bin Packing with Three Items per Bin
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We prove that bin packing is NP-hard to approximate within an additive factor of $o(\ls\OPT)$, even when all item sizes are arbitrarily close to $1/3$. This gives the first lower bound for bin packing with an additive factor that depends explicitly on the optimum value. In addition, we give a polynomial-time reduction from any bin packing instance into one with item sizes arbitrarily close to $1/3$, preserving its additive configuration-LP gap up to constant factors. Thus, in the sense of additive configuration LP gap and up to a constant, we confirm the conjecture that 3-partition instances are the hardest bin packing instances. In particular, we obtain an unconditional $Ω(\ls\OPT)$ gap for 3-partition instances. We build on the recent OpenAI construction that uses five items per bin and rules out any constant additive gap.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Bounds for $β$-TSP
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) asks for a minimum-length Hamiltonian cycle in a complete weighted graph. Its approximability depends on the edge lengths: unrestricted instances admit no constant-factor approximation unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, metric instances admit Christofides' $3/2$-approximation, and fixed-dimensional Euclidean instances admit a PTAS. We study $β$-TSP, where the edge lengths satisfy $ \ell_{uw}\leqβ(\ell_{uv}+\ell_{vw}) \qquad \forall\,u,v,w\in V\ \text{pairwise distinct}, \quad β\in\left[\tfrac{1}{2},1\right]. $ The condition arises naturally in various settings, for example, when metric travel times are combined with positive service times at the vertices. The previous best approximation algorithm, due to Böckenhauer et al., ranges from $1$ at $β=1/2$ to $3/2$ as $β$ approaches $1$. We obtain a strictly better guarantee for every $1/2<β<1$ by combining two simple constructions whose guarantees counterbalance each other. We also improve the best known approximation hardness bound for every $1/2<β<1$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Precedence Constraint Scheduling on a Fixed Number of Machines
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a deterministic exact algorithm for $P_m\mid\mathrm{prec},p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$ for every fixed $m\ge3$. The algorithm constructs an optimum schedule in $$
  O(L)+m^{O(m^2)}\, n^{6m^2+13m+1} \, {\log n} $$ elementary RAM operations, where $n \ge 2$ is the number of jobs and $L$ is the binary input length. Its word size is $O(m^2 \log n)$ bits. An implementation with a fixed number of tapes uses $O(L)+m^{O(m^2)} \, n^{12m^2+26m+2} \, \log^3 n$ steps. For three machines the respective polynomial degrees are $94$ and $188$, apart from the displayed logarithmic factors.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Effective Horizons for Prophet Inequalities with Discounted I.I.D. Rewards
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study prophet inequalities for $n$ i.i.d. base rewards subject to multiplicative discounts across $S$ phases. For equal-length phases and a common discount factor $\widetildeγ$, we characterize the optimal competitive ratio of single-quantile policies as $n\to\infty$ with $S$ and $\widetildeγ$ fixed. The resulting sharp guarantee describes the dependence on the phase parameters: it recovers $1-1/e$ without discounting and approaches $1/2$ in the worst-case regime. We also establish a distribution-free comparison that bounds the discounted prophet by a fractional i.i.d. maximum with effective horizon $B$, the sum of the discount weights across all observations. The comparison yields acceptance probability $1/B$, determined only by the phase profile. This calibration attains the canonical optimum even among single-quantile policies that may choose their acceptance probability using the known base distribution. The comparison also gives guarantees for heterogeneous discounts and unequal phase lengths. A complementary optimal-stopping upper bound establishes the same limiting optimum of $1/2$ for arbitrary stopping rules in the canonical model. Finally, the same effective-horizon calibration sets acceptance probability $1-\widetildeγ$ under infinite-horizon geometric discounting. This explicit quantile rule attains Boshuizen's (1994) known optimal worst-case ratio $1/(1+\widetildeγ)$ without solving a Bellman equation.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Prophet Secretary for Matroids and XOS Valuations: A Separation at 1-1/e and a 0.6767 Guarantee for I.I.D. Weights
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Ehsani, Hajiaghayi, Kesselheim, and Singla (SODA 2018) give $(1-1/e)$-competitive algorithms for matroid prophet-secretary and prophet-secretary with XOS valuation functions. In this work we show that these two guarantees have different limits. For every matroid, we give a randomized $(1-1/e+\varepsilon_0)$-competitive algorithm, where $\varepsilon_0=10^{-6}$. The guarantee holds for independent nonnegative values with finite expected optimum. For explicitly given finite distributions with rational values and probabilities, the algorithm has polynomial worst-case running time in the matroid independence-oracle model. The oracle tests whether a queried set is independent. The algorithm makes $O(N^4)$ such queries in expectation and $O(N^4\log(N+2))$ in the worst case, where $N$ is the number of elements.
  We further consider the i.i.d. version of this problem and provide a $0.6767$ competitive ratio for every matroid with i.i.d.\ nonnegative weights from a known distribution. This guarantee even holds in fixed arrival order (a.k.a. i.i.d. matriod prophet inequalities), even when the algorithm learns the order only as the elements arrive.
  For combinatorial auctions with XOS valuations, however, we show that $1-1/e$ is the optimal competitive ratio. We give an explicit family of finite instances showing that no online algorithm can guarantee a larger competitive ratio than $1-1/e$, even when the buyers' valuations are i.i.d., every additive clause has coefficients in $\{0,1\}$, and computation is unrestricted. Thus the matroid improvement exploits structure absent from general allocation with XOS valuations.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Pairwise Reconnection for Cost-Distance Steiner Trees
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Uniform Cost-Distance Steiner Tree Problem asks for a rooted tree that minimizes the connection cost plus a weighted sum of root-to-terminal distances. We develop an algorithm that constructs two candidate trees: one based on direct connections to the root and another that pairs selected vertices and connects each pair to the root. The algorithm selects the tree with the smaller objective value. The resulting randomized algorithm achieves expected approximation factors of $1.698$ in the spanning case and $2.041$ in the general case, and it can be derandomized in polynomial time. The pairwise matching analysis charges part of the augmentation cost directly to the connection and delay costs of an optimal solution, rather than only to the separated lower bound used in previous analyses. This allows the $1.698$ factor to fall below the maximum multiplicative gap of $1+1/\sqrt{2}$ between the optimum value and that lower bound.
  We give instance families with approximation-ratio lower bounds approaching $1+1/\sqrt{2}$ for cut-and-reconnect algorithms that start from a minimum spanning tree and $3/2$ for the present algorithm. Finally, we show that the Uniform Cost-Distance Steiner Tree Problem and the Steiner-tree version of the Cable-Trench Problem are approximation equivalent up to an arbitrarily small additive loss.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Variable-Occurrence Bounds and Exponential Separations for Moser--Tardos and WalkSAT on 3-CNF
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We establish a sharp variable-occurrence threshold for polynomial expected-time convergence for the Moser--Tardos algorithm and the pure random-walk WalkSAT on 3-CNF formulas. For every formula with $m$ clauses and at most two occurrences per variable, both algorithms terminate in $O(m)$ expected updates. This occurrence bound is sharp: we construct an infinite family with at most three occurrences per variable on which both algorithms require $2^{Θ(\sqrt{m})}$ expected updates. Surprisingly, this dynamical transition occurs strictly below the classical NP-completeness threshold at variable-occurrence degree four.
  We further establish exponential separations between the two algorithms on satisfiable 3-CNF formulas. On one family, WalkSAT terminates in $O(m^4)$ expected flips, whereas MT requires $2^{Ω(m)}$ expected resampling steps. On another, MT terminates in $O(m)$ expected resampling steps, whereas WalkSAT requires $2^{Ω(m)}$ expected flips. These constructions exploit the different ways in which single-variable flips and simultaneous resampling propagate local violations. Our results show that the algorithms' expected running times are incomparable even up to polynomial overhead on the same inputs.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Load Balancing with Item Fragmentation and More Bins than Items: Linear-Time and Exact
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study a fundamental load-balancing problem in which $N$ items of strictly positive integer sizes with total size $W$ must be assigned to $B$ bins, with items allowed to be divided into integer-size fragments across bins. Each bin must receive a load of either $\lfloor W/B \rfloor$ or $\lceil W/B \rceil$, ensuring that the loads of any two bins differ by at most one unit. Under this constraint, the objective is to minimize the maximum number of distinct item fragments placed into any single bin. This problem is NP-hard and there exists an $(\mathrm{OPT}+1)$-approximation algorithm that runs in $O(N \log N + B)$ time [Kobert et al., 2014]. The existing algorithm is employed by several widely used production codes for phylogenetic reconstruction.
  Here, we focus on the case $B \ge N$, that is, bins are at least as numerous as items. This setting arises pervasively in modern parallel and distributed systems, as well as in iterative algorithms that rebalance their workload at every step. In this context, bins are machines or machine cores, and items represent computational tasks (jobs). Our central contribution is a remarkably simple $O(N)$-time algorithm that computes an optimal assignment in this setting; this assignment is encoded using $O(N)$ space. In particular, we prove that an optimum always exists in which every bin receives at most two fragments and provide a characterization of when one fragment per bin suffices. Our result strictly improves the $(\mathrm{OPT}+1)$-approximation of Kobert et al. in the many-bins setting and, together with it, yields a strongly polynomial-time $(\mathrm{OPT}+1)$-approximation algorithm for the general setting, as it removes the dependency on the number $B$ of bins.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximate Total Weighted Completion Time with Convex Controllable Processing Times
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the single-machine scheduling problem with controllable processing times to minimize the total weighted completion time, focusing on the setting where a job's processing time is a convex function of its allocated continuous resource. The computational complexity of this problem represents a long-standing open question, as it is currently neither known to be polynomial-time solvable nor NP-hard. While we do not fully resolve this complexity question, we provide several insights into the problem's approximability. On the positive side, we present a polynomial-time $e \le 2.719$-approximation algorithm, alongside a quasi-polynomial approximation scheme for instances where the largest parameter value is polynomially bounded by the instance size. On the negative side, we demonstrate that simple sorting rules, which are optimal for certain special cases in the literature, cannot guarantee a constant-factor approximation for the general case.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: The results of this manuscript are superseeded by the paper "Dual Techniques for Scheduling on a Machine with Varying Speed" by Megow and Verschae, SIDMA 2018

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: PaB-tree: Parallel B+-tree with Batch Updates
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The B+-tree is a ubiquitous search index due to its provable I/O (cache) efficiency. Yet unlike batch-parallel binary search trees, which are both fast and widely available, no batch-parallel B+-tree offers strong empirical performance together with provable, near-optimal I/O efficiency. Prior B+-tree-based designs are either parallel but purely theoretical, with no high-performance implementation, or concurrent indexes such as the Bw-tree and Masstree, which run an order of magnitude slower on batch updates.
  We present PaB-tree, the first batch-parallel B+-tree with guarantees on work, span, and cache complexity alongside strong practical performance. Its core challenge -- repairing node overflows and underflows without eroding the tree's I/O advantage -- is resolved by one simple invariant: a repair never touches a sibling and is always pushed to the parent. A Promote primitive reduces batch construction and insertion to repeated node promotion, and batch deletion to reinsertion. Batch updates take O(B log_B n) work and O(log_B n) I/O per element, matching the sequential B+-tree bounds, with polylogarithmic span. Against highly-optimized parallel and concurrent baselines, PaB-tree delivers the best overall performance trade-off: up to 1.4x faster on construction and up to 3.6x faster on batch insertion than the strongest baseline, while preserving B+-tree query efficiency.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Bounds for Paging with Delay and Joint Replenishment with Varying Opening Costs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study weighted paging with delay, a generalization of classical paging in which requests may be served after their arrival, incurring delay costs while awaiting service. This model allows the algorithm to delay service and batch service requests over time, but also introduces significant challenges due to overlapping requests. While the problem is well understood in the unweighted setting, where optimal $O(\log k)$-competitive algorithms are known, the weighted case remains more elusive. The best previously known randomized algorithm, due to Gupta, Kumar, and Panigrahi, achieves an $O(\log k \log n)$-competitive ratio, leaving a gap between weighted and unweighted settings. We obtain a randomized $O(\log k)$-competitive algorithm, matching the lower bound inherited from classical paging.
  The core of our approach is a structural decomposition that separates the evolution of the cache over time from scheduling additional page loads, so as to make the solution feasible. We develop this approach first for paging with time windows, the special case in which each request must be served within a specified time interval. Given a sequence of cache configurations, we reduce the problem of augmenting this sequence to a feasible solution to a variant of the Joint Replenishment Problem with deadlines (JRP-D) with time-dependent opening costs. We design a constant-competitive online algorithm for this variant under a prediction model whose required information is available online in our paging reduction. Combining this algorithm with an existing online construction of cache configurations yields an $O(\log k)$-competitive algorithm for paging with time windows. We then extend the framework to obtain the same guarantee for weighted paging with a general delay function.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Vertex Deletion on $H$-Induced-Minor-Free Graphs: Subexponential FPT Algorithms and Approximation Schemes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study vertex-deletion problems on string graphs and, more generally, on graphs excluding a fixed graph as an induced minor. For every fixed graph $H$, fixed nonnegative integer $t$, and fixed monadic second-order formula $φ$, we consider the problem of finding a minimum-cardinality set $S$ such that $G-S$ has treewidth at most $t$ and satisfies $φ$. This captures classic problems such as Vertex Cover, Feedback Vertex Set, and deletion to graphs of any fixed bounded treewidth. We give an algorithm with running time $2^{k^{2/3} \log^{O(1)} k}n^{O(1)}$ on $H$-induced-minor-free graphs, where $k$ is the optimum deletion-set size. This resolves in the affirmative the open problem highlighted by Bonnet and Rzążewski [Algorithmica 2019] and Berthe, Bougeret, Gonçalves, and Raymond [ICALP 2025] regarding the existence of a subexponential parameterized algorithm for Feedback Vertex Set on string graphs. Our algorithm significantly improves over existing parameterized algorithms for more restricted classes of problems on more restricted classes of graphs. When the property defined by $φ$ is hereditary, we also obtain a quasi-polynomial time approximation scheme, namely an algorithm that produces a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate solution in quasi-polynomial time. Both the sub-exponential algorithm and the quasi-polynomial time approximation scheme build on the same new structural and algorithmic insights.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: On the Communication Complexity of Shortcut Set Computation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A recent breakthrough of Kogan and Parter (SODA '22) provided the first polynomial improvement in decades on the size/diameter tradeoff available for shortcut sets. However, algorithmic applications of shortcut sets have mostly not taken advantage of these new bounds. A barrier is that many shortcut set applications occur in \emph{decentralized} settings, and we generally lack decentralized algorithms implementing the Kogan-Parter bounds.
  To this end, we study the \emph{communication complexity} of constructing Kogan-Parter shortcut sets. The edges of an $n$-node directed graph are split between two players, Alice and Bob, who are also given a target diameter $D$. Our main result is a protocol that, for $D \le n^{1/3}$, allows Alice and Bob to agree on a shortcut set matching the Kogan-Parter tradeoff between size and diameter, while exchanging only $\Oish(n^2 / D^2)$ bits of communication. We also provide (non-matching) lower bounds on the communication complexity required to find a correct $D$-diameter shortcut set of any size.
  The main technical ingredient for the upper bounds is a low-communication protocol for finding a \emph{path cover}, a common subroutine in shortcut set constructions that has attracted some independent interest. Our protocol crucially avoids applications of Menger's theorem or antichain decompositions, as often done in prior work. On the lower bounds side, we relate the communication complexity of the shortcut set problem to the size of bridge-free path systems.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Global Sinkhorn Convergence and Spectral Stability of Matrix Scaling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a global spectral bound for the Sinkhorn--Knopp (SK) algorithm. Let $A$ be a row-stochastic nonnegative $n\times n$ matrix admitting a finite doubly stochastic scaling $B$. Define \[
  g=1-s_2(B)^2>0,
  \qquad
  D=\min\left\{\|(u,v)\|_\infty:
  B=\operatorname{diag}(e^u)A\operatorname{diag}(e^{-v})\right\}. \] From the standard initialization, SK achieves total marginal $\ell_1$ error $\varepsilon$ in \[
  O\!\left(\frac{D+\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)}{g}\right) \] iterations. A scale-invariant potential contracts globally according to the spectrum of $B$. The linear dependence on $D$ is necessary in the fixed-gap regime: we construct strictly positive inputs with constant input and endpoint spectral gaps, $D=Θ(n)$, and an $Ω(n)$ iteration lower bound at error $n^{-2}$. Our upper bound gives $O(n)$ iterations on this family.
  We next give spectral certificates for scalability and short scaling distance. For a row-stochastic input $A$ with positive column sums $c_j$, set \[
  K=\frac{\max_jc_j}{\min_jc_j},\qquad
  σ=s_2\!\left(A\operatorname{diag}(c)^{-1/2}\right). \] The input-only condition $\sqrt K\,σ<1$ certifies exact scalability and polynomial scaling distortion, with $D=O(\log n)$ for fixed $K$ and a fixed positive spectral margin. Given a finite scaling $B$, the weaker condition $\sqrt K\,σs_2(B)<1$ gives the same structural bounds. With a constant endpoint gap, these bounds imply logarithmic SK iteration complexity. Boundary constructions show that the strict spectral inequalities cannot uniformly be replaced by nonstrict ones.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Greedy Superstring Conjecture Is False
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In the Shortest Common Superstring problem (SCS), one is given a finite set of strings and is asked to find a shortest string containing every input string as a substring. Since the problem is NP-hard, various approximation algorithms have been proposed for it. The currently best known approximation ratio is $2.466$ due to Englert, Matsakis, and Veselý; a better approximation ratio $2$ has been announced by OpenAI just recently. In 1988, Tarhio and Ukkonen introduced a simple greedy algorithm that iteratively takes two strings with the longest overlap and merges them together. They showed that the greedy algorithm may produce a superstring that is about two times longer than the optimal one and conjectured that this bound is tight. This has become known as the Greedy Superstring Conjecture and has remained open for almost four decades. The best known upper bound on the approximation ratio of the greedy algorithm is $3.396$ due to Englert, Matsakis, and Veselý. In this paper, we present a series of results tightening the bounds of the greedy algorithm, with the main contributions being as follows: 1. We refute the Greedy Conjecture by constructing a family of instances for which a lower bound on the approximation ratio tends to $2.4$. 2. We prove that the greedy algorithm is $3$-approximate. 3. For input strings of fixed length $k$, we prove that the approximation guarantee is exactly $9/5$ for $k=3$ and at least $2$ for all $k \ge 6$.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Preliminary versions of the results of this paper are contained in arXiv:2608.20018v2, arXiv:2609.27921v2, and arXiv:2609.01365v1

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: As Easy as Rank One: Optimal Algorithms for Matroid Secretary and Single-Sample Matroid Prophet
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We resolve the matroid secretary conjecture in its strong form and the single-sample matroid prophet inequality problem, achieving competitive ratios $e$ and $2$, respectively. Both ratios are optimal, even for rank-one matroids.
  For matroid secretary, our ordinal algorithm accepts the elements of the canonical optimum independently, each with probability $1/e$. It needs only the number of elements in advance and uses an expected polynomial number of independence queries on arrived elements. For single-sample matroid prophet inequalities, our algorithm uses one sample per independent value distribution and $O(n^2)$ independence queries on a known $n$-element matroid. It works for every arrival order fixed independently of the samples, values, and algorithmic randomness. The selected elements and their values have exactly the joint distribution obtained by independently retaining each element--value pair in the canonical optimum of a fresh product draw with probability $1/2$.
  Our main algorithms maintain a reference state whose greedy solution contains every accepted element. Its updates, made even after rejections, preserve exact distributional invariants. A short reversible-update argument gives a $4$-probability-competitive secretary algorithm, already resolving the original conjecture; a related invariant gives the optimal single-sample prophet inequality. For secretary, we characterize the distributions achievable by ordinal algorithms through a finite polytope. A continuous-time formulation then lets us design an accepted-set distribution achieving the optimal ratio $e$ and realize it efficiently. We also obtain guarantees for matroid intersections.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: This paper merges and extends arXiv:2609.14555, arXiv:2609.19118, and arXiv:2609.30421

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Sparse Predict and Demote: Optimal Scheduling with Minimal Size Advice
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Knowledge of job sizes is crucial for optimizing the mean response time in single-server scheduling. However, predictions of job sizes are typically inexact and may be costly to obtain. Thus, a long-standing research question is: what is the minimal information about job sizes required to obtain near-optimal mean response time? We introduce a novel policy, \emph{Sparse Predict and Demote (SPD)}, and prove that it achieves order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic while requiring only one-bit job-size predictions for a vanishing fraction of arrivals. SPD achieves heavy-traffic order-optimality even in situations when predictions are (i) inexact up to any fixed multiplicative error bound, and (ii) costly, i.e., the server is used to compute predictions and is thus unavailable to serve jobs while processing prediction queries. Finally, we use numerical experiments to illustrate that SPD maintains near-optimal performance beyond the heavy-traffic regime.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Regev's Reduction Reaches Reconstruction
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Regev's reduction uses a quantum Fourier transform to carry out reductions between various problems related to lattices and codes. We apply it to the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions of certain classical spin glass Hamiltonians, which can equivalently be thought of as cost functions for average-case instances of an optimization problem called $D$-regular max-$k$-LINSAT. This problem becomes hard at low temperature. Here, we use a quantum decoding algorithm called Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM) to solve the decoding problem arising from Regev's reduction. Our main contribution is a proof that the minimum temperature reachable using Regev+BPQM is exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold temperature for noisy channels transmitting signals on a tree network. This equality can be understood via Renes' duality between classical and quantum channels, which we use to show that quantum decoding is possible exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem is impossible. M{é}zard and Montanari identified this reconstruction temperature with a dynamical glass transition predicted by the one-step replica-symmetry breaking (1RSB) cavity equation. It is conjectured that local samplers such as Metropolis Monte Carlo and Glauber dynamics cannot equilibrate efficiently below this reconstruction temperature but may do so above it; our large numerical experiments show close agreement with this prediction across hundreds of different problem parameters. Therefore, our results rigorously show that Regev+BPQM reaches a temperature for which, to our knowledge, there is no matching classical guarantee, and brings Regev+BPQM to the conjectured limit of efficient Gibbs sampling by classical local dynamics.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Trichotomy of Regular Property Testing
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Property testing is concerned with the design of algorithms making a sublinear number of queries to distinguish whether the input satisfies a given property or is far from having this property. A seminal paper of Alon, Krivelevich, Newman, and Szegedy in 2001 introduced property testing of formal languages: the goal is to determine whether an input word belongs to a given language, or is far from any word in that language. They constructed the first property testing algorithm for the class of all regular languages. This opened a line of work with improved complexity results and applications to streaming algorithms. In this work, we show a trichotomy result: the class of regular languages can be divided into three classes, each associated with an optimal query complexity. Our analysis, which reasons directly and combinatorially on automata, yields effective characterizations of all three classes using so-called minimal blocking sequences.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Full version of the ICALP 2025 paper, revised for Logical Methods in Computer Science. 52 pages

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Randomized Greedy MIS Is Fast at Every Node of a Tree
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Randomized Greedy MIS (RGMIS) algorithm computes a maximal independent set (MIS) by processing the vertices in a uniformly random order and greedily adding each vertex to the independent set whenever possible. Despite its simplicity, this algorithm has proved effective in a range of parallel, distributed, and dynamic settings. For sufficiently small maximum degree, Nguyen and Onak (FOCS~'08) and Yoshida, Yamamoto, and Ito (STOC~'09) showed that a recursive simulation of RGMIS can be used to estimate the sizes of matching and vertex cover in sublinear time. The key subroutine in their approach is the following local query procedure: given a vertex $v$, to determine whether $v$ belongs to the MIS, recursively evaluate the neighbors of $v$ that precede $v$ in the random order. If any such neighbor is found to belong to the MIS, the procedure immediately concludes that $v$ is not in the MIS; otherwise, it concludes that $v$ is in the MIS.
