Companion to arXiv:2608.03473, arXiv:2608.09761, arXiv:2609.10600, arXiv:2610.08854 and arXiv:2610.30168

Programming Languages.title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
Programming Languages.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal Injectivity of the SparseStack
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
An Oblivious Subspace Injection (OSI) is a random sketching matrix that reliably preserves the minimum singular value of any fixed subspace with high constant probability, requiring only a one-sided spectral lower bound without controlling upper singular values. While classical Oblivious Subspace Embeddings (OSEs) fundamentally require row sparsity $Ω(\log r)$ at linear sketch dimension $k = O(r)$, we show that one-sided injectivity permits strictly sparser sketches, establishing matching (up to $\log\log r$ factors) upper and lower bounds of $\tildeΘ(\sqrt{\log r})$.
  First, we prove that the SparseStack sketch achieves constant injectivity at linear dimension $k = Θ(r)$ with row sparsity only $ζ= O(\sqrt{\log r})$, well below the $Θ(\log r)$ barrier where standard operator-norm concentration fails. Second, we establish a matching lower bound: any isotropic random sketching matrix satisfying a mild row-overlap condition requires row sparsity $ζ= Ω(\sqrt{\log r / \log \log r})$ to achieve linear-dimension injectivity, confirming that the $\sqrt{\log r}$ scale is fundamental.
  To bypass the lack of an operator-norm upper bound when $ζ= O(\sqrt{\log r})$, we decouple the sketch into two independent halves and introduce three techniques: (i) a uniform lower bound for flat vectors via randomized rounding, controlling discretization error using solely the Frobenius norm; (ii) a Gaussian truncation and minimax duality argument showing that all non-flat vectors escaping injectivity in the first half concentrate on a single universal coordinate subset $I \subseteq [n]$ of size $O(r/ζ)$, bypassing union bounds over supports; and (iii) a two-tier coordinate isolation analysis in the second half that suppresses collisions to $e^{-Ω(ζ^2)} \ll 1/r$, reliably preserving these heavy coordinates.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Query-Optimal and Gate-Efficient Lindbladian Simulation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a quantum algorithm for Lindbladian simulation given a block encoding of the Hamiltonian $H$ and a projected unitary encoding of the stacked jump operator $B=\sum_{k=1}^m \lvert k\rangle\otimes L_k$, with normalization factors $α_H$ and $α_B$, respectively. For evolution time $t$, set $τ=(α_H+α_B^2)t$. The algorithm approximates the evolution channel to diamond-norm error $\varepsilon$ using $O\!\left(τ+\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log\!\left(e+\log(1/\varepsilon)/τ\right)}\right)$ oracle queries, matching the query lower bound for Hamiltonian simulation. The number of additional one- and two-qubit gates is linear in the query complexity up to polylogarithmic factors. The query- and gate-complexity bounds extend to Lipschitz-continuous time-dependent Lindbladians under coherent time-indexed oracle access. Our construction uses a one-query transducer that implements a product of rational approximations to short-time evolution when supplied with a catalyst. We bound the error from omitting the catalyst by exploiting orthogonality between different sequences of Kraus labels. The gate implementation combines a compressed Kraus-label representation, which stores only the positions and values of the nonzero labels, with the rotation factorization of Chen et al.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Flows in High Degree Places: Sublinear Spanning Tree Congestion
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The congestion of a spanning tree $T$ of graph $G$ is the maximum congestion of an edge of $T$ if each edge of $G$ is routed on $T$. Prior work showed that obtaining a minimum congestion spanning tree is NP-hard to approximate within $6/5$, yet the only known approximation algorithm is a trivial $n/2$-approximation from returning any spanning tree of the graph. We give a simple poly-time $\tilde{O}(n^{6/7})$-approximation for minimum congestion spanning tree on $n$-vertex graphs. We obtain this result via a $\tilde{O}(m^{2/3})$-approximation, where $m$ is the number of edges. Our algorithm is based on a new \textit{flow-or-degree decomposition} which deletes a small number of edges so that each remaining component either has low degree or admits a low congestion flow. We also show that, assuming the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis, it is NP-hard to $O(1)$-approximate this problem, even on graphs of constant maximum degree.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Transposition Is Nearly Optimal for IID List Update
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The list update problem is one of the oldest and simplest problems in online algorithms: A set of items must be maintained in a list while requests to these items arrive over time. Whenever an item is requested, the algorithm pays a cost equal to the position of the item in the list. In the i.i.d. model, where requests are drawn independently from a fixed distribution, the static ordering by decreasing access probabilities $p_1\ge p_2\ge \dots \ge p_n$ achieves the minimal expected access cost $\mathrm{OPT}=\sum_{i=1}^n ip_i$. However, $p$ is typically unknown, and approximating it by tracking access frequencies creates undesirable overheads.
  A 50-year old conjecture by Rivest states that the Transposition rule (swap the requested item with its predecessor) is optimal among memoryless algorithms. While known to be false in the strict sense, prior research provided asymptotic confirmation of Rivest's conjecture for restricted distributions. We show that for all distributions, Transposition has stationary expected access cost at most $\mathrm{OPT}+1$, confirming Rivest's conjecture up to an unavoidable additive constant, and showing near-optimality even among algorithms with memory. More abstractly, it yields a purely memoryless procedure to approximately sort probabilities via sampling.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a workhorse algorithm for continuous optimization. It is a folk belief among deep learning practitioners that learning rate decay in SGD substantially improves performance. However, it has remained unclear whether learning rate decay offers an asymptotic advantage for global nonconvex optimization. We answer this question in the affirmative by demonstrating a natural class of nonconvex functions for which, we prove that SGD with learning rate decay requires exponentially fewer gradient queries for global optimization than SGD with any fixed learning rate in the small-step size regime. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exponential advantage that has been demonstrated for learning rate decay. The class of functions we consider includes many popular benchmark nonconvex functions. Our results provide a robust explanatory theory for the empirically observed benefits of learning rate decay for global optimization. We show that annealing performs the non-logconcave sampling task associated to the optimization problem in polynomial time, via a novel application of weak Poincaré inequalities.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Computing EF1 Allocations under Budget Constraints in Polynomial Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the fair allocation of indivisible items to agents with budget constraints and additive valuations. Each agent compares its own bundle with the subsets of another bundle that fit its budget. An allocation is envy-free up to one item (EF1) if, for every agent and every nonempty subset under comparison, removing an item of maximum value to that agent eliminates its envy. We require EF1 both between agents and towards the charity, which contains all unallocated items. EF1 allocations exist, but computing them in polynomial time has remained open even for homogeneous valuations. We resolve this problem with a polynomial-time algorithm for EF1 allocations under heterogeneous valuations. We also prove that detecting an EF1 violation is NP-complete. Equivalently, checking whether a given allocation is EF1 is coNP-complete. Finally, we give polynomial-time algorithms for envy-freeness up to any item (EFX) both when each agent's valuation is proportional to item size and when each agent has a fixed number of distinct positive item values. As an application, for homogeneous valuations and any $\varepsilon>0$, we obtain an EF1 allocation with at least a $(1/2-\varepsilon)$ fraction of the maximum social welfare in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Smoothed Analysis of Nash Equilibrium and Fixed Point Computation, and Efficiency of the Homotopy Method
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study, under a smoothed analysis perspective, the complexity of three PPAD-complete problems: computing Nash equilibria, computing fixed points, and solving variational inequalities. We consider a general perturbation model that bounds the probability density of the quantities evaluated by our algorithms. As special cases, it captures worst-case games perturbed by small random per-action costs, and worst-case maps perturbed by a small random affine function.
  Under these models, we show that classical algorithmic paradigms, cover-based search and homotopy path-following provably outperform the worst-case state-of-the-art. For games with a constant number of players and $n$ strategies per player, a recursive cover-based algorithm computes an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium using $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot 2^{O(n)}$ expected payoff-vector computations, compared to the worst-case runtime tradeoffs of $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot n^{O(n)}$, $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(n)}$, $2^{O(\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)}$, and $2^{O(n)}\mathrm{poly}(\log(1/\varepsilon))$. For fixed points and variational inequalities of bounded and Lipschitz maps on the $n$-dimensional $\ell_2$ unit ball, the same approach runs in expected time $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot 2^{O(n)}$, compared to the worst-case $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(n)}$; the $2^{Ω(n)}$ factor is necessary by prior work [Rubinstein, 2017]. For general smooth maps, we further analyze the classical predictor--corrector homotopy method, for which only qualitative convergence guarantees were previously known, showing that under perturbations the homotopy path is well conditioned and has length $2^{O(n)}$, so that the method finds an $\varepsilon$-approximate solution in time $2^{O(n)}\cdot\mathrm{poly}(1/p)/\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-p$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: No Exponential Quantum Advantage for Decoded Quantum Interferometry with Local Quantum Decoders
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) reduces optimization of sparse linear constraint problems, and sampling from their Gibbs measures, to decoding a linear code from a quantum state. We study DQI on random $D$-regular $k$-sparse instances with $k\ge3$, for which local decoders such as belief propagation with quantum messages (BPQM) are commonly used. Such decoders estimate a typical codeword symbol using only the qudits within logarithmic distance of it. Our main insight is that the thresholds of the decoding problem induced by DQI correspond to phase transitions of the Gibbs measure that are well studied in statistical physics: tree reconstruction for local decoders and, for Max-$k$-XORSAT, condensation for the optimal decoder. This insight allows us to prove two main results. First, we prove an information-theoretic obstruction: no local decoder can recover the codeword with high probability above the tree reconstruction threshold. Conversely, we show that a decoder based on BPQM reaches this threshold. Since the cavity method predicts that local Markov chains equilibrate rapidly up to the same threshold, we expect DQI with local decoders to give no exponential speedup for sampling and no advantage in approximate optimization with amplitude functions that depend only on the number of violated constraints. Second, we consider the optimal decoder (the pretty-good measurement, for which no efficient implementation is known) and show that it succeeds exactly below the condensation threshold. The condensation threshold thus provides a tight upper bound on the performance of DQI with these amplitude functions, providing a strict refinement of the limit that Jordan et al.\ derived from the Holevo bound. Our results point to efficient nonlocal decoders that succeed between the two thresholds as the only viable path to a quantum advantage with DQI on these instances.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Polynomial-Space Quantum Algorithms from Classical Branching: Colouring, Domination and Monotone Local Search
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give quantum algorithms for exponential-time problems on $n$ vertices or elements, with bounded error, polynomial space and no quantum random access memory. Our results are these. (1) 4-Colouring in quantum time $O(1.3032^n)$, from a polynomial-space branching algorithm with polynomial-space terminal algorithms; with the branching algorithm alone, $O(1.3100^n)$. The previous best bound in this model, to our knowledge, is $O(1.3231^n)$. (2) $k$-Colouring below the previous best bound for $k \in \{5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11\}$ and $13 \le k \le 18$, from $O(1.4518^n)$ for $k = 5$ to $O(1.9233^n)$ for $k = 18$. (3) Dominating Set in $O(1.2235^n)$, against the previous $O(2^{n/2})$, Independent Dominating Set in $O(1.1583^n)$, and Edge Dominating Set and Minimum Maximal Matching in $O(1.1501^n)$. (4) A quantum form of monotone local search: if the extension problem has a backtracking tree with $c^k$ nodes up to polynomial factors, the problem is solved in quantum time $(2 - 1/c)^{n/2}$ up to polynomial factors. This gives Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3081^n)$, Subset and Group Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3229^n)$, Cluster Vertex Deletion in $O(1.2033^n)$, 3-Hitting Set in $O(1.2405^n)$, Proper Interval Vertex Deletion in $O(1.3541^n)$, Multicut on Trees in $O(1.1647^n)$ and Min-Ones $d$-SAT in $O^*((2-1/d)^{n/2})$. (5) Quantum exponential-time approximations below the quantum exact bounds, such as a 1.1-approximation for Vertex Cover in $O(1.0555^n)$ and for Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.2161^n)$. The colouring exponents for $k \ge 6$ come from an evaluation of a known reduction recursion, computed in floating point with a margin.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Wolfe's Minimum-Norm-Point Method Generalizes the Simplex Method
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Wolfe's method computes the point of minimum Euclidean norm in the convex hull of finitely many points. The method is parameterized by an insertion rule and it has been an open problem whether Wolfe's original rule guarantees a polynomial number of iterations (De Loera, Haddock, and Rademacher; STOC'18). We resolve this question by proving an exponential lower bound. In fact, we establish a tight connection to the simplex method for linear programming that allows us to transfer many lower bounds for simplex pivot rules to corresponding insertion rules of Wolfe's method. These include not only Wolfe's linopt rule via Dantzig's pivot rule, but also many other classical, randomized and history-based rules. As a corollary, we obtain the first exponential example for the Lawson-Hanson algorithm for nonnegative least squares, as well as PSPACE-hardness of deciding whether the linopt rule ever uses a given point.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Better Bounds For Graph Reconstruction
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The goal in graph reconstruction problems is to learn an initially unknown graph using only a few queries of a specific type. Possibly the most natural query type is retrieving the distance between any two vertices of a connected, undirected, and unweighted graph. For a bounded-degree graph on $n$ vertices, Kannan, Mathieu, and Zhou [TALG 2018] showed a randomized algorithm that uses only $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{3/2})$ such queries. On the lower bound side, it is only known that any randomized algorithm needs $Ω(n\log n)$ queries. We make a significant step forward to bridging these bounds by designing a randomized algorithm that uses $n^{4/3+o(1)}$ queries. This requires extending the original approach based on Voronoi diagrams into a recursive procedure that partitions a cell into smaller cells. While such a recursive approach has been used in the related graph verification problem, in the more general graph reconstruction problem we need to operate without knowing the graph, which requires a new (and more technical) approach.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: GreedTok Is a 0.3287-Approximation for Tokenization, Within 3% of the Best Possible Constant
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A tokenizer's vocabulary is chosen once and used on every input, so it matters how much compression a greedy vocabulary can lose. GreedTok (Lim et al., 2025) picks $k$ tokens one at a time, each time the string that saves the most tokens; its worst-case ratio was open. We prove that GreedTok saves at least 0.3287 of the optimal number of tokens saved, on every corpus and budget, while junction corpora show that no constant above 0.3387 is possible. The lower-bound proof is written out in full and uses no computer certificates. Its key idea is to track the order of greedy's choices: given that order, the pattern greedy leaves inside an optimal token depends on two numbers, and an induction peels off one chosen string at a time; without the order, a needed inequality fails for a 20-character token. Over 256 symbols, GreedTok's ratio exceeds 0.33861 for every $k\ge 104{,}910$, and over $k^c$ symbols with $c<1/2$ it is at least 0.4386 in the limit. We also show that the objective is APX-hard: it has no PTAS unless P = NP.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 57 pages, 5 figures. Code, checkers and supplement: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24073514

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Greedy Byte-Pair Encoding Achieves 0.391 of the Optimum, Past the One-Third Barrier for Packing-Based Analyses
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds most language-model tokenisers by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols. How much shortening can this greedy rule lose against the best $k$ merges? Kozma and Voderholzer proved that greedy achieves at least one third of the optimal shortening; the best known upper bound is $(1-e^{-2})/2\approx 0.432$. We show that one third is a barrier for packing-based analyses, which see the optimum only through a pair packing, and we prove that greedy achieves at least $0.391$ of the optimum on every input, with any tie-breaking. The key idea is rule determinism: all copies of a rule of the optimum spell the same letters, so when one greedy replacement destroys three of the optimum's merge points, half a unit can be refunded on each side. A weaker bound, $0.374$, has a short proof that needs no computer; $0.391$ adds a certificate in exact arithmetic. We also show that the worst-case ratio is exactly $3/4$ for two merges and at most $7/12$ for three.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimizing the Steady-State Travel Time of Nash Flows over Time with Capacity Increases
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study budgeted capacity augmentation for single-source single-sink \NFOTs under constant inflow $u_0$. The goal is to increase capacities on arcs subject to a global budget constraint in order to minimize the steady-state travel time in the network. We show that this problem is weakly NP-hard on series-parallel networks and provide an exact pseudopolynomial algorithm as well as a fully polynomial algorithm that attains the optimum travel time for budget $B$ while spending at most $B + \varepsilon\cdot\max\{B,u_0\}$. On general networks the problem becomes strongly NP-hard. Moreover, unless $\text{P} = \text{NP}$, for every fixed $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, no polynomial-time algorithm can achieve the optimal steady-state travel time while exceeding the budget by at most a factor of $n^{1-\varepsilon}$. Lastly, we give structural properties about steady-state travel time under varying arc capacities. We identify capacity thresholds determined by subsets of $s$-$t$-cuts and show that the travel time is constant in the interior of the cells resulting from the corresponding hyperplane arrangement.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Single-Exponential Algorithms for Directed Feedback Vertex Set on Planar Digraphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We consider Directed Feedback Vertex Set on planar digraphs, parameterized by the solution size $k$. We give a randomized algorithm with one-sided error running in time $(2+\sqrt5)^k n^{O(1)}= 4.24^k n^{O(1)}$, and a deterministic algorithm running in time $8.04^k n^{O(1)}$. Both algorithms use polynomial space. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first single-exponential fixed-parameter algorithms for Directed Feedback Vertex Set on planar digraphs. This contrasts with general digraphs, where the best known algorithms run in time $2^{O(k\log k)}(n+m)$, and whether a $2^{o(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}$-time algorithm exists remains a major open problem. Our main tool is an exact Euler-type counting identity for plane digraphs. It shows that every small solution must carry a large share of the vertices whose in- and out-arcs alternate in the embedding, while solutions avoiding such vertices can be computed by reducing to Directed Feedback Arc Set, which is known to be solvable in polynomial time on planar digraphs via the Lucchesi-Younger theorem.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Sampling Colorings on $G(n, d/n)$ via Glauber Dynamics
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the mixing time of Glauber dynamics for sampling uniformly from the proper $q$-colorings of sparse Erdős-Rényi random graphs $G(n,d/n)$. Our main result establishes that with probability $1-o(1)$ over the draw of $G$, Glauber dynamics is rapidly mixing for every $q\geq d+d^{1/2+\varepsilon}$, given any fixed $0<\varepsilon\leq1/2$ and any sufficiently large fixed $d$. In particular, the surplus of colors above $d$ is sublinear and close to $\sqrt{d}$. The achieved color range therefore approaches the tree uniqueness threshold and improves over the previously best achievable number of colors $q > 1.763 d$ due to Efthymiou, Hayes, Stefankovic, and Vigoda [SODA 2018]. Moreover, our mixing-time bound is $O(n^{2+o_d(1)})$, and hence almost quadratic as $d\rightarrow\infty$.
  Our proof is based on establishing a spectral gap for block dynamics resulting from a suitable decomposition of $G(n,d/n)$ into blocks and singleton vertices, ensuring that every high-degree vertex is encapsulated within a block. Our main technical contribution is a novel way of establishing rapid mixing of block dynamics via an integrated Bochner-Bakry-Émery approach, which we expect to have applications beyond sampling colorings. We further devise a new block decomposition of $G(n,d/n)$ that strengthens and simplifies similar constructions used in previous work. Finally, to compare block and Glauber dynamics, we establish a novel recursive separator decomposition of tree-like blocks, together with a coupling argument that avoids the need for nearly uniform color marginals at vertices adjacent to hubs. This comparison argument might be of independent interest.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Existence of Maximin Share Allocations is $Δ_2^P$-complete
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The maximin share (MMS) guarantee has become one of the central fairness benchmarks for allocating indivisible items. Since Kurokawa, Procaccia, and Wang [EC'14, JACM'18] showed that exact MMS allocations need not exist, a substantial literature has developed around the existence and computation of approximate MMS allocations, including the recent work of Heidari, Kaviani, Seddighin, and Shahrezaei [SODA'26]. In contrast, a fundamental complexity question posed more than a decade ago by Bouveret and Lemaître [JAAMAS'16] has remained unresolved: how hard is it to decide whether an exact MMS allocation exists?
  For additive valuations, Lonc and Truszczynski [JAIR'20] established membership in the complexity class $Δ_2^P$ (also known as $P^{NP}$), but no hardness result was known. For the more general class of 2-additive valuations, Bouveret and Lemaître established NP-hardness, leaving a substantial gap to the $Δ_2^P$ upper bound. Moreover, the complexity of MMS existence for additive and $k$-additive valuations was posed as open questions.
  We resolve this longstanding question by proving that deciding the existence of an MMS allocation for additive goods is $Δ_2^P$-complete, even for five agents.
  Additionally, we prove weak coNP-hardness for three agents, thereby establishing a precise dichotomy with the known existence guarantee for two agents, and strong coNP-hardness when the number of agents is unrestricted. Furthermore, our strong hardness construction yields an inverse-polynomial gap in the optimal MMS approximation ratio, ruling out an FPTAS for approximating this ratio unless P=NP. Finally, we show that all these results for goods extend to the chores setting through a polynomial-time transformation that preserves MMS existence.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 58 pages; this version strengthens the main result for additive valuations; abstract shortened to meet arXiv requirements

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: How Hard Is Tokenisation? Algorithms and Complexity Beyond NP-Hardness
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Given a collection of strings and a vocabulary budget, how well can we minimize its total token count, and how does the answer change with the tokenisation model? For binary direct tokenisation, previous work proved APX-hardness but left constant-factor approximability unresolved \citep{kastreva2026}. We rule out every polynomial-time $M^{1-\varepsilon}$ approximation, for fixed $\varepsilon>0$, unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, even on distinct equal-length strings with $K=m-1$. Here $M$ is the total input length and $m$ is the number of input strings. We complement this lower bound with a deterministic polynomial-time $O(M/\log M)$ approximation algorithm and stronger bounds for selected vocabulary budgets. For the different objective of maximizing compression savings, GreedTok was shown to attain a constant fraction of the optimum on unrestricted alphabets \citep{baliga2026}; we establish a deterministic EPTAS for direct savings on every fixed alphabet and analyze greedy selection by true marginal gains. For exact optimization, we give a binary direct algorithm running in $2^{O(n\log\log n/\log n)}\poly(I)$ time, where $n$ is the total length of the distinct input strings and $I$ is the input encoding length. Finally, we resolve two unary merge-model hardness questions left by the bounded-alphabet study \citep{kastreva2026}: standard unary bottom-up tokenisation is APX-hard, and unary optimal pair encoding is strongly NP-complete, strengthening the previously known weak hardness.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Strong Backdoor to Forests is FPT: Tight Linear-Time FPT for Essentially General SAT
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In a seminal work, Gaspers and Szeider [FOCS 2013] gave a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) approximate algorithm for finding a strong backdoor of size at most $k$ to incidence treewidth at most $t$, for a given CNF-formula $φ$. In particular, their algorithm runs in $f(k,t) |φ|^3$ time, and finds a strong backdoor to treewidth at most $t$, of $φ$, of size at most $2^k$ whenever there exists one of size at most $k$. Determining whether the detection of strong backdoors to bounded incidence treewidth is FPT parameterized by $k+t$ was left open in their work and this has been repeatedly posed as an open question by Gaspers and Szeider, for example in [The Multivariate Algorithmic Revolution and Beyond 2012] and more recently in [Computer Science Reviews 2025], even for incidence forests and when the input is a $3$-CNF formula. We answer this question affirmatively.
  We show that strong backdoors to forests can be found in linear-FPT time on arbitrary non-tautological CNF formulas (not just on 3-CNF formulas). Given such a formula $φ$ and a budget $k$, our algorithm finds a strong backdoor to the class of forests, of size at most $k$, or correctly reports that none exists, in $2^{2^{O(k)}} |φ|$ time. Moreover, we show that our result is as tight as it can get. First, we show that finding strong backdoors to treewidth $t$ for any $t \geq 2$ is W[1]-hard, even on non-tautological 3-CNF formulas. Second, the running time of our algorithm is tight: it is linear in the input size and a better than double-exponential dependence on $k$ in the running time would imply a $2^{o(N/\log N)}$-time algorithm for solving 3-SAT on $N$ variables, which would beat even the very recently claimed sub-exponential algorithm for solving 3-SAT by OpenAI and Anthropic.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Balanced spanning forests of graphs: Hardness and solving methods
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The balanced connected $k$-partition problem (\textsc{bcp}) is a classic problem, which consists in partitioning the set of vertices of a vertex-weighted connected graph into a collection of~$k$ classes such that each class induces a connected subgraph of \emph{roughly} the same weight. In this study, we investigate edge-weighted variants of $\textsc{bcp}$, where, given a connected graph $G$, a positive integer $k$, and edge weights, the goal is to compute a spanning $k$-forest~$\mathcal{T}$ of $G$ (i.e., a forest with exactly $k$ trees) that minimizes the weight of the heaviest tree in~$\mathcal{T}$ in the min-max version, or maximizes the weight of the lightest tree in~$\mathcal{T}$ in the max-min version. We show that both versions of this problem are $\NP$-hard on complete graphs with $k=2$, unweighted split graphs, and unweighted bipartite graphs with $k\geq 2$ fixed. Moreover, we prove that these problems do not admit subexponential-time algorithms, unless the Exponential-Time Hypothesis fails. We focus on the min-max version and devise a tight $k$-approximation algorithm, compact and non-compact integer {linear programming} formulations, branch-and-cut, and branch-and-price algorithms. Finally, we present the outcomes of an experimental study on the performance of different solution methods. The source code of the complete implementation of the proposed algorithms is also available.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A 1.764-competitive algorithm for online fractional vertex cover on forests
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study online fractional vertex cover on forests under edge arrival. We give a deterministic algorithm with competitive ratio at most $4 - \sqrt{5} \approx 1.764$, which simultaneously produces an online fractional matching with competitive ratio of at least $1/(4 - \sqrt{5}) \approx 0.566$. This improves on the previous best competitive ratios of $11/6 \approx 1.833$ and $5/9 \approx 0.555$, respectively.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Competitive Bounds for Online Matching on Forests
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the online matching problem, its fractional relaxation, and the fractional online vertex cover problem on forests whose edges arrive one at a time in an arbitrary order. Matching decisions are irrevocable, and vertex-cover weights can only increase over time. For online matching, we present a randomized algorithm with expected competitive ratio $4/7$ against an oblivious adversary, improving the previous $5/9$ guarantee. We also present a deterministic algorithm that simultaneously maintains a $4/7$-competitive fractional matching and a $7/4$-competitive fractional vertex cover. This deterministic algorithm improves the previous $5/9$ guarantee for fractional matching and the $11/6$ guarantee for fractional vertex cover. We prove that $4/7$ is optimal for both randomized and fractional matching, even on growing trees of maximum degree four.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Instance-Optimality of Single-Pair Personalized PageRank
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We consider discounted random walks in a directed simple graph $G=(V,E)$. Such a walk terminates at each step with a constant probability $α\in (0,1)$ and otherwise continues to a uniform random out-neighbor. Given a pair $(s,t)\in V^2$, we denote by $π(s,t)$ the probability of such a discounted random walk starting at $s$ terminates at $t$. This probability is referred to as the Personalized PageRank (PPR) of $t$ with respect to $s$. The problem of estimating $π(s,t)$ within a constant multiplicative factor with constant success probability for a given vertex pair $(s,t)$ is called the single-pair PPR estimation problem.
  We investigate the instance-optimality of single-pair PPR estimation in directed graphs. We present a new algorithm that aims at instance-optimal running time up to polylogarithmic factors. In other words, no correct algorithm can run faster than our algorithm on any valid graph by more than a polylogarithmic factor. We show that our algorithm is instance-optimal in the standard adjacency-list query model if $n$ is not known (as is often the case for most of the large networks to which PPR is applied). When $n$ is known, our algorithm is still instance-optimal for sparse graphs. For denser graphs, when $n$ is known, we show that no algorithm can achieve general instance-optimality.
  For the multiplicative approximation of PPR, we also improve the worst-case complexity from $O(mn\log n)$ to the near-optimal $O(m\log n)$. This is not only for the single-pair discussed above, but also for the single-source and single-target variants of the PPR estimation problem.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Longest Unbordered Factors in Linear Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A border of a string is a nonempty proper prefix that is also a suffix. A string is unbordered if it has no border. The length of a longest unbordered factor is closely related to the smallest period of the string. While the smallest period can be computed in linear time, the best previously known algorithm for computing a longest unbordered factor takes $O(n \log n)$ worst-case time for a string of length $n$. Whether this computational problem can be solved in worst-case linear time has remained open. In this paper, we resolve this open problem for integer alphabets of size $n^{O(1)}$ by presenting an algorithm that computes all occurrences of longest unbordered factors in $O(n)$ worst-case time. Our algorithm uses a combinatorial property of longest unbordered factors and scans the input string in both directions to capture all occurrences achieving the global maximum without computing the local maximum at every starting position.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Lumberjack: Better Differentially Private Random Forests through Heavy Hitter Detection in Trees
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Random forests are widely used in fields involving sensitive tabular data, but existing approaches to enforcing differential privacy (DP) typically degrade performance to the point of impracticality. In this paper, we introduce Lumberjack, a differentially private random forest algorithm that achieves substantially higher utility by constructing large random decision trees and then applying aggressive, privacy-preserving pruning to retain only sufficiently populated nodes. A key component of our approach is a novel $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP heavy hitter detection algorithm for hierarchical data, whose error is $O_{\varepsilon,δ}(\sqrt{\log h})$ for trees of height $h$ and may be of independent interest. This favorable scaling enables the use of significantly deeper trees than in prior work, leading to improved expressiveness under privacy constraints. Our empirical evaluation on benchmark datasets shows that Lumberjack consistently outperforms prior DP random forest methods, establishing a new state of the art. In particular, our approach yields substantial improvements in the privacy-utility trade-off for practical privacy budgets. Our findings suggest that carefully designed DP random forests can close much of the utility gap, highlighting a promising and underexplored direction for future research.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Induced Cycles of Many Lengths
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Let $G$ be a graph and let $\mathrm{cl}(G)$ be the number of distinct induced cycle lengths in $G$. We show that for $c,t\in \mathbb N$, every graph $G$ that does not contain an induced subgraph isomorphic to $K_{t+1}$ or $K_{t,t}$ and satisfies $\mathrm{cl}(G) \le c$ has bounded treewidth. As a consequence, we obtain a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding whether a graph $G$ contains induced cycles of at least three distinct lengths.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Power of Migration on Identical Machines is Two
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the power of migration in preemptive scheduling on identical parallel machines with time windows. If an instance admits a migratory schedule on $m$ machines, how many machines are needed to schedule it without migration? Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs (2001) showed that $6m-5$ machines suffice and gave a polynomial-time construction using $12m-5$ machines, whereas $2m-1$ machines may be necessary. We close this gap, which has been open for more than 25 years: $2m-1$ machines always suffice, and a corresponding non-migratory schedule can be computed in strongly polynomial time.
  Our proof has two main technical ingredients. First, we introduce supercanonical schedules and prove that the conflict graph of every such schedule on $m$ machines is $(2m-1)$-colorable. The key property is that whenever a job pauses, the jobs running alongside it just before and just after the pause separate the jobs processed entirely during the pause from the rest of the conflict graph. We use these separators and Kempe exchanges to compute a coloring in polynomial time. Second, we construct a supercanonical schedule with polynomially many processing blocks by shrinking job windows as far as possible while preserving feasibility and solving a min-cost flow problem.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Bounds for Sublinear Metric Steiner Tree
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the metric Steiner tree problem we are given an $n$-point metric space $(V,w)$ and a set $T\subseteq V$ of terminals, and we seek the smallest weight $\mathrm{OPT}$ of a tree that spans $T$ and may use points of $V\setminus T$. We study sublinear algorithms in the distance-oracle model, where the algorithm knows $V$ and $T$ upfront and can query the distance function $w$. The objective is to estimate $\mathrm{OPT}$ while querying significantly fewer than $n^2$ distances.
  The minimum spanning tree on $T$ estimates $\mathrm{OPT}$ within a factor $2$, and its weight can be approximated with $\widetilde{O}(n)$ queries. The natural question that has been studied is therefore the query complexity of estimating $\mathrm{OPT}$ within a factor strictly below $2$. Chen, Khanna, and Tan [SODA 2023] gave such an algorithm using $\widetilde{O}(n^{13/7})$ queries, and a lower bound of $\widetildeΩ(n^{6/5})$. Later Mahabadi, Roghani, Tarnawski, and Vakilian [ITCS 2025] improved the algorithm to $\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})$, and Mahabadi, Tarnawski, and Vakilian [ITCS 2027] improved the lower bound to $\widetildeΩ(n^{7/5})$.
  In this work we settle the above question. We give an algorithm that estimates $\mathrm{OPT}$ within a factor $2-η_0$, for an absolute constant $η_0>0$, with query (and time) complexity $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$. We also show that the exponent $3/2$ is tight.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: How Far Must a Test Explore? Certifying Composable Read-Write Interfaces from Their Own Random Edits
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Random tests of stateful code check laws, like reading back a written value, at states that random writes reach. The laws hold at every state exactly when the code behaves like a record with hidden data, so a pass is taken as evidence. This can fail: the laws can hold at every sample while the code is far from any record. The laws are local, but behaving like a record is global. Self-testing and stability theorems bridge this gap when the query distribution is controlled by the tester or preserved by the tested maps, but here it is generated by the tested writes, which need not be invertible.
  We ask how far a test must explore. An interface has $m$ binary variables, each with a read and two writes; in a record, reads return their bits and writes set only their bits. Samples are the ends of geometric runs of mean $\ell$ of uniformly random writes from a start distribution; a tester adds its own write chains of depth $d$. The distance is the least, over records with hidden data, of the largest probability that a read or write differs from it at a sample.
  From one start state, law checks at $O(m^2\log m/ε)$ samples certify, at fixed confidence, any threshold $ε$ after geometric runs of every positive mean, while runs of fixed positive length can pass at distance $1/2$. For the worst start distribution, take $ε=m^{-β}$ with fixed $0<β\le1$. For $d\le cm$ with fixed $c<1/2$, a polynomial budget of samples and writes exists exactly when $\ell=Ω(m)$, where law checks suffice. With no runs, the least depth for this budget is $(1/2+o(1))m$. Counting samples alone, in the worst case at $ε=1/(32m)$ and $d\le m/16$, the critical mean for a polynomial budget is $Θ(m\log(m/d)/\log m)$, by exhaustive search. So one start state needs only law checks, and the worst case at these thresholds needs exploration linear in $m$ if writes are counted.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Efficient Adaptive Data Analysis over Dense Distributions
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Modern data workflows are inherently adaptive, repeatedly querying the same dataset to refine and validate sequential decisions, but such adaptivity can lead to overfitting and invalid statistical inference. Adaptive Data Analysis (ADA) mechanisms address this challenge; however, there is a fundamental tension between computational efficiency and sample complexity. For $T$ rounds of adaptive analysis, computationally efficient algorithms typically incur suboptimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ sample complexity, whereas for arbitrary distributions, algorithms with $O(\log T)$ sample complexity are computationally intractable under standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work, we shed light on this trade-off by identifying a natural class of data distributions under which both computational efficiency and logarithmic sample complexity in $T$ are achievable. We propose a computationally efficient ADA mechanism that attains $O(\log T)$ sample complexity, optimal in its dependence on $T$, when the data distribution is dense with respect to a known prior. This setting includes, in particular, feature-label data distributions arising in distribution-specific learning. As a consequence, our mechanism also yields a sample-efficient (i.e., $O(\log T)$ samples) statistical query oracle in the distribution-specific setting. Moreover, although our algorithm is not based on differential privacy, it satisfies a relaxed privacy notion known as Predicate Singling Out (PSO) security (Cohen and Nissim 2020) whenever the number of its possible update transcripts is polynomial in the sample size. Our results thus reveal an inherent connection between adaptive data analysis and privacy beyond differential privacy.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Counting Hypertriangles through Hypergraph Orientations
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Counting the number of small patterns is a central task in network analysis. While this problem is well studied for graphs, many real-world datasets are naturally modeled as hypergraphs, motivating the need for efficient hypergraph motif counting algorithms. In particular, we study the problem of counting hypertriangles - collections of three pairwise-intersecting hyperedges. These hypergraph patterns have a rich structure with multiple distinct intersection patterns unlike graph triangles.
  Inspired by classical graph algorithms based on orientations and degeneracy, we develop a new theoretical framework that generalizes these concepts to hypergraphs and yields provable algorithms for hypertriangle counting.
  We implement these ideas in DITCH (Degeneracy Inspired Triangle Counter for Hypergraphs) and show experimentally that it is faster on all but one small instance, achieving speedups of up to 100x, and is 6-100x more memory-efficient than existing state-of-the-art methods.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Ranking and Unranking Permutations in Heap's Order
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Heap's algorithm is a permutation generation method with very low constant overhead. Its element-interchanging mechanism, however, prevents the standard factorial-base Lehmer code from being applied directly, and to our knowledge no explicit Rank/Unrank algorithm for the Heap order has been published. This paper describes the block structure of Heap's algorithm in terms of rearrangement operators: the net effect of a block-internal traversal is a tail-preserving operator and the block-boundary swap is a top-level swap operator, and together they yield a closed-form recurrence for the block transitions. On this basis a bottom-up Unrank algorithm and a top-down Rank algorithm are built from one and the same closed-form in-block mapping; both run in $O(n^3)$ time and $O(n)$ space and require no factorial-scale precomputed table. The supporting proofs use a synchronized strong induction on the dimension to establish the bijectivity of the trailing-element mapping, closed forms for the final arrangement and for the trailing sequence, the dichotomy of its cycle structure, and the reciprocity of Rank and Unrank. The Heap order is in fact the colex order of the mixed-radix code.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Pseudometric-Weighted Correlation Clustering via Spectral Preclustering
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study \emph{pseudometric-weighted correlation clustering}, in which pairs have arbitrary positive or negative labels and nonnegative disagreement weights satisfying the triangle inequality. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, we give a randomized polynomial-time $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation, improving the previous factor of $10/3$. The algorithm constructs an explicit feasible solution to the cluster LP with polynomial support and value at most $(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the minimum integral clustering cost. Our main contribution is a weighted preclustering construction that witnesses a near-optimal clustering while bounding the total weight of admissible edges by $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}$. We obtain admissibility certificates from random walks, where the factor-two Ptolemy's inequality for pseudometrics reduces the required length of walks from $O(\log n)$ to a constant. We then bound the rounding error separately at each vertex and use the triangle inequality to control its weighted cost. Sampling and coverage corrections produce an exactly feasible solution, and the factor-two rounding completes the approximation algorithm.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Function Inversion Reporting
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the Function Inversion problem, the goal is to invert a function $f:[N] \to [N]$ in two phases. In the preprocessing phase, the offline algorithm computes an advice string of length $S$ bits. In the online phase, the online algorithm receives the advice and a challenge $y \in [N]$, and the goal is to find a preimage $x \in [N]$ such that $f(x) = y$ in time $T$. The problem was initially studied in cryptography, but in recent years it has found various applications to data structure problems. Yet, several of the applications require a variant of Function Inversion, known as Function Inversion Reporting, where the goal is to output all preimages of the challenge $y$.
  In this paper, we study the Function Inversion Reporting problem in a systematic way by unifying and improving existing algorithms. As a result, we obtain improved data structures for several problems including 3SUM-Indexing Reporting, Range Reporting, Approximate Nearest Neighbor, Jumbled Indexing Reporting, and Gapped String Indexing Reporting.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Improved $(1+2e)$-Approximation Algorithm for Metric Data Placement
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the metric data placement problem with site-capacity constraints and fixed installation costs, aiming to minimize the total cost of placing data (resources) and accessing their nearest copies. We develop a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm based on a natural linear programming relaxation of the problem. Starting from an optimal fractional solution, we construct multiscale metric-ball partitions independently for each resource and connect overlapping balls at consecutive levels to form a flow network. The resource layers are then coupled through shared site-capacity arcs, allowing us to obtain an integral placement by minimizing a surrogate cost over a single min-cost circulation. By optimizing the choice of ball radii, we establish an approximation factor of $1+2e\approx 6.44$. To our knowledge, this is the best approximation guarantee for the metric data placement problem since its introduction by Baev and Rajaraman in 2001.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Differentially Private Verification of Distribution Properties
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A recent line of work initiated by Chiesa and Gur and further developed by Herman and Rothblum investigates the sample and communication complexity of verifying properties of distributions with the assistance of a powerful, knowledgeable, but untrusted prover. In this work, we initiate the study of differentially private distribution property verification. After all, if we do not trust the prover to help us with verification, why should we trust it with our sensitive sample? We map a landscape of differentially private verification of properties of distributions. In the non-private case it is known that one-round private-coin protocols can have substantially lower complexity than public-coin (AM) protocols. In contrast, the possibility for improvement in differentially private interactive proofs depends on the privacy parameter regime and model. Drawing on connections between privacy and replicability and privacy amplification techniques in the literature we show:
  1. There exists a reduction from any one-round $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differentially private private-coin protocol to a differentially private AM protocol for the parameter regime $\varepsilon = O(1/\sqrt{s})$ and $δ= O(1/s^{5/2})$ with approximately the same privacy and sample and communication complexities. In the local model, this is relaxed to $\varepsilon = O(1/\sqrt{\log s})$
  2. However, when the privacy guarantee is very relaxed ($\varepsilon \in Ω(\log s)$), private coins indeed reduce sample and communication complexities.
  We also obtain a computationally efficient Merlin-Arthur proof for privately testing whether samples are drawn from a product distribution and prove that its sample complexity is optimal up to a $polylog N$ factor by reducing uniformity testing to independence testing with Boolean attributes and appealing to known lower bounds on sample complexity for private uniformity testing.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Fast Algorithm for Subspace Convolution
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A cornerstone result in Boolean lattice theory is the subset-zeta transform, which computes the $f$-weighted subset summation problem $(Z f)(B)=\sum_{A\subseteq B}f(A)$ for all $ B\subseteq[n]$ in $O(N \log N)$ additions instead of the naïve $O(3^n) = O(N^{\log_2 3})$, where $N=2^n$.
  This paper studies the algebraic analogue of this problem--the subspace summation problem--where subsets are replaced by linear subspaces in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$. Surprisingly, we show that this problem admits a similar $Θ_q(N_q \log N_q)$-time algorithm, where $N_q$ is the number of subspaces. This improves substantially (in both theory and practice) over lattice-based algorithms ([BHK+16, KKW16]), which are known to be optimal for addition-only algorithms over $\mathbb R$. We prove similar runtimes for inversion, rank-constrained sums and span convolution. We describe two main applications:
  Fast linear algebra on Grassmann graphs: Matrix--vector multiplication for arbitrary distance-invariant kernels on $N$-vertex Grassmann graphs in $O_q(N\log N)$ arithmetic operations, together with fast spectral projections and exact solutions of the corresponding linear systems.
  Graph coloring of low binary cut-rank graphs: An $n^{2^{r^2/4+O(1)}}$-time algorithm for computing the chromatic number and chromatic polynomial of an $n$-vertex graph, given a rank-decomposition of width $r$. We also give quantitative reductions from satisfiability and monotone constraint problems.
  Experiments show speedups in measured running time of up to $18$ over the covering-pair algorithm for the zeta transform, $190$ over Poisson summation for rank-constrained sums, and $22$ over the distance-matrix recurrence for Grassmann kernel multiplication. Lean 4 formalizations of the transform identities, arithmetic operation bounds, and graph-coloring constructions accompany the paper [PW26].
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 35 pages, 2 figures. Code, experiments, and Lean 4 formalizations: https://github.com/shlomi-perles/subspace-convolution

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Compact enumeration for scheduling one machine
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A Variable Parameter (VP) analysis, that we introduce here, aims to give a precise algorithm time complexity expression in which an exponent appears solely in terms of a variable parameter. A variable parameter is the number of objects with specific problem-dependent properties. Here we describe two VP-algorithms, an implicit enumeration algorithm and a polynomial-time approximation scheme for a strongly $NP$-hard problem of scheduling $n$ independent jobs with release and due times on one machine to minimize the maximum job lateness. For the problem considered, a variable parameter is the number of a special kind of the so-called ``emerging'' jobs. A partial solution without these jobs is constructed in a low degree polynomial time, and an exponential time procedure (in the number of variable parameters) is carried out to augment it to a complete optimal solution. In the alternative time complexity expressions that we derive, the exponential dependence is solely on some job parameters. Applying the fixed parameter analysis to these estimations, a purely polynomial-time dependence is obtained. Both, the intuitive probabilistic estimation and an extensive experimental study support an intuitively evident conjecture that the total number of the variable parameters is far less than $n$. In particular, its ratio to $n$ asymptotically converges to 0.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: This is the old version of the paper that has been substantially modified. Subsequent updates will appear here: arXiv:2211.02107v2

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Combinatorial optimization with bounded subdeterminants
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We take a first step toward a broader study of classical combinatorial optimization problems through the maximum subdeterminants of their standard integer programming formulations, yielding new positive results for several famous (NP-hard) problems. An integer matrix is totally $Δ$-modular if every square submatrix has determinant of absolute value at most $Δ$. For every fixed $Δ$, it has been known that maximum clique, maximum stable set, and minimum vertex cover can be solved in polynomial time on instances for which the coefficient matrix of the natural formulation is totally $Δ$-modular. We extend this list by showing that the same holds for many other problems, including the weighted versions of maximum cut, the traveling salesman problem, feedback vertex set, odd cycle transversal, dominating set, max 2-sat, induced matching, and cluster vertex deletion, as well as for $k$-colorability and graph isomorphism.
  Our proofs reveal several new ways in which bounded subdeterminants impose combinatorial structure: they bound the size or maximum degree of the input graph, bound packings of cycles and other obstructions, or yield decompositions into tractable graph classes such as forests, chordal graphs, graphs of bounded treewidth, and graphs of bounded linear mim-width.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Beyond the First Hit: Towards Tight Guarantees for $k$-means++
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove $R_k\le\frac{1163}{233}+2.108\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge3$ by a computer-assisted argument, and $R_k\le5+2.3139\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge2$ by a short analytic argument; here $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number. Since $H_{k-2}\le1+\ln k$, this lowers the leading coefficient of $\ln k$ from $5$ to $2.108$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$ exactly; both are suprema that are approached but not attained. On the lower side we prove $R_k\ge2(1+H_{k-1})$ for every $k$, and give a second family of lower bounds that is larger than this for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We instead track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit: a cluster left with a large residual cost is likely to be sampled again before it accumulates much of the logarithmic charge, and each repeat repairs it.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 48 pages, 1 figure (3 panels). Exact-arithmetic certificate data and verification code included as ancillary files

Graphics.title: DinoComplete: 3D Shape Completion with Distilled Semantic Priors and State Space Models
Graphics.summary: 3D shape completion from partial scans remains challenging for unseen categories and noisy real-world observations, where geometry alone is often insufficient for inferring missing structure. We present DinoComplete, a deterministic and efficient shape completion framework that augments geometric reconstruction with voxel-aligned semantic priors distilled from DINO features. First, we construct multi-view DINO feature volumes aligned with ShapeNet data and train a student network to predict dense semantic features directly from incomplete shapes. These predicted features capture global structure and part-aware semantic context while remaining aligned with the underlying geometry. We then integrate these distilled features into a completion network, where geometric and semantic voxel representations are fused through voxel state-space modeling. To enable efficient long-range reasoning without sacrificing resolution, we introduce a Multi-Scale Voxel Mamba module that refines the fused features by combining full-grid and chunk-wise sequence modeling. Experiments on unseen ShapeNet categories and ScanNet objects show that DinoComplete achieves competitive completion quality than prior deterministic and generative based completion methods while using relatively fewer parameters, requiring lower memory, and achieving faster inference. Our results demonstrate that distilling semantic priors from visual foundation models improves generalization and robustness in 3D shape completion.

Graphics.title: Spaghetti Splatting: Differentiating Curvilinear Dirac Masses via Convolution
Graphics.summary: In production systems, 3D geometry is represented by primitives such as points, lines, and triangles, as rendering hardware is optimized to generate images from them very efficiently. Learning such primitives from images by volume rendering is challenging, as they are Dirac masses defined at infinitesimal locations in space. EWA splatting, Poisson reconstruction, and 3D Gaussian Splatting overcome this by convolving Dirac masses with a low-frequency kernel, a recipe that generalizes along two axes: the kernel and the primitive. As points and triangles have already received significant attention, we investigate this recipe for curvilinear primitives, and introduce Spaghetti Splatting. We approximate curves by polylines whose convolution converges to that of the continuous curve, and volume render each segment so that connected segments composite without overcounting at their joints. For fast training and inference, we linearize the camera projection per segment, which also accommodates kernels beyond Gaussians, such as Beta kernels. As a point is a curve of zero length, our representation is a strict superset of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It remains competitive with the state-of-the-art on general scenes, outperforms methods specialized to line-like geometry, natively supports anti-aliasing, and produces long connected strands that are directly amenable to physics simulation.

Graphics.title: PL Morse-Cerf Theory for Topological Analysis of Time-Varying Scalar Fields
Graphics.summary: Morse-Cerf theory studies the evolution of critical points in one-parameter families of smooth functions defined on a manifold. This paper describes an adaptation of Morse-Cerf theory of smooth functions to one-parameter families of piecewise-linear (PL) functions. The vertex diagram and Cerf diagram are introduced as topological descriptors that represent evolution of the PL function. The characterization of a crossing in the vertex diagram based on the homology of the lower links of vertices leads to the definition of a topological descriptor for time-varying scalar fields. Algorithms and methods for computing, querying, and comparing Cerf diagrams support its application towards the analysis of time-varying scalar fields. Stability theorems on the comparison measure provide a guarantee of robustness. Experimental results on multiple scientific datasets demonstrate its practical utility.
Graphics.comment: Extended journal version of the previous IEEE VIS 2025 Short Paper, PrePrints https://doi.org/10.1109/VIS60296.2025.00024

Graphics.title: Explicit LOD-Conditioned Anisotropic Filtering for Neural Texture Compression
Graphics.summary: Neural texture compression (NTC) stores material textures compactly, but the dominant feature-pyramid design receives no filtering from the GPU texture unit: it learns each material at a fixed UV and level of detail and has no explicit anisotropic-filtering (AF) mechanism. Setting the filter from the footprint aspect ratio alone is not enough: a single input cannot carry both the shape of the footprint and its size, so the image is too blurry near the camera by the same amount at every distance. Our method, AF-NTC, instead conditions the decoder on the same three bounded values a hardware sampler uses: minor-axis scale (LOD), aspect ratio, and major-axis orientation. These drive a tap line along the major axis and a level blend across the minor axis, and we train against anisotropically filtered ground truth. At $25\%$ of a full BC7 mip chain, AF-NTC beats the no-AF trilinear-BC7 baseline on all ten material--scene pairs we compare ($+1.3$ to $+7.6$\,dB), and it is $0.0$ to $3.4$\,dB below the $4\times$-larger anisotropic-BC7, depending on the material.

Graphics.title: Dynamic Elliptical Graph Factor Models via Riemannian Optimization with Geodesic Temporal Regularization
Graphics.summary: Inferring time-varying graphs from high-dimensional nodal observations is challenging when windows contain fewer samples than nodes, observations are heavy-tailed, and the dependence drifts multiplicatively over time. We propose the dynamic elliptical graph factor model (\textsc{Degfm}), combining: an elliptical likelihood that down-weights outliers; a low-rank-plus-diagonal (LRaD) parameterization of each precision matrix, shown to be the posterior precision of a field conditioned on a few aggregate linear measurements; and a temporal regularizer given by the squared affine-invariant distance between consecutive precision matrices, capturing multiplicative evolution and invariant to node rescaling and to the choice between precision and covariance. Estimation on a product of quotient manifolds is solved by a safeguarded Riemannian conjugate-gradient method with closed-form temporal gradients via generalized eigendecompositions. We prove that (i) LRaD is locally identifiable modulo orthogonal transformations under a tangent-space transversality (coherence) condition; (ii) with rank-preserving Armijo backtracking, the solver is well defined and converges to critical points with $\min_{k<K}\|\grad F(θ^{(k)})\|^2=\mathcal{O}(1/K)$; (iii) a localized estimator obeys a finite-sample oracle inequality whose error scales with the intrinsic dimension $pr+p-r(r-1)/2$ times an effective temporal dimension decreasing from $1$ to $1/T$ as coupling strengthens, quantifying the variance reduction and bias of temporal coupling, and extending to misspecified non-LRaD models; (iv) for Student-$t$ observations, the local restricted strong convexity is proved rather than assumed, with curvature of order $ν/(p+ν)$ shown unimprovable; and (v) partial-correlation graphs are recovered exactly by thresholding. Experiments on synthetic data, S\&P~500 returns, and HCP fMRI data validate the approach.

Graphics.title: X-SiT: Inherently Interpretable Surface Vision Transformers for Dementia Diagnosis
Graphics.summary: Interpretable models are crucial for supporting clinical decision-making, driving advances in their development and application for medical images. However, the nature of 3D volumetric data makes it inherently challenging to visualize and interpret intricate and complex structures like the cerebral cortex. Cortical surface renderings, on the other hand, provide a more accessible and understandable 3D representation of brain anatomy, facilitating visualization and interactive exploration. Motivated by this advantage and the widespread use of surface data for studying neurological disorders, we present the eXplainable Surface Vision Transformer (X-SiT). This is the first inherently interpretable neural network that offers human-understandable predictions based on interpretable cortical features. As part of X-SiT, we introduce a prototypical surface patch decoder for classifying surface patch embeddings, incorporating case-based reasoning with spatially corresponding cortical prototypes. The results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in detecting Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia while additionally providing informative prototypes that align with known disease patterns and reveal classification errors.

Graphics.title: Mitigating SM-Level Load Imbalance in 3D Gaussian Splatting on GPUs
Graphics.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic, real-time rendering on commodity GPUs and is increasingly adopted in generative world models and autonomous driving simulators. However, existing optimizations rely on algorithmic changes that often require retraining, or on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants. In this paper, we identify a fundamental inefficiency in GPU-based 3DGS rendering: severe SM-level load imbalance caused by uneven workloads across screen tiles. This imbalance creates a long execution tail, leaving most SMs idle while a few process computationally intensive tiles, particularly in large-scale urban scenes. To address this, we present a software-defined GPU scheduling approach that mitigates the execution tail. Our approach uses a persistent kernel to schedule heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs. A lightweight per-frame policy determines when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline. Our approach requires neither retraining nor specialized hardware and can be applied orthogonally to existing optimizations across diverse 3DGS variants. Averaged per scene, it accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene, and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.

Graphics.title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation
Graphics.summary: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.

Graphics.title: Real-Time Volumetric Light Transport Inference without a Path
Graphics.summary: We present a real-time method for reconstructing fully integrated pixel radiance in rendered volumetric media under direct and ambient environmental illumination, using compact, low-cost scene features and statistics. Unlike Monte Carlo denoising pipelines for volumetric rendering, which depend on computationally expensive path-traced radiance estimates, our approach directly infers the final light-transport solution from inexpensive primary-ray and environment sample evaluations. We show that these features form a near-sufficient representation of the scene, enabling accurate reconstruction at substantially lower computational cost. Using an attention-augmented image-to-image network, we demonstrate that complete pixel radiance can be inferred directly from these auxiliary features, without requiring the original radiance signal. Operating in image space also provides a more stable computational cost as the camera zooms into or out of the volume, with substantially less dependence on volume density than approaches based on explicit multiple-scattering simulation. We demonstrate real-time performance and high reconstruction accuracy in challenging volumetric cloud scenarios.

Graphics.title: Architectural Textured Proxy Generation
Graphics.summary: Textured proxy models are a fundamental representation for architectural scenes, enabling efficient rendering while preserving visual fidelity. Existing approaches construct such proxies through a sequential pipeline in which geometry is first abstracted from a dense reconstruction and textures are later projected from input images. This geometry-only formulation neglects image evidence during proxy generation, leading to misalignment of structural features such as facades, edges, and their intersections across views. As a result, inconsistencies are deferred to a downstream correction stage during texturing, where the underlying geometric structure can no longer be reliably recovered. In this work, we introduce an image-guided proxy formulation in which proxy generation is jointly constrained by both the dense reconstruction and the input aerial images. By incorporating image derived structural cues directly into the construction process, the proxy is optimized to align with observed features across views from the outset, rather than relying on post hoc correction that may be infeasible. This shift from a geometry-only to an image-guided paradigm produces proxies that are inherently consistent with the input imagery, enabling more accurate geometry and more coherent texture mapping. We realize this formulation through a framework that extracts structural priors from images and dense geometry, and enforces their consistency during proxy optimization. The resulting proxies exhibit improved alignment of structural features, reducing artifacts such as edge duplication, texture drift, and cross view inconsistencies. Experiments on diverse architectural scenes demonstrate that our approach produces compact, geometry texture aligned proxies with substantially improved visual fidelity compared to existing methods.

Graphics.title: A Unified Interactive Framework for Real-Time Three-Dimensional Cellular Automata Simulation in XR
Graphics.summary: Integrating three-dimensional cellular automata (3D CA) into extended reality (XR) requires coordinated simulation, volumetric data management, rendering, and interaction under variable hardware constraints. This paper presents a hybrid study combining a critical review of existing approaches with a unified architecture for real-time 3D CA in XR. The proposed five-layer architecture integrates voxel and rule management, parallel computation, interoperability middleware, visualization, and XR interaction. Its key principles include hardware-aware execution, asynchronous simulation-rendering, adaptive fidelity, and cross-engine interoperability. An analytical evaluation framework is defined to assess performance, latency, scalability, memory efficiency, simulation correctness, and interaction quality. The proposed framework provides a foundation for developing portable and interactive 3D CA systems across desktop and mobile XR platforms.

Operating Systems.title: BunshinRL: Splitting Live Agent Workspaces for Memory-Efficient Agentic RL
Operating Systems.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers.
