BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.

Hardware Architecture.title: Beyond Host-Side Control: HBM Controller Partitioning Across Host and HBM Base Dies
Hardware Architecture.summary: Recent generations of high bandwidth memory (HBM), such as HBM4, allow the base die of the memory stack to be manufactured using a logic process that can accommodate more complex controller functions next to the DRAM. We present the first systematic quantitative study of function-level controller placement between the host and the HBM4 base die on a silicon interposer. We divide the controller into its main functions and evaluate four placements, from a complete host controller to a complete base die controller, with intermediate placements that move maintenance or scheduling to the base die. We extend Ramulator 2 with HBM4 timing and maintenance, model a die-to-die (D2D) link with timing checks at the DRAM interface, and compose area, energy, and temperature from synthesized controller blocks, modeled storage, and interface data. A provisioned D2D link preserves per-stack bandwidth and adds about twice its one-way delay to unloaded latency. Maintenance moves to the base die with no bandwidth cost and frees host command slots, and the freed share grows with stack height. Replacing the wide interface with a D2D link saves 61% of host shoreline and 16.85 mm2 of host area per stack. The D2D link dominates the added base die area and power, and the base die runs cooler under streaming with link energy below 0.4 pJ/bit. Shared control delivers up to 1.72x the throughput of static partitioning between two requestors.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Accepted to IEEE International 3D Systems Integration Conference (3DIC)

Hardware Architecture.title: Augur: An Online Learning-based Hardware Data Prefetcher using Reservoir Computing
Hardware Architecture.summary: Machine-learning-based hardware prefetchers can learn complex access patterns, but practical deployment demands online adaptation, low-latency inference, and modest hardware cost. We present Augur, a hardware delta prefetcher based on next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC) that meets all three requirements. Augur formulates delta prediction as a history-based regression problem. It constructs a fixed-size reservoir from hashed delta features over a short context window and predicts the next delta using a single dot product. The model is updated online via one-step SGD and requires no offline pre-training, no workload-specific tuning, and no floating-point arithmetic. A key technical insight makes this practical: replacing the integer multiplications traditionally used to generate nonlinear reservoir features with bitwise AND operations removes all feature-generation multipliers while preserving the joint context encoded in hash-derived features. Because Augur regresses a continuous delta rather than classifying into a fixed action set, it can predict any delta in [-64, 63]. Augur pairs the reservoir with a simple Markov-based delta predictor for simple delta patterns and employs multi-layered filtering and adaptive lookahead to suppress wasteful prefetches. Evaluated on 169 traces spanning GAP, Ligra, PARSEC, SPEC CPU 2006, SPEC CPU 2017, and AI workloads, Augur outperforms the state-of-the-art ML-based delta prefetcher by 2.9%, 4.5%, and 5.3% in geomean speedup on 1-, 4-, and 8-core systems, respectively, while achieving ~2x higher prefetch accuracy and 37.8% fewer overpredictions. Augur is practical to implement at 35 KB storage, 0.32 sq. mm area, and 32.7 mW in 12 nm.

Hardware Architecture.title: Bit-level Perceptron Prediction for Indirect Branches
Hardware Architecture.summary: Modern software uses indirect branches for various purposes including, but not limited to, virtual method dispatch and implementation of switch statements. Because an indirect branch's target address cannot be determined prior to execution, high-performance processors depend on highly-accurate indirect branch prediction techniques to mitigate control hazards. This paper proposes a new indirect branch prediction scheme that predicts target addresses at the bit level. Using a series of perceptron-based predictors, our predictor predicts individual branch target address bits based on correlations within branch history. Our evaluations show this new branch target predictor is competitive with state-of-the-art branch target predictors at an equivalent hardware budget. For instance, over a set of workloads including SPEC and mobile applications, our predictor achieves a misprediction rate of 0.183 mispredictions per 1000 instructions, compared with 0.193 for the state-of-the-art ITTAGE predictor and 0.29 for a VPC-based indirect predictor.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Author manuscript of Proceedings of the 46th International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA '19), pp. 27-38 (2019). 12 manuscript pages plus publication-notice page

Hardware Architecture.title: AutoC2V: Synthesis-Guided LLM Training for QoR-Optimized C++-to-Verilog Generation
Hardware Architecture.summary: High-level synthesis (HLS) can translate C/C++ kernels into register-transfer level (RTL) designs, yet generating high-quality hardware still relies heavily on manual pragma tuning and repeated synthesis evaluation. We propose AutoC2V, a C++-to-Verilog generation framework driven by real synthesis feedback that enables large language models (LLMs) to directly generate RTL with improved quality of results (QoR) from synthesizable C++ kernels. We construct training data from real synthesis results, including synthesizable C++ source code, the corresponding Verilog RTL, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives. Using this dataset, we align the model toward synthesis-aware RTL generation through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To reduce the high cost of repeatedly invoking real synthesis during GRPO, we design the QoR Prediction Reward Model (QoR RM), which predicts latency and resource metrics by encoding RTL into long-context semantic representations, thereby providing low-cost and continuous QoR reward signals for policy optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoC2V not only substantially improves RTL functional pass rates, but also achieves superior latency and resource optimization compared to the unfine-tuned base model, representative HLS optimization approaches (HLSPilot, LLM-DSE, and AutoDSE), and advanced general-purpose commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek v4 Pro, and GLM-5.2). These results indicate that combining real synthesis data with efficient QoR reward modeling can further improve the ability of LLMs to generate high-quality RTL.

Hardware Architecture.title: RTLREX: LLM-Guided Framework for Exact High-Level RTL Recovery
Hardware Architecture.summary: Hardware designs may be available only as gate-level netlists or input-output descriptions when the original register-transfer-level (RTL) design and documentation are not accessible. Low-level representations obscure word-level computation and its finite-width behavior. Recovering high-level RTL from such representations therefore helps engineers understand a circuit's functionality and enables RTL rewriting and resynthesis. A plausible function model is also insufficient unless the generated RTL is equivalent to the original circuit for all input combinations. In this paper, we present RTLREX, a large language model (LLM)-guided framework that coordinates domain-specific tools for function recovery, RTL generation, independent verification, and cost-guided rewriting. Independent verification establishes equivalence between the recovered RTL and the original circuit. The LLM uses tool feedback to select further analyses, revise candidate RTL, and propose syntax-cost reductions. Experiments on 30 benchmarks from Problem A of the ICCAD 2022 CAD Contest show that RTLREX recovers equivalent high-level RTL for all benchmarks, surpassing the state-of-the-art method WolFEx in recovery coverage. On benchmarks recovered by both methods, RTLREX reduces mean syntax cost by 20.5% relative to WolFEx. On complete truth-table benchmarks from the IWLS 2026 Contest, our framework reduces mean syntax cost by 95.7% relative to an LLM agent baseline on the benchmarks validated by both methods.

Hardware Architecture.title: Fixed-Capacity Causal Models with Parallel Recovery for GPU Lossless Compression
Hardware Architecture.summary: GPU lossless compression requires both compact complete frames and fast checked recovery. We evaluate fixed-capacity causal byte-bank representations under a shared 512-row probability budget, select a single representation via a pre-payload complete-cost proxy charging both empirical cross-entropy and compressed model tables, and align two rANS states per 8\,KiB chunk with the causal byte banks. Independent byte banks decode concurrently, whereas intra-word conditional banks decode in two ordered phases. On ten structured imaging and electrophysiology inputs, split-bank execution lowers aggregate median encode-plus-recovery time by 13.10\% for 0.18\% additional frame bytes, and reduces complete encoding cost by 44.16\% relative to a matched native-CPU model control while supporting a standalone CUDA-free CPU receiver. In a twelve-configuration GPU comparison, Split GPX produces 5.75\% and 7.11\% smaller complete frames than Zigshuffle + nvCOMP Zstd at 35.14\% and 19.03\% lower paired cost for 64\,KiB and 8\,KiB requests. For multi-channel sample-interleaved waveforms, extending causal differencing with zero-oracle GPU stride screening (strided-residual) reduces holdout 12-lead PTB Diagnostic ECG frames by 49.89\% (from 71.47\% to 35.81\% of raw bytes, 37.20\% smaller than Zigshuffle + Zstd-1 and 46.67\% smaller than OpenZL-9) while preserving byte parity across all single-stream benchmarks.

Hardware Architecture.title: PENSA: A Spatial Accelerator for BitNet b1.58 Inference on an HBM-equipped AMD Alveo FPGA
Hardware Architecture.summary: Ternary large language models (tLLMs) replace general multiplication in dominant linear layers with sign-controlled accumulation, shifting hardware bottlenecks toward packed-weight delivery, reduction, and operator occupancy. PENSA is an end-to-end FPGA accelerator for the BitNet b1.58 2B4T model on an AMD Alveo U50. Two row-partitioned ternary matrix engines consume packed TQ1_0 weights from eight independent high-bandwidth memory (HBM) pseudo-channels, each processing 1,280 ternary weights per cycle through sign selection and integer reduction. The sequencer, attention, and vocabulary-projection units remain resident on the FPGA, while two-stream interleaved scheduling overlaps sequences across the persistent pipeline to form the Penta-Unit. At 104.1~MHz, PENSA achieves 58.09 tok/s at context 128 and 24.60 tok/s at context 2048, corresponding to 2.14-3.14$\times$ the throughput of a same-model Xeon E-2356G baseline. The resulting system demonstrates end-to-end FPGA execution of 2B-scale BitNet topology without modifying its model structure.

Hardware Architecture.title: TsetlinKWS: A 65nm 16.58uW, 0.63mm2 State-Driven Convolutional Tsetlin Machine-Based Accelerator For Keyword Spotting
Hardware Architecture.summary: The Tsetlin Machine (TM) has recently attracted attention as a low-power alternative to neural networks due to its simple and interpretable inference mechanisms. However, its performance on speech-related tasks remains limited. This paper proposes TsetlinKWS, the first algorithm-hardware co-design framework for the Convolutional Tsetlin Machine (CTM) on the 12-keyword spotting task. Firstly, we introduce a novel Mel-Frequency Spectral Coefficient and Spectral Flux (MFSC-SF) feature extraction scheme together with spectral convolution, achieving a record-high accuracy of 87.35% for TM-based models on the 12-keyword spotting task. Secondly, we develop an Optimized Grouped Block-Compressed Sparse Row (OG-BCSR) algorithm that delivers a remarkable 9.84$\times$ reduction in model size, significantly improving the storage efficiency of CTMs. Finally, we propose a state-driven architecture tailored for CTMs, which simultaneously exploits data reuse and sparsity to attain high energy efficiency. The full system is evaluated in 65 nm process technology, consuming 16.58 $μ$W at 0.7 V with a compact 0.63 mm$^2$ core area. TsetlinKWS demonstrates a Power-Performance-Area (PPA) product of 60.2 and requires only 907k logic operations per inference, corresponding to 1.4$\times$ and 10$\times$ reductions, respectively, compared with state-of-the-art KWS accelerators. These results position the CTM as a highly efficient candidate for ultra-low-power speech applications.

Hardware Architecture.title: EmbodiedIntentBench: Benchmarking Intent-Driven Runtime Adaptation for Mobile Robotic Missions
Hardware Architecture.summary: Mobile robotic sensing systems must adapt to operator requirements, limited resources, changing connectivity, and observation opportunities shaped by physical motion. Evaluating runtime strategies therefore requires assessing whether their decisions fulfill mission objectives, beyond isolated perception accuracy or execution efficiency. We present EmbodiedIntentBench, a benchmark for intent-driven runtime adaptation in mobile robotic missions. It represents mission intent through structured contracts for coverage, temporal evidence, reporting, urgency, and resources, and couples simulated unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) workloads with causal, resource-accounted execution. Computation decisions affect mission time, resource use, and which observations can contribute evidence. We evaluate fixed and adaptive perception strategies in multi-phase missions and under changing urgency, connectivity, and battery conditions. In the multi-phase Depot study, a configuration with 87.5% full-bank target recall across visible target observations completes only 1 of 16 missions, whereas a lower-recall configuration completes 14. In an ablation, ignoring execution-induced observation loss increases aggregate mission success and reverses the ordering of two runtime strategies. Replays using Jetson AGX Orin CPU and GPU profiles change the relative success of local and remote strategies. In selected Jetson GPU-profile replays, intent-driven adaptation reduces modeled task energy by up to 28% with unchanged mission success. EmbodiedIntentBench provides an extensible framework for evaluating runtime decisions against mission fulfillment under physical and resource constraints.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Paper is currently under review. Authors' version posted for personal use and not for redistribution

Hardware Architecture.title: Embedded Blockchain Infrastructure Management (eBIM): A RISC-V-Empowered Hardware--Software Co-Design Framework Towards Trustworthy Blockchain
Hardware Architecture.summary: Blockchain systems are shifting from decentralized ledgers for digital assets to general-purpose trust infrastructures for verifiable computation, decentralized physical resources, and automated infrastructure management. However, deploying these systems through third-party Blockchain-as-a-Service (BaaS) offerings may introduce dependencies involving operational control, confidentiality, and infrastructure governance. Meanwhile, blockchain execution and verification impose demanding requirements on cryptographic processing, isolation, and reproducibility. RISC-V offers an open, extensible instruction set architecture that enables co-design of software execution environments and domain-specific security hardware. Inspired by the embedded identity and provisioning model of an embedded subscriber identity module (eSIM), this survey proposes embedded Blockchain infrastructure management (eBIM) as a conceptual hardware-software co-design framework that organizes existing RISC-V-enabled technologies into a hardware-anchored blockchain infrastructure stack. We systematically review RISC-V-based smart-contract execution, trusted execution environments, zero-knowledge virtual machines, and cryptographic acceleration, and analyze their relationship to blockchain requirements, including deterministic execution, verifiability, extensibility, and secure key management. Based on this evidence, we distinguish currently demonstrated capabilities from the proposed eBIM integration vision and identify major open challenges, including system-level benchmarking, blockchain-oriented cryptographic extensions, TEE security, post-quantum migration, and deployable hardware-software co-design. The survey provides an architectural reference for researchers and designers investigating open and verifiable blockchain infrastructure.

Programming Languages.title: A Calculus for Units of Measure with Conversion
Programming Languages.summary:
Programs that compute with physical quantities often need to convert between units of measurement, and as the Mars Climate Orbiter showed, these conversions can be a rich source of errors. Meanwhile, typed unit calculi, our most rigorous formalisms for checking physical units in a program, have excluded unit conversions. Through this exclusion, they have established a powerful property: well-typed programs are invariant under rescaling (no program can depend on how big a meter is). But losing the ability to convert between units is a significant cost. In contrast, practical languages provide conversion but no invariance theorem. We present $Λ_S$, a typed lambda calculus with conversion, quantification over units and dimensions, and vectors and linear maps with per-component units, and we determine exactly how much invariance survives conversion. For terms without unit constants we prove two abstraction theorems: (i) a convert-free term is invariant under every rescaling; (ii) a term with conversions is invariant under every rescaling that scales all units of one dimension by the same factor. The condition in (ii) cannot be weakened: under any other rescaling, some conversion of a nonzero value is not invariant.
  For first-order programs, a verified decision procedure returns one of three verdicts: it certifies that no error in the declared conversion factors can change the program's answer, names the accumulated ratio through which such an error would scale it, or declines. A verified checker decides whether unit declarations are consistent and determine every conversion factor, and extracts each factor exactly. We also prove adequacy, erasure, and the $n$-variable Pi theorem of dimensional analysis with conversion. Every theorem is mechanized in Lean 4, and the evaluator compiles to a native binary.

Programming Languages.title: Representing Tensors as Compositions for Efficient Computation on Sparse and Structured Data
Programming Languages.summary: We propose a new mathematical formalism in which all kinds of tensors and of operations on those tensors are represented as simple function compositions. Tensors are functions from indices to values. An element-wise operation (e.g. an activation function) is a composition with a function applied to values; re-indexing (e.g. reshape, transposition) is a composition with a function applied to indices; and a reduction is a composition with both an index function, mapping each index to several indices, and a reduction operation (e.g. product, sum, max). Combined with tensor stacking, these compositions can represent most interesting kinds of tensors (e.g. dense, jagged, all kinds of sparsity patterns, matrix factorizations), as well as lazy versions of almost every operation available in modern tensor computation frameworks, including einsums between tensors of any kind. Identities between compositions can then be used to rewrite such expressions into equivalent ones, without evaluating them. For instance, the product of two sparse matrices can be rewritten so that only products between non-zero values are computed, turning a sparse problem into a dense one. Using this algebra as the intermediate representation of a tensor computation engine would shift the focus from defining operations on tensors (e.g. einsum between sparse tensors) to defining an algebra on index functions. This should reduce the codebase complexity from $\mathcal{O}(mn^2)$, with $m$ the number of binary operations between tensors and $n$ the number of tensor types, to $\mathcal{O}(m + k^2)$, with $k$ the number of types of index functions. A draft implementation of a tensor computation framework based on this algebra is publicly available.

Programming Languages.title: For Generalised Algebraic Theories, Two Sorts Are Enough
Programming Languages.summary:
Generalised algebraic theories (GATs) allow multiple sorts indexed over each other. For example, the theories of categories or Martin-L{ö}f type theories form GATs. Categories have two sorts, objects and morphisms, and the latter are double-indexed over the former. Martin-L{ö}f type theory has four sorts: contexts, substitutions, types and terms. For example, types are indexed over contexts, and terms are indexed over both contexts and types. In this paper we show that any GAT can be reduced to a GAT with only two sorts, and there is a section-retraction correspondence (formally, a strict coreflection) between models of the original and the reduced GAT. In particular, any model of the original GAT can be turned into a model of the reduced (two-sorted) GAT and back, and this roundtrip is the identity.
  The reduced GAT is simpler than the original GAT in the following aspects: it does not have sort equalities; it does not have interleaved sorts and operations; if the original GAT did not have interleaved sorts and operations, then the reduced GAT won't have operations interleaved between different sorts. In a type-theoretic metatheory, the initial algebra of a GAT is called a quotient inductive-inductive type (QIIT). Our reduction provides a way to implement QIITs with sort equalities or interleaved constructors which are not allowed by Cubical Agda. An instance of our reduction is the well-known method of reducing mutual inductive types to a single indexed family. Our approach is semantic in that it does not rely on a syntactic description of GATs, but instead, on Uemura's bi-initial characterisation of the category of (finite) GATs in the 2-category of finitely complete categories with a chosen exponentiable morphism.

Programming Languages.title: Lipschitz-Based Robustness Certification Under Floating-Point Execution
Programming Languages.summary:
Lipschitz-based certification checks a neural network's robustness with a small numerical computation: milliseconds per input, and small enough to be formally verified. Its soundness is proved for execution in real arithmetic, whereas deployed networks execute in floating point, so rounding must be accounted for in the network and in the certifier itself.
  We show that the conservatism of Lipschitz-based certification does not absorb the rounding in the network's execution: we exhibit counterexamples to a formally verified real-arithmetic certifier that computes in exact arithmetic, and show that an adversary who controls the weights can make it issue false certificates for ordinary test images at standard perturbation bounds. We present the first Lipschitz-based certification method that is both efficient and sound with respect to floating-point execution. It keeps the real-arithmetic network's Lipschitz constant and bounds separately how far the floating-point outputs can depart from the real-arithmetic ones, through a compositional theory of the deviation that also rules out overflow; pre-deployment measurements of a high-precision execution tighten the bound. Its spectral norms come from a float64 Gram iteration proved never to under-estimate the true norm.
  We mechanise the theory in Rocq and implement it in a certifier, evaluated on dense image, tabular and many-class classifiers. It rejects every certificate a counterexample refutes and certifies entire test sets at milliseconds per instance on a CPU, losing relatively few real-arithmetic certificates, many of which the measurement reclaims. At float32, ERAN's GPUPoly, to our knowledge the only other public floating-point-sound verifier for networks of our size, loses most of its certificates on most of our models to its own rounding accounting; ours does not, and is more than an order of magnitude faster.

Programming Languages.title: Language-Based Agent Control
Programming Languages.summary: This paper introduces language-based agent control (LBAC), a new programming model for agentic applications that brings techniques from programming languages and language-based security to the problem of agent control. In conventional programming, combinations of static typing and runtime enforcement have long been used to guarantee that well-typed programs satisfy user-specified policies, including policies for access control, information flow, data provenance, and more. The key idea behind LBAC is to extend these guarantees to agentic applications by requiring agents to generate programs that are themselves well-typed in the context of the surrounding scaffolding code. Unsafe programs are rejected by the typechecker before execution, allowing policies to apply uniformly across the entire application, including both agent-generated behavior and developer-written scaffolding. At the same time, LBAC preserves substantial expressiveness: agents may perform arbitrary side-effect-free computation and recursively invoke subagents, which retain full tool access subject to the same--or potentially more restrictive--policies. We demonstrate LBAC with three case studies: I/O sandboxing via filesystem capabilities, data provenance, and information-flow control.

Programming Languages.title: Crustify: Repository-Level Generation of Safe Rust Bindings with LLM Agents and Coverage-Guided Testing
Programming Languages.summary:
Wrapping C code in a safe Rust interface lets Rust applications use it without writing unsafe code, until the code itself is migrated to Rust. Such bindings are tedious and error-prone to write, however: their internals use unsafe code that the Rust compiler does not check, so a single mistake can introduce undefined behavior (UB), and they have so far been written mostly by hand.
  We present Crustify, an agentic co-translator that generates safe Rust bindings for repository-level C libraries. Crustify schedules a target's types and symbols into dependency-ordered waves of independent batches that agents bind concurrently. Its agents derive the ownership and lifecycle contract of every pointer and type they wrap, check each binding with coverage-guided equivalence and UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, and review every wave. They build on three tools that we contribute: (a) ffibox, Rust primitives for C/Rust interop that mirror Box, Arc, and Vec for C objects without ever forming a reference to memory that C may alias; (b) Wavefront, a neuro-symbolic static analyzer that orders a target's items by their dependencies, including those that casts and type-erased pointers hide; and (c) ffimap, a rustc-based analysis that maps the unsafe surface of bindings.
  On libgit2 and ffmpeg, with one developer in the loop, Crustify generated safe bindings for 41.9% and 42.8% of their public APIs in about 51.9 and 58.9 hours. On the interface consumers are expected to use, only 1.6% and 0.4% of the bindings' public functions are unsafe, and only 0.1% and 0.6% have a raw pointer in their signature. Their tests cover 98.92% and 99.07% of the Rust code and 45.95% and 67.20% of libgit2 and of ffmpeg's libavutil, and the reviewers fixed 8 and 13 defects that caused UB reachable from Rust. To our knowledge, this is the first work to automate the generation of safe Rust bindings for C libraries.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Solving Large Rubik's Cubes within a Factor of $2.37+o(1)$ of Optimal
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We design optimized algorithms to solve the $n \times n \times n$ Rubik's Cube within $30.5 n^2 / \lg n + o(n^2 / \lg n)$ moves. This upper bound is asymptotically within a factor of $2.37$ of the known lower bound, which applies to almost all instances. The constant $30.5$ is also the first explicit constant factor for the known upper bound of $O(n^2 / \lg n)$, where the implicit constant of the previous algorithm was $1.01 \cdot 10^{40}$ (ten duodecillion). Thus we improve the upper-bound constant by a factor of more than $3.30 \cdot 10^{38}$ (330 undecillion). Our algorithm runs in time linear in the input size $N = Θ(n^2)$, and uses $O(\sqrt{N} \lg N)$ extra space (beyond the state of the cube). Our implementation is the first practical cube solver to generate solutions of length $O(n^2/\lg n)$. Our latest solver outperforms existing solvers for $n$ as small as $840$.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 41 pages, 18 figures, 16 tables. Project page: https://largecubebench.org

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Hadamard Flattening and Gaussian Pooling Sketch for Least Squares with Coordinate-wise Guarantee
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Randomized sketch-and-solve algorithms accelerate overconstrained $\ell_2$ regression by replacing the input with a much smaller, randomly projected problem. While standard subspace embeddings nearly preserve the regression cost, coordinate-wise accuracy is more delicate: rather than the objective value, we want the solution vector itself to be close to the optimum in $\ell_\infty$ norm. Specifically, we seek $x'\in\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\|x'-x^\star\|_\infty\leq\fracε{\sqrt d}\|Ax^\star-b\|_2\|A^\dagger\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ is the design matrix, $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$ the label vector, $x^\star$ the optimal solution and $A^\dagger$ the pseudo-inverse of $A$. Price, Song and Woodruff introduced this problem and claimed that the subsampled randomized Hadamard transform (SRHT) with $O(ε^{-2}d^{1+Θ(\sqrt{\log\log n/\log d})})$ rows achieves this guarantee; we point out a gap in the proof. Song, Ye, Yin and Zhang later claimed $O(ε^{-2}d\log^3 n)$ rows, but their proof relies on an independence assumption that does not hold in general, and we exhibit an explicit instance on which it fails.
  To achieve a truly nearly-linear-in-$d$ row count, we introduce a new fast, dense randomized transform combining a randomized Hadamard flattening, a random permutation, and balanced, disjoint Gaussian pooling. Conditioned on the Hadamard-and-permutation stage, the sketched problem becomes an exact Gaussian regression whose noise is independent of the entire sketched design, exactly what Song, Ye, Yin and Zhang's argument was missing. Our sketch yields the $\ell_\infty$ guarantee with $m=O(ε^{-2}d\log d)$ rows, using one Hadamard pass with padded internal dimension $N=\widetilde{O}(n+ε^{-2}d^3)$. It is also efficient to apply: $(SA,Sb)$ can be computed in $O(Nd\log N)=\widetilde{O}(nd+ε^{-2}d^4)$ time.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Improve presentation and add more discussions on prior work. Abstract shortened to meet arxiv requirement

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Sublinear Time Quantum Sensitivity Sampling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We present a unified quantum sensitivity sampling framework that streamlines coreset construction for many classical approximation problems, significantly speeding up clustering, regression, and low-rank approximation. We assume $n,d\geq\mathrm{poly}(k/ε)$ and, for regression, $n\geq\mathrm{poly}(d)$:
  - $k$-median/$k$-means: For $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we build an $ε$-coreset of input points of size $\tilde O(k^{4/3}ε^{-2})$ (resp. $\tilde O(k^{3/2}ε^{-2})$) in time $\tilde O(ε^{-1}n^{0.5}dk^{1.67})$ (resp. $\tilde O(ε^{-1}n^{0.5}dk^{1.75})$). Our better $d$- and linear $1/ε$-dependence improve on [Xue, Chen, Li and Jiang, ICML'23] for $d\geqΩ(k^{7/3})$ (resp. $Ω(k^{2.5})$).
  - $\ell_p$ regression: For $\min_x\|Ax-b\|_p$, $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, we build an $ε$-coreset of size $\tilde O_p(d^{\max\{1,p/2\}}ε^{-2})$ in time $\tilde O_p(n^{0.5}d^{1.5}ε^{-1})$ for $p\leq 2$ and $\tilde O_p(n^{0.5}d^{p/4+1}(ε^{-1}+d^{0.5}))$ for $p>2$, matching [Liu and Ji, ICML'26] for $p\leq 2$ and improving on the prior best quantum sampling approach [Apers and Gribling, SICOMP'26] for all $p>2$.
  - Low-rank approximation: We give the first quantum sublinear-time algorithm for Frobenius-norm rank-$k$ approximation of $A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ free of data-dependent parameters, running in $\tilde O(n^{0.5}dk^{0.5}ε^{-0.5})$ time with factored output (plus $\tilde O(nk^2ε^{-2})$ to materialize them). We also give sublinear algorithms for kernel and tensor variants.
  - Lower bound: For generic sensitivity sampling with total sensitivity $S$, any quantum algorithm outputting an $ε$-coreset of size $o(\sqrt{nS})$ needs $Ω(\sqrt{nS})$ queries, so our query complexity is optimal up to $\mathrm{poly}(ε^{-1},\log n)$ and VC-dimension factors.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: NeurIPS 2026, abstract shortened to meet arxiv requirement

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tunnels: Compressing the Solution Subgraph of Regular Path Queries
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Regular path queries (RPQs) are increasingly expected to return the paths that match them, not only their endpoints. Since the number of matching paths can be exponential or infinite, a standard way to deliver them (PMR) is the subgraph $\Hs$ of the product between the graph and the query automaton that contains exactly the nodes lying on some solution path. We show that $\Hs$ can be compressed much further when the graph is available to the decoder: most of $\Hs$ can be regenerated by re-running small parts of the traversal, and only the places where the traversal would waste significant effort on dead branches need to be stored. We formalize this as \emph{tunnels}: regions of $\Hs$ that are re-expanded from a stored entry point with a bounded amount of extra work, either an absolute budget or one proportional to the output produced. We handle the three classes of RPQs: constant-to-variable, constant-to-constant, and variable-to-variable. In the latter, we study the combination of tunnels with cutting the query at a selective articulation point of the automaton and encoding the answer as a union of Cartesian products of leftward and rightward traversals. Our experimental results show improvements of 2 to 3 orders of magnitude over the baseline space of PMR, for an acceptable increase in traversal time.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Asymptotic Bounds on the Size of Order Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Order graphs were introduced by Arroyuelo et al.\ (TODS 2024) as a generalization of the ring index, to support worst-case optimal joins on relations of arity $d$ while storing few columns: the index stores one column per edge, so its size is proportional to the number of edges of an order graph. It was known that the minimum number of edges lies between $Ω(2^d\sqrt d)$ and $O(2^d d)$, and the lower bound had been claimed to be $42$ for $d=6$. We first exhibit an optimal order graph with only $40$ edges for $d=6$, and show that the proof of that lower bound holds only for unions of cycles, whereas order graphs can be smaller than the smallest set of cycles. We give a corrected statement and proof that holds for every order graph: there must be at least $\max_m\binom dm\lceil m/2\rceil$ edges. This bound is $40$ (hence tight) for $d=6$. We then settle the asymptotic question: the minimum size is $Θ(2^d\sqrt d)$. This is obtained via an explicit construction, based on symmetric chain decompositions of the Boolean lattice, with at most $(d-1)\binom{d}{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}+2^d$ edges. The upper bound is within a factor $4+O(d^{-1/2})$ of the lower bound, and both numerically and asymptotically better than trie switching. Finally, we cast the problem as a set cover with connectivity constraints, which yields an exact ILP formulation and a greedy heuristic. With them we find optimal order graphs for $d\le 6$ in the bidirectional and for $d \le 7$ in the unidirectional model, showing that our lower bounds are tight there, and improve the best known order graphs for $d=7$ and $8$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Improved Algorithm for Quantified Boolean Formulas
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Quantified Boolean formula (QBF), the quantified version of Boolean satisfiability (SAT), is a fundamental problem in constraint solving. Due to the $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete nature of QBF, designing theoretically efficient QBF algorithms is much harder and receives less attention in academia. In this work, we present a new algorithm based on memoized search, which solves QBF with $n$ variables and $m$ clauses in $1.685^m\cdot\text{poly}(n)$ time and space. This is the first improvement over the $1.709^m\cdot\text{poly}(n)$ bound by Williams in over 20 years. Our technique is based on the minimum vertex cover of the conflict graphs, which was proposed to study the parameterized complexity of SAT. We extend this idea to QBF and further show that QBF is slicewise polynomial-time solvable using this parameter.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Simple Computer-Assisted Proof of the 5/6-Bound for Real-Period Pinwheel Scheduling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In pinwheel scheduling with real periods, an instance consists of $n$ tasks with real periods $1\le a_1\le a_2\le\cdots\le a_n$. The goal is to find a schedule that assigns one task to each day indefinitely such that, for every task $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and every positive integer $\ell$, task $i$ occurs at least $\ell$ times in every block of $\lceil\ell a_i\rceil$ consecutive days. Given an instance $(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n)$, its dimension is $n$, its density is $\sum_{i=1}^n1/a_i$, and its potential is $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}1/a_i$. We prove that every real-valued instance of density at most 5/6 admits a periodic schedule of period length less than $4\cdot2^n$. For integer periods, the 5/6 density bound was a long-standing conjecture settled by Kawamura using a computer-assisted proof [STOC 2024, PNAS 2026]. Our result confirms the real-period conjecture of Fujiwara, Miyagi, and Ouchi [DMTCS 2026]. Our computer-assisted proof builds on Kawamura's ideas while using fewer explicit schedules. It combines dimension reduction by folding with nine satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) checks over linear real arithmetic. A set of 14287 explicit periodic schedules contains a schedule for every instance of dimension at most 8 and density at most 5/6, and for every instance of dimension 9 and potential at most 5/6. Folding is used to reduce every instance of larger dimension and potential at most 5/6 to an instance of dimension 9 and the same potential bound. We also prove that every real-valued instance with minimum period at least 4 and density at most 17/20=0.85 admits a periodic schedule of period length less than $19\cdot2^n$. The density bound 17/20 is tight and improves the 0.84-bound of Mishra, Rho, and Kleinberg [arXiv 2025] for integer periods. It also resolves the $a_1=4$ case of Kawamura's 2025 conjecture that integer-valued instances of density at most $1-(a_1-1)/(a_1(a_1+1))$ are schedulable.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Online Interval Selection with Binary Predictions: Optimal Consistency and a Continuous Robustness Tradeoff
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study online interval selection with binary predictions of membership in a final optimal solution. Requests arrive in arbitrary order; accepted requests may be revoked, but rejected or revoked requests cannot be recovered. With rewards proportional to interval length, the best consistency under finite strict robustness is $d=(3+\sqrt5)/2$ when both guarantees hold almost surely on each fixed input, including for randomized algorithms. A continuous lower bound forces consistency strictly above $d$ at every robustness budget below $4\varphi+3\approx9.472$, whereas our deterministic algorithm attains $d$ with exact robustness $\varphi^5\approx11.090$, where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. Each held interval inherits a ledger recording positive prediction mass lost through irrevocable decisions. Tuning the replacement costs and both special thresholds gives a continuous family with exact consistency throughout and exact robustness on two parameter intervals, including $(C,R)=(25/9,10)$ and $(4,7)$. Randomization permits expected consistency approaching one with finite expected robustness, whereas almost-sure robustness forces expected consistency strictly above two at every finite budget.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 45 pages, 4 figures. Streamlined appendix and clarified proof sketches and advice diagnostics. Includes ancillary evidence tables. Extended diagnostics remain available in v1

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Close and Sort: Exact Maximum-Likelihood Aggregation of Cyclic Rank-Two Preferences
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Pairwise probabilities arise in rank aggregation, recommendation, and human or LLM evaluation, yet converting them into a maximum-likelihood list is a weighted Kemeny problem and is NP-hard in general. Known exact algorithms for rank-two tournaments use only comparison signs and do not optimize this likelihood. We show that the weighted problem is exactly solvable when the skew-symmetric log-odds matrix $W_{ij}=\log(p_{ij}/p_{ji})$ has rank two, including when the induced preferences contain cycles. Writing $W_{ij}=\det(h_i,h_j)$ and adding the closing vector $h_0=-\sum_i h_i$ turns the objective into twice the signed area of a closed polygon. This geometry yields CloseSort, which polar-sorts the $n+1$ edge vectors, cuts after $h_0$, and returns a global maximum-likelihood order in $O(n\log n)$ time from the factors. The same geometry identifies the runner-up and gives a stability certificate beyond exact rank two. When the smallest determinant $δ$ of two consecutive edges in the closed angular cycle is positive, it is exactly the best-to-runner-up log-likelihood gap. For $W=W_0+E$, the CloseSort order of $W_0$ has regret at most $\sum_{i<j}|E_{ij}|$ on $W$ and remains optimal whenever this sum is below $δ$, a worst-case tight threshold. In 5,120 determinant-logit simulations, increasing the observations per pair from 4 to 64 raises the fraction on which rank-two projection outperforms the empirical plug-in optimum from 68.6% to 85.7%. On 3,600 Arena-Hard LLM-judge profiles drawn from 63 systems and ten judges, the leading rank-two component captures 89.2% of the log-odds energy. On profiles containing a directed majority triangle, CloseSort reduces normalized regret by 44% relative to Borda and improves the mean normalized objective over each of eight baselines. With factors supplied, it is 8,407 times faster than exact dynamic programming on 18-item rankings.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 20th ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining (WSDM 2027). Code: https://github.com/sarinstein-yan/close-and-sort

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Smoothed Score Queries and the Complexity of Sampling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the query complexity of sampling from high-dimensional Gaussian distributions using gradient information. In the standard oracle model, exact gradients expose only matrix-vector products with the precision matrix, leading to polynomial approximation barriers and a characteristic $\sqrtκ$ dependence on the known spectral range. We show that this barrier disappears when the sampler is allowed to query smoothed scores, namely gradients of the logarithms of the Gaussian-convolved densities. For a centered Gaussian target with precision matrix $Λ$, a smoothed-score query at noise level $τ$ gives access to the resolvent $(Λ+τ^{-1}I)^{-1}$. Combining geometrically spaced noise levels with sinc-quadrature rational approximation, we obtain a sampler with $q=O((\logκ+\log(e\sqrt d/δ_{\rm TV}))\log(e\sqrt d/δ_{\rm TV}))$ smoothed-score queries for total variation error $δ_{\rm TV}$, improving the condition-number dependence from $\sqrtκ$ to logarithmic. We also study finite-bit gradient oracles. Using coordinatewise quantization of the transformed smoothed-score answers and a final dithering step, we obtain a sampling scheme whose total communicated gradient information is polylogarithmic in $κ$; in particular, for fixed dimension and accuracy, the bit complexity is $O(\log^2κ)$. To complement these upper bounds, we introduce a channel-synthesis, or reverse-Shannon, converse technique for sampling lower bounds. This converts total-variation simulation guarantees into communication requirements and yields an $Ω(d\logκ)$ bit lower bound for $d\ge2$ and fixed total variation error below one, as $κ\to\infty$. Together, these results identify smoothed scores as a provably more informative oracle for sampling and give nearly matching upper and lower bounds for its finite-bit complexity.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Lower Bounds Above $\sqrt{3}$ for Online Makespan Minimization on Four Identical Machines
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
For deterministic online makespan minimization, $m = 4$ identical machines is the smallest case whose optimal competitive ratio is open: it is known only to lie between $\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73205$ and $26/15 \approx 1.73333$. We prove a lower bound of $14383/8304 \approx 1.73206$ using a single branching layer, and refine the construction with a second, mirrored branching layer to obtain $14350/8283 \approx 1.73246$, closing about a third of the gap.
  Our constructions are the first branching adversaries for $m = 4$ machines, and the first explicit lower bounds for online makespan minimization in which the adversary presents jobs in non-monotone order of size.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dimension-Free Sinkhorn for Optimal Transport: Bypassing Extremal Costs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Sinkhorn--Knopp (SK) algorithm is a cornerstone method for matrix scaling and entropically regularized optimal transport (EOT). Despite its empirical efficiency, existing bounds for achieving marginal accuracy $\varepsilon$ deteriorate severely in the presence of extreme entries, bottlenecked either by the global maximum regularized cost $η\|C\|_\infty$ (where $η$ is the regularization parameter and $C$ the cost matrix) or the matrix's minimum-to-maximum entry ratio $ν$. These bounds may be overly sensitive to rare extreme entries that do not dominate the overall matrix structure.
  We identify a broad structural regime in which the dependence on the magnitude of global extreme entries can be circumvented. For EOT, we introduce well-boundedness, a local mass property that captures the row- and column-wise bulk structure of the underlying matrix while maintaining robustness against scattered entrywise outliers. We prove that, governed by this structural condition, SK converges to the target transport plan for a problem of dimension $n$ in $O(\log n + \log(1/\varepsilon))$ iterations. This complexity bound is independent of the maximum regularized cost $η\|C\|_\infty$. A computationally negligible pre-scaling step eliminates this dimensional dependence, reducing the iteration complexity to a strictly dimension-free $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$.
  Beyond EOT, we establish a sharp phase transition for general $(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v})$-scaling governed by a critical matrix density threshold. We prove that when a matrix's density exceeds this threshold, the iteration complexity is strictly independent of $ν$. Conversely, when the density falls below this threshold, the dependence on $ν$ becomes unavoidable; in this sub-critical regime, we construct instances where SK requires $Ω(n/\varepsilon)$ iterations.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: DASHQuant: Provable Quantization with a Single Randomized Hadamard Transform
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Vector quantization via random projection followed by scalar quantization is a fundamental primitive in machine learning, with applications ranging from similarity search to federated learning and KV cache compression. While dense random rotations yield clean theoretical guarantees, they require $Θ(d^2)$ time. The randomized Hadamard transform $HD$ reduces this cost to $O(d \log d)$, but its discrete structure complicates analysis and leads to weaker or purely empirical compression guarantees. In this work, we introduce DASHQuant (Dithered Accelerated Single-Hadamard Quantization), a provable variant of this approach. Specifically, the quantizer applies $HD$ to the input vector and adds a random dithering before quantizing, injecting additional randomness at negligible cost. We prove that this approach is unbiased and provides mean squared error bounds that asymptotically match those achievable with truly random rotation matrices. In particular, we prove that a dithered version of TurboQuant, and a special case of EDEN, achieves mean squared error $\bigl(π\sqrt{3}/2 + o(1)\bigr) \cdot 4^{-b}$ at $b$ bits per coordinate, where the $o(1)$ term vanishes uniformly over all unit vectors and all dimensions as the number of quantization levels grows.

Graphics.title: 3D Point Splatting for mmWave Radar Novel View Synthesis
Graphics.summary: Solving novel view synthesis (NVS) for millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar requires a renderer that is physically faithful, complex-valued, and multi-viewpoint-tractable. No prior method achieves these three properties simultaneously. Differentiable Monte Carlo (MC) ray tracers implement the radar forward model directly with explicit material modeling and complex outputs, but a joint fit across views takes over an hour per scene. Optical-NVS ports of NeRF, hash grids, and 3D Gaussians train fast but discard phase and replace explicit material modeling with opaque learned features, restricting them to power-only range-azimuth (RA) magnitudes. We propose 3D Point Splatting (3DPS), the first differentiable point splatting renderer for radar, derived directly from the standard solid-angle form of the radar equation. Each oriented 3D point carries a material model built on ITU-R P.2040 permittivity and slab reflection, evaluated in closed form, with the resulting complex phasor splatted into range bins through a precomputed point spread function (PSF). The complex-valued output makes the renderer product-agnostic. The same optimized scene yields analog-to-digital converter (ADC), complex range profile (CRP), and RA outputs through standard fast Fourier transform (FFT) pipelines without retraining for each format. On six outdoor ColoRadar scenes, 3DPS reaches 0.587 mean Pearson correlation on held-out RA images. This is between 1.7x and 5.2x the three optical-NVS baselines (RadarSplat, Radar Fields, DART) and 1.3x the mmIR ray tracer at 1/25 of its wall-clock time. Training takes approximately 3 minutes per scene on a single RTX 4090. Project page: https://3d-point-splatting.github.io/
Graphics.comment: Accepted to the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026. Project page: https://3d-point-splatting.github.io/

Graphics.title: Quadratic Bezier Splatting with Structural Initialization for Efficient Painting Rendering
Graphics.summary: Stroke-based rendering is often optimized as a pixel-level reconstruction task. This over-reliance on global error reduction not only degrades strokes into fragmented curves due to a lack of structured planning, but also allows locally defective primitives to be concealed by overlapping layers. To address these issues, we introduce a model-guided framework for stroke-audited rendering. Our framework uses Quadratic Bezier Splatting to analytically model continuous curved strokes with efficient differentiable alpha compositing. Built on this renderer, a feedforward multi-scale stroke decoder provides a structural initialization with learned stroke-scale allocation, while test-time stroke optimization supplies the reconstruction capacity needed for high-fidelity refinement. We further propose a single-stroke audit mechanism that explicitly evaluates local stroke quality, preventing defective primitives from surviving optimization through layer-wise compensation. Compared with existing methods, our approach achieves coherent layouts, improves PSNR by up to 5.46 dB, yields a 16% more compact representation, and accelerates combined renderer forward and backward computation by a factor of 220.3.

Graphics.title: PLS-GS: Probabilistic Lidar Scaffolds for Compact, Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting
Graphics.summary: While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is typically optimized from images only, many robotics and mapping applications provide both camera and high-definition LiDAR data, combining rich visual appearance with accurate geometric structure. We introduce PLS-GS, a probabilistic LiDAR scaffold for Gaussian Splatting that exploits this complementary sensing setting to construct a compact 3DGS representation aligned to the measured surface. PLS-GS fits a Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model jointly over position and color, yielding a continuous and adaptive scaffold that eliminates the need for discrete scene partitioning such as voxel grids or octrees. The fitted mixture then guides the renderable 3DGS Gaussians: each rendering Gaussian is associated with a GMM component and constrained in the local surface frame induced by that component's covariance. A Mahalanobis support loss bounds the deviation of the rendering Gaussians from the corresponding LiDAR-derived surface. Across five large outdoor scenes, PLS-GS places primitives markedly closer to the LiDAR measurements than both image- and LiDAR-initialized baselines, while employing substantially fewer primitives, yielding a considerably more compact model and faster rendering. At matched capacity, PLS-GS places primitives closer to the LiDAR measurements, with comparable rendering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/k-harikumar/PLS-GS.
Graphics.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. Main paper and supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/k-harikumar/PLS-GS

Graphics.title: Action Transfer Across Character Body Plans in Latent-Action World Models: An Empirical Study of Animated Characters
Graphics.summary: Latent-action world models learn actions from video without labels, and recent methods aim to share these actions across bodies. Transfer between 2D characters with different body structures remains underexplored. In this paper, we study whether an action learned from one character can make a character with a different body perform the same action. A cat, a blob and a human can all jump, but each moves its body in its own way. The usual transfer gain mixes body motion with screen movement and can assign a perfect score to a model that ignores its action. To address this, we introduce a transfer score that compares the correct action with wrong ones from the same source. We test five training objectives on a new synthetic benchmark of 2D cartoon characters with six body plans, the standard Sprites benchmark, and 431 selected animal and human animations from DeformingThings4D. With a fixed camera, a baseline that only copies the source's screen movement scores 0.71, as high as most learned models. In contrast, with a camera that follows the body, the best model reaches only 0.46 for an unseen animal family and 0.20 for humans. With this camera, a linear probe identifies the action class of unseen animal families with 66% to 86% balanced accuracy (chance 17%). The learned actions therefore retain information about which action is performed, but the correct action closes only part of the prediction error gap for a new character.

Graphics.title: Good Token Hunting: A Hitchhiker's Guide to Token Selection for Visual Geometry Transformers
Graphics.summary: Visual geometry transformers have become powerful architectures for multi-view 3D reconstruction, enabling joint prediction of multiple 3D attributes in a feed-forward manner. However, their computational cost grows quadratically with the input sequence length due to the global attention layers inside these models. This limits both their scalability and efficiency. In this work, we address this challenge with a simple yet general strategy: restricting the number of key/value tokens that each query interacts with during global attention. To achieve effective token selection, we introduce a two-stage framework. First, an inter-frame selection step operates at the frame level to identify frames that should be preserved. Second, an intra-frame selection step further discards more redundant tokens within the selected frames. Our analysis highlights the advantage of a diversity-based strategy for inter-frame selection, which ensures broad coverage of the scene. For intra-frame selection, we show that layer-aware sparsification is necessary, with the selection process guided by the entropy of the global attention pattern. Our approach offers a superior speed-accuracy trade-off compared to existing solutions. Extensive experiments show that it accelerates visual geometry transformers by over 85% for scenes with 500 images while maintaining, or even improving, baseline performance, which hints that how our token selection strategy can play a crucial role in future applications of visual geometry transformers. Our project website is available at https://zsh2000.github.io/good-token-hunting.github.io.

Graphics.title: Squeezing Capacity from Multimodal Large Language Models for Subject-driven Generation
Graphics.summary: Subject-driven image generation aims to synthesize new images that preserve the identity of the given subject while following textual instructions. Existing approaches often encode text and reference images separately. This limits cross-modal reasoning abilities and causes copy-paste artifacts. Recent frameworks that connect multimodal models and diffusion models improve instruction following, but largely overlook identity preservation. To address these limitations, we condition diffusion models on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that jointly encode text and reference images, and augment it with VAE-based identity conditioning. A novel Dual Layer Aggregation (DLA) module is designed to aggregate multi-level MLLM features for optimal conditioning, and a multi-stage denoising strategy is applied to progressively balance the semantic information from MLLM and fine-detail identity from VAE during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach harmonizes multimodal understanding with identity preservation, mitigates copy-paste issues, and achieves superior performance regarding human preference on subject-driven image generation. Our project website is available at https://zsh2000.github.io/squeeze-mllm-subject-gen/.

Hardware Architecture.title: Compute Regeneration through Re-Productization: Reorganizing Retired Edge AI Silicon into a Delivered Multilingual Service Robot
Hardware Architecture.summary: Useful edge hardware can lose product support while retaining substantial computation. We treat this as systems design: compute regeneration here means re-productization, retaining the compute module while redesigning the surrounding product organization. Our case is GEdgeBot, a multilingual service robot built around a retired 32 GB Jetson AGX Xavier. A source-grounded inventory shows the box alone supplies inference, while the combined system exposes five on-device AI services, a seven-language speech chain, three sensing domains, and one deterministic seven-byte control boundary. AI and orchestration stay on the Xavier; finite motor-pulse generation on an STM32F407. Audits cover the six-mode control state machine, readiness barriers and sound orientation. Historical single-prototype measurements report 1,782 MB GPU memory with YOLO, Whisper-small, and NLLB-200 resident, a direct-control p99 deviation rising from 0.24 to 49.93 ms under concurrent AI load, and six of six trigger-to-follow demonstrations at 4.35 s mean latency, with conversational voice unavailable. A November campaign restores an isolated inference stack, re-measures AI workloads, and repeats control-frame runs. Driving two execution organisations with the same 6,000 measured 50 ms frame intervals shows the finite-pulse boundary removes host jitter from the pulse train but not the command start phase; its stopping bound is host-enforced, while the MCU 16-bit pulse field is unclamped. A six-check static audit exposes a host--MCU queue mismatch, and a 14-scenario replay executes the audited main() dispatcher across six modes with zero physical device opens and 54 contract-checked frames. Results support an existence claim and a reproducible architectural hypothesis, not fleet-level reliability. The 208 direct-control ratio remains unreplicated; MCU waveform capture and on-site fault injection remain open.

Hardware Architecture.title: Practical Deep Learning-Based Block Demapping for mmWave MIMO Systems
Hardware Architecture.summary: Deep learning is expected to play a central role in 6G systems, by enabling data-driven physical layer designs that can adapt to practical wireless impairments. This is particularly important for millimetre-wave (mmWave) multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, which are strongly affected by residual channel distortions, interference, and hardware non-idealities that are difficult to capture with analytical models. In this paper, we propose a deep learning-based soft demapper that performs block-wise processing of received symbols instead of conventional symbol-wise detection. The demapper employs a one-dimensional convolutional neural network to learn temporal structure induced by practical propagation and hardware effects, while producing soft bit outputs compatible with soft-decision decoding stages. The proposed approach is trained and evaluated for a 4$\times$4 wideband mmWave MIMO system at 60~GHz, using an over-the-air dataset collected across multiple days and settings. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over a conventional soft-decision demapper, including up to a 2.6$\times$ reduction in bit error rate for 16QAM and up to a 17.6$\times$ reduction for 64QAM under real over-the-air mmWave MIMO conditions. The proposed demapper is further implemented on a Zynq RFSoC platform using a reconfigurable convolution engine and fixed-point arithmetic, achieving an approximately 34.3$\times$ speedup compared to a processor-based implementation, and demonstrating that learning-based demapping can be deployed efficiently on resource-constrained edge hardware.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Submitted for publication to IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications

Hardware Architecture.title: Same Error, Different Recovery: How Delivery Changes LLM Agent Behavior
Hardware Architecture.summary: A tool-using language model must decide whether to retry a failed call, correct it, or stop and tell the user. The error text alone may not be enough: the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation. We isolate this delivery problem by varying placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure. Two studies with plans fixed before data collection, across 13 open models from 3B to 70B parameters, compare the next action and subsequent task completion, with exact deterministic reruns. A new user turn that retains the failed exchange avoids the severe stopping failure observed in Llama models when that exchange is removed. It is non-inferior to history rewriting in pooled synthetic comparisons, but is not best for every model. We implement this form as an opt-in recovery layer within a deterministic inference engine and evaluate it on public benchmarks and a coding agent. On ToolMaze, it raises success on explicit errors by 14.2 points with 7-8B models and 10.5 points with 32-70B models; Loud/Quiet, 24 multi-turn tasks with visible failures and silent corruption, scored by final-state agreement, shows no measurable gain. A client given the exact fault kind performs better still. The findings support delivery as a distinct factor in recovery, not an engine-exclusive solution or a universal retry policy.

Hardware Architecture.title: CU-3D: A Scalable Legality-Aware RTL-to-GDS Flow for 3D-IC Physical Design
Hardware Architecture.summary: Face-to-face (F2F) hybrid bonds shorten interdie connections, but data, clock, and power-grid (PG) connections must be realized together. CU-3D is a RTL-to-GDS physical design flow based on commercial EDA tools. It derives role-compatible hybrid-bond (HB) sites from a 17-metal ASAP7-based technology model, complete HB footprints, and constructed PG geometry. To coordinate partitioning with placement flexibility, Scaled refines an inherited 2D placement, whereas Fresh places the receiving die first and uses its pin locations and clock loads to guide placement of the other die. Data and clock HB assignments are jointly optimized while retaining alternative data sites and reserving capacity for subsequent PG assignment. The selected HB sites and stacks are preserved during 3D clock-tree synthesis, supply-aware cell insertion, and routing. Across eleven designs, including a 133-macro processor, the flow achieves zero backend DRC violations and passes signal-connectivity checks. Nine paired designs admit lower-footprint, lower-power implementations; four improve setup WNS. On JPEG, early joint planning gains 87 ps and mobility-aware partitioning gains 346 ps. Path analysis explains why cell-delay savings can outweigh net-delay increases.

Hardware Architecture.title: A Per-Step Load-Balancing Engine for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
Hardware Architecture.summary: In expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts serving, a layer finishes only when the most loaded GPU of its group does. Token routing shifts at every decode step and concentrates on a few experts, so most of the group's reserved GPU time waits on stragglers. Recovering that time means re-deciding, at every layer of every decode step, how each replicated expert's tokens divide between its copies. The exact linear-program solvers that make this decision optimally take longer than many of the layers they serve, and their working set outgrows GPU shared memory at deployment scale. We introduce Relief, a bidirectional pairwise relaxation that makes the linear program unnecessary, coming within a fraction of a point of the per-step optimum in a few passes of integer halving over the token counts. We build and measure three deployments, CUDA kernels on the serving GPU, the same verified engine on an FPGA over PCIe, and a fixed-function block beside the accelerator. On decode routing from three open MoE families, Relief holds the balance near the per-step optimum at every group size and layer time measured. Scored as effective utilization relative to that optimum, the kernel alone matches or exceeds every deployable scheme at every group size, from the hundred-microsecond layer on. The on-die engine widens that lead at every point, recovering up to 37.3 percentage points over the deployed static placement, while adding 0.02% of a current accelerator's transistors.
Hardware Architecture.comment: An anonymous version of this manuscript was submitted to HPCA 2027 on August 1, 2026. The original submission PDF and its SHA-256 checksum are archived at https://github.com/SuanNaiShuiGuoLao/relief-paper-archive

Hardware Architecture.title: MOSAIC: Efficient Mixture-of-Agent Scheduling via Adaptive Aggregation and Inference Concurrency
Hardware Architecture.summary: Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) systems improve reasoning accuracy by routing each query to multiple expert LLMs and aggregating their outputs. Efficiently executing this workload on limited GPU resources has bottlenecks. Skill-based routing creates skewed expert demand, and combining instruction-tuned LLMs with long-reasoning models results in extreme variability in generation lengths. Consequently, traditional scheduling strategies suffer from significant GPU idling and throughput collapse due to load imbalances. We present MOSAIC, a scheduling framework for accelerating batch-oriented MoA workloads. MOSAIC uses two-stage workload-aware scheduling: an expert placement stage, where an integer linear program (ILP) decides expert placement, followed by a query-sequencing stage that schedules requests based on predicted output lengths. Additionally, MOSAIC uses confidence-aware adaptive aggregation, leveraging inter-expert agreement to bypass the heavy aggregator LLM for consensus queries. On a 4-GPU system, MOSAIC achieves 2.7-3.4x end-to-end speedups over round-robin scheduling and reduces the mean time-to-answer by 3.9-7.8x, while matching accuracy within +/-1pp.

Hardware Architecture.title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms.
  In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.

Hardware Architecture.title: PRISM: Preference-based Reward and Uncertainty-Integrated Synthesis Minimization for RTL PPA Optimization
Hardware Architecture.summary: This paper introduces a budget-aware, multi-objective framework (called PRISM) for RTL optimization that improves power, performance, and area (PPA) while sharply limiting expensive commercial synthesis tool calls. Starting from a synthesizable baseline and functional testbench, the method iterates through LLM-driven rewrite generation, fast compile/simulation equivalence filtering, low-cost proxy feature extraction, and selective commercial synthesis tool (Synopsys Design Compiler (DC)) evaluation. To prioritize which candidates deserve high-quality synthesis, we train a preference-based reward model using pairwise ranking supervision derived from commercial synthesis tool outcomes, and combine ensemble uncertainty with a diversity-aware acquisition rule to avoid early bias and redundant evaluations. A key advantage is that PRISM maintains a best-tradeoff set G of non-dominated designs throughout the run: G preserves the best solutions found so far, is fed back into generation and refinement, and enables consistent, cumulative improvements rather than repeatedly restarting from the baseline. Across RTLLM v2.0 modules, the approach consistently yields post-synthesis gains under fixed commercial synthesis tool call budgets, and ablations confirm that reward-guided selection and candidate dropping are central to sample-efficient progress. PRISM efficacy is evaluated across multiple technology nodes (7 nm, 15 nm, and 45 nm) using identical pipelines without retraining.

Hardware Architecture.title: When Is High-Bandwidth Flash Cost-Effective for LLM Inference?
Hardware Architecture.summary: Can high-bandwidth flash (HBF) make LLM inference cheaper than adding GPUs? By storing weights closer to the GPU than SSD, HBF may reduce the number of GPUs needed for model capacity. However, this integration is only justified if it meets service targets and its cost is recovered. We simulate this integration using public component data across nine dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, five workloads, two GPU platforms, and 1--100 GPUs. At fixed demand, HBF reduces the minimum GPU count to meet a service target in 98 of 468 comparisons; majority of them are paused and short sessions, 63 remain cost-effective at half a GPU price per HBF stack. For single short-chat users, HBF enables large MoEs, e.g. DeepSeek V3 and Kimi K2, to meet a relaxed service target on one RTX~4090 GPU, where conventional serving fails. At fixed GPU count, HBF improves throughput in 48\% of matched comparisons below 16 GPUs and 13\% at larger counts. Even at 100 RTX~4090-scale GPUs, cascaded HBF raises offline throughput by 16.4--26.5$\times$ for three large MoEs. We found savings and throughput gains arise in different scenarios.

Hardware Architecture.title: ICLayout-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Custom Circuit Layout Design
Hardware Architecture.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are being explored for circuit design, but their ability to produce high-quality custom layouts has not been extensively evaluated. ICLayout-Bench is a benchmark in which agents use electronic design automation (EDA) tools to construct and optimize GDSII layouts from transistor-level circuit netlists. These layouts are evaluated using physical verification, parasitic extraction, and post-layout simulation. Layouts that pass the physical and functional checks are scored on electrical performance and area. The benchmark includes 165 tasks across 13 process design kits (PDKs), covering technology nodes from 3 nm to 180 nm. The tasks span analog, mixed-signal, and digital circuits in open-source and commercial EDA flows. The experiments evaluate 22 configurations spanning seven models on 21 public and 19 private tasks. Mean layout scores range from 4.22 to 80.26 on public tasks and from 1.43 to 67.01 on private tasks, on a 100-point scale. Higher reasoning effort does not consistently improve mean scores, and configurations with comparable scores can incur substantially different model costs.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables, including appendices. Project page: https://lizhangmai.github.io/ICLayout-Bench Code: https://github.com/lizhangmai/ICLayout-Bench Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/lizhangmai/ICLayout-Bench

Hardware Architecture.title: Priority-Aware Deficit Round Robin for AXI4 Bandwidth Fairness in ASAP-7nm Process
Hardware Architecture.summary: Modern systems-on-chip place real-time clients, processor cores and bulk data engines on the same AXI4 interconnect, where they contend for shared slaves. AXI4 fixes the ordering rules and carries a 4-bit quality of service (QoS) field, but leaves the service policy to the implementer, and that policy determines how long each master waits and how much bandwidth it receives once a slave saturates. We propose a QoS-aware deficit round robin (DRR) architecture that charges each grant in beats, and benchmark it against two architectures built behind the same port list: round robin, and QoS priority with anti-starvation aging. Charging in beats recovers bandwidth fairness while leaving every burst whole, so the address phase is issued once and locality for memory access is preserved. All three are driven by the same deterministic traffic generator and taken from RTL to GDSII on the ASAP7 7-nm predictive PDK. Under a 1:16 burst-length mismatch, the round robin and QoS architectures both hold the beat ratio between the two competing masters at 1:16, while our design brings it to 1:1 at full load. Mean read latency for the priority master falls from 95 cycles under round robin to 67 with QoS and 37 with QoS-aware DRR. At 500 MHz this serves the priority master in 74 ns against 190 ns. The measurements give a per-policy price and a traffic-based guide for choosing among the three.

Programming Languages.title: Quantifier Elimination and Craig Interpolation, Quantitatively
Programming Languages.summary:
Quantifier elimination (QE) and Craig interpolation (CI) are central to various state-of-the-art automated approaches to hardware- and software verification. They are rooted in the Boolean setting and are successful for, e.g., first-order theories such as linear rational arithmetic. What about their applicability in the quantitative setting where formulae evaluate to numbers and quantitative supremum/infimum quantifiers are the natural counterpart to Boolean quantifiers? Applications include establishing quantitative properties of programs such as bounds on expected outcomes of probabilistic programs featuring non-determinism and analyzing the flow of information through programs.
  In this paper, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first QE algorithm for possibly unbounded, $\infty$- or $(-\infty)$-valued, or discontinuous piecewise linear quantities. They are the quantitative counterpart to linear rational arithmetic, and they are a popular quantitative assertion language for probabilistic program verification. We provide rigorous soundness proofs as well as upper bounds on the size of the output. Moreover, we present two applications of our QE algorithm. First, our algorithm yields a quantitative CI theorem: Given arbitrary piecewise linear quantities $f,g$ with $f \models g$ (i.e., $f$ is at most $g$ at every variable valuation), both the strongest and the weakest Craig interpolants are quantifier-free and effectively constructible. Such interpolants lie between the two quantities and use only their common free variables. Second, we apply our QE algorithm to computing minimal and maximal expected outcomes of loop-free probabilistic programs featuring unbounded non-determinism, and to checking inductivity of candidate upper bounds on minimal and maximal expected outcomes of probabilistic loops featuring unbounded non-determinism.

Programming Languages.title: Quantitative Verification of Infinite-State Networks
Programming Languages.summary:
Many network protocols and distributed systems combine recursion, unbounded local state, and quantitative behaviour such as cost, latency, or reliability. Existing decidability results for networks of pushdown systems are largely qualitative, and do not extend to quantitative analyses, which must jointly track traces and weights.
  We present a framework for the quantitative verification of acyclic networks of weighted pushdown systems. Finitely summarising a recursive network component requires collapsing the infinite family of runs obtained by pumping its nested loops, and doing so exactly, rather than by over-approximation, is a standing difficulty.
