Then we show how to address the limitation and provide an alternative tripod reordering mechanism that reduces the upper bound on the queue number of planar graphs to $33$. As a corollary, bipartite planar graphs have queue number at most $22$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Source Assignment: Hardness, Approximation, and Parameterized Algorithms
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In Source Assignment, each pointer represents a substring of a common reference string and may have several possible source occurrences. The goal is to choose one source for each pointer while minimizing the number of distinct reference boundaries used by the selected sources. The problem was introduced by Qiu and Kingsford (Bioinformatics 2021) in the context of compact genome-graph construction. We distinguish \emph{Explicit Source Assignment}, where admissible source sets are given explicitly, from \emph{Complete Source Assignment}, where all occurrences of each pointer string are available.
  We show that Explicit Source Assignment has an exact value-preserving formulation as cardinality Set Cover with Pairs. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, it cannot be approximated within $(1-\varepsilon)\ln p$ unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, even over a binary alphabet when all pointers have length one, while known algorithms for Minimum-Weight Multicolored Subgraph give an $O(\sqrt{q\log p})$-approximation for arbitrary pointer lengths. Our main hardness result proves that Complete Source Assignment is APX-hard even over a binary alphabet, with equal pointer lengths and at most two sources per pointer. For edge-disjoint equal-length instances, we give a $3/2$-approximation and a $1.12585$-approximation when each pointer has at most two sources. We also introduce the rainbow-path length $λ$: the problem is polynomial-time solvable for $λ\le2$, and for $λ\le3$ we obtain a $(9/8+\varepsilon)$-approximation.
  We further give a polynomial-time test for deciding whether abstract source sets can be realized exactly as complete occurrence sets over an unrestricted alphabet. Finally, we give exact fixed-parameter algorithms for several structural parameters, and show that Complete Source Assignment is fixed-parameter tractable in the alphabet size and maximum pointer length.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Combinatorial Boolean Matrix Multiplication in $n^3 / 2^{Ω(\sqrt{\log n})}$ Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
For over fifty years, combinatorial algorithms for Boolean matrix multiplication (BMM) and triangle detection saved only polylogarithmic factors over cubic time. At STOC 2024, Abboud, Fischer, Kelley, Lovett, and Meka broke this barrier with a deterministic $O(n^3 / 2^{Ω((\log n)^{1/7})})$-time algorithm, and asked whether $n^3 / 2^{Ω(\sqrt{\log n})}$ time is achievable. We answer this question in the affirmative, giving deterministic combinatorial algorithms for both BMM and triangle detection running in $O(n^3 / 2^{Ω(\sqrt{\log n})})$ time.
  Following Abboud et al., we decompose $(A,B)$ into pairs of submatrices $(A_k,B_k)$, called \emph{pieces}, each of which is either sparse or pseudorandom in a sense that forces $A_k\star B_k$ to be nearly all-ones on its vertex sets. Whereas their decomposition produces $2^{O(d^7)}$ pieces at regularity parameter $d$, we obtain $2^{O(d^2)}$ pieces, directly improving the runtime exponent from $(\log n)^{1/7}$ to $\sqrt{\log n}$. Prior work found pseudorandom pieces by repeatedly restricting to denser submatrices, paying worst-case vertex losses at each step that compounded across nested recursion levels, together with an expensive derandomization step. We eliminate the extra powers of $d$ by matching the vertex loss at each step to the size of its density jump so losses telescope across scales, derandomizing witness search via $L_d$-norm estimation so the sampler length stays $2^{O(d)}$, and bounding overlap across the recursion with a fractional density-weighted volume budget rather than raw submatrix volume.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 27 pages. Condensed version; the full version (46 pages, with additional results and the Lean 4 formalization) is available at https://github.com/lockqueue/bmm

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Sublogarithmic Competitive Algorithm for Online Graph Exploration
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In online graph exploration, an agent must visit every vertex of an unknown weighted graph and return to its start, learning the incident edges at each vertex it visits. On $n$-vertex graphs, the best known competitive ratio has been $O(\log n)$, achieved by several algorithms, among them the hierarchical depth-first search of Megow, Mehlhorn, and Schweitzer. We give an algorithm with competitive ratio ${(2+o(1))}\ln n/\ln\ln n$ for known~$n$. Like hierarchical depth-first search, it groups the edges into geometric weight classes and searches depth-first between components of lighter edges. Unlike it, the agent tours each component along a minimum spanning tree for the original weights, so only crossings between components pay for rounding, and the base $b$ of the weight class can grow with~$n$. The leading constant $2$ is tight for our choice of base. Without knowing $n$, restarts with increasing size guesses give upper bounds with leading constant $4$ for a fixed schedule and $2$ in expectation for a randomly shifted schedule. If the weights lie in a known range $[1,2^k]$ with $k\ge4$, choosing $b=k/\log_2 k$ gives a competitive ratio of $O(k/\log k)$ without knowing $n$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Multiple-Choice Secretary Problem with Predictions
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the multiple-choice secretary problem, in which candidates arrive in uniformly random order and the goal is to select at most $k$ candidates to maximize their total value. We consider a setting where predictions of individual candidate values are available before any candidate arrives. Fujii and Yoshida's Learned Kleinberg algorithm achieves competitive loss $O(\min\{\log k/\sqrt{k},\eps\})$, where $k$ is the selection capacity and $\eps$ is the maximum multiplicative prediction error. We remove the logarithmic factor through a sharper analysis of the same switching algorithm with a retuned threshold. The resulting competitive ratio is at least $\max\{0,1-\min\{32/\sqrt{k},4\eps\}\}$. In particular, exact predictions ($\eps=0$) achieve the offline optimum on every arrival order.

Graphics.title: A Lightweight Differentiable Method for Real-Time Skin Rendering and Digitization
Graphics.summary: Inverse rendering for skin typically relies on offline path tracing to estimate physical properties, which fail to map directly to the approximate shaders utilized in interactive applications, such as game engines. We bridge this gap by directly estimating subsurface scattering parameters tailored for real-time rendering pipelines. We introduce a differentiable Screen-Space Subsurface Scattering (SSSS) framework that enables the joint optimization of spatially varying base textures and scattering distances. To account for local variations in skin thickness, we estimate these parameters across distinct facial regions, generating a blended profile map ready for production runtime engines. Our pipeline utilizes a low-cost, single-light, single-view capture setup designed for accessible and practical appearance acquisition. Optimization is driven by a masked loss function targeting regions where subsurface scattering effects are dominant. We validate our approach on a real-world dataset of $45$ individuals across the Monk Skin Tone Scale, ensuring demographic generalization. Furthermore, we complement this evaluation with synthetic data, a multi-light setup validating our single-light assumption, and a tilted-view configuration confirming angular consistency. Results demonstrate that our method effectively recovers scattering parameters from lightweight inputs, yielding realistic skin appearance directly compatible with standard real-time shaders.
Graphics.comment: 20 pages, 25 figures; includes 6 pages of supplementary material. Accepted to Computers and Graphics

Graphics.title: Linear-size graphs at every strict dismantling level
Graphics.summary: Dismantling reduces a graph to one vertex by successive deletions. At level zero, a vertex is eligible if one of its neighbours is adjacent to all its other neighbours. At level $k\geq1$, its neighbours must induce a graph dismantlable at level $k-1$. A graph has strict level $k$ if it admits a reduction at level $k$ and none at level $k-1$. For every $k\geq1$, we construct a graph of strict level $k$ with $3k+8$ vertices. Each step adds three vertices: the neighbours of one induce the preceding graph, and the other two provide the adjacencies used to rule out other first deletions at the lower level. A second construction gives a graph of order $4k+4$ at strict level $k$. Together the two families give the upper bound $\min\{4k+4,3k+8\}$ on the least order at strict level $k$.

Graphics.title: Exploring Cross-Reality Transitions between Projections and Head-Mounted Displays for Immersive Digital Art
Graphics.summary: Immersive exhibitions increasingly combine large-scale projections with mixed reality (MR) head-mounted displays (HMDs), but how users perceive transitions across these heterogeneous visualization environments remains underexplored. We investigate cross-reality (CR) object- and scene-level transitions in a hybrid immersive art installation spanning projection, augmented reality (AR), and virtual reality (VR). In a within-subjects study (N=24), we compared a calibrated condition with a bundled inconsistency condition introducing noticeable differences in spatial alignment, visual appearance, and cross-device latency. This contrast was used not to establish perceptual thresholds or hardware targets, but as a diagnostic probe to make transition disruptions more perceptible and discussable. The inconsistency condition reduced presence and increased workload. Interviews showed that spatial misalignment disrupted action-outcome predictability, appearance mismatch reduced aesthetic coherence, and latency weakened perceived responsiveness. Effects also varied by asset type: rigid static assets exposed inconsistencies more clearly, animated skeletal assets shifted attention toward motion, and particle effects often masked small discrepancies. These findings clarify how users perceive projection-MR transitions and support asset-aware design strategies for coherent hybrid immersive art. We also release HUICRSync, an open-source Unreal Engine plugin for prototyping projection-MR CR experiences.

Graphics.title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control
Graphics.summary: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.

Graphics.title: Physics-Driven Extraction of Dynamic Fluid Asset from Monocular Video with Generative 3DGS
Graphics.summary: Existing methods for dynamic 3D scene synthesis from video rely on per-frame deformation fields optimized through pixel-level reconstruction losses. While effective for closed systems such as elastic solids, these approaches face challenges with open systems like fluids where material continuously enters and exits the scene, topology changes freely, and no stable point correspondence exists across frames. We propose a simulation-driven alternative that optimizes the parameters of a fluid simulator to reproduce dynamics observed in a single-view video, rather than fitting per-point deformation to pixel values. Our framework leverages generative 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models to obtain initial fluid geometry including unseen surfaces, estimates a physically grounded velocity field from surface motions with a physics-constraint correction algorithm, and converts it into a divergence-free, grid-based representation. A differentiable Affine Particle-In-Cell (APIC) simulation then optimizes effective simulation parameters, such as viscosity, boundary conditions, and inflow/outflow velocities, to match the observed dynamics. Because the dynamics are governed by forward simulation, the output assets are inherently editable, interactive, and temporally extendable, which reconstruction-based approaches cannot readily provide. Stage-wise ablations confirm that each stage is necessary, and hyperparameter sweeps show the pipeline to be robust without sensitive per-scene tuning. Our method handles various liquid fluids, including inviscid and viscous types, demonstrating the potential for automatically creating simulation-ready 3D fluid assets from readily available internet videos.
Graphics.comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics. 21 pages (18 pages + 3 pages supplementary material), 28 figures

Graphics.title: Pygmalion Effect in Vision: Image-to-Clay Translation for Reflective Geometry Reconstruction
Graphics.summary: Understanding reflection remains a long-standing challenge in 3D reconstruction due to the entanglement of appearance and geometry under view-dependent reflections. In this work, we present the Pygmalion Effect in Vision, a novel framework that metaphorically "sculpts" reflective objects into clay-like forms through image-to-clay translation. We then introduce a dual-branch design in which a BRDF-based reflective branch and a clay-guided branch share the same Gaussian geometry but operate through independent rendering paths. The clay-guided branch, supervised by the synthesized clay images, provides reflection-free geometric guidance that complements the photometric supervision of the BRDF branch. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets show consistent improvements in both geometry and photometric metrics. Beyond technical gains, our framework reveals that seeing by unshining, translating radiance into neutrality, can serve as a powerful inductive bias for reflective object geometry learning.

Graphics.title: Deformable Texture Maps: Compiling Dynamic Microgeometry into Neural Textures
Graphics.summary: Deformable material surfaces, such as cloth, owe their appearance to fine-scale geometries that restructure under deformation. Even when coarse simulation models efficiently recover this microstructure, explicitly instantiating and rendering it remains expensive. We introduce Deformable Texture Maps (DTM), a representation that compiles deformation-driven microgeometry into a continuous and compact neural texture. Our model maps texture coordinates and local deformations to intrinsic maps describing opacity, surface normals, depth, and material identity. This captures the occlusion and visibility changes generated by deformation. At runtime, these maps provide a common texture-space representation of deformation-driven fine-scale structure that can be evaluated directly on coarse deforming surfaces. Since our representation encodes geometric attributes rather than radiance, lighting and material response remain decoupled from the learned model. This allows us to apply relighting, as well as shading and material editing without retraining. We further introduce a persistent texture-space rendering strategy that caches these intrinsic maps and selectively updates them as deformation changes. This effectively decouples neural evaluation from frame rendering and enables their reuse across frames and conventional rendering effects. We demonstrate our approach on yarn-based textiles, where non-linear material stretch and shear induce changes in yarn geometry, spacing and occlusion. We build our model by, first, sweeping tileable yarn patches through deformation space, then, rendering the detailed geometry into a canonical texture-space, and finally, compressing the resulting maps into a single neural representation. Our resulting model can be evaluated directly on arbitrary coarse garment meshes and integrated with conventional shading pipelines, keeping appearance authorable at render time.

Graphics.title: Patch-Based Generalized Neural Texture Upscaling
Graphics.summary: We propose a lightweight neural texture upscaling method. A single generalized MLP is trained on a diverse collection of texture patches and integrated into the texture sampling stage, upscaling low-resolution textures on-the-fly at rendering time. Because the model is generalized rather than overfit to specific content, no per-asset training is required - the same model applies to any existing scene without modifying texture data or the asset pipeline. Storing lower-resolution base textures reduces disk footprint, upscaling at sampling time eliminates the need to store high-resolution textures in VRAM, and sharing a single set of model weights across all textures ensures non-divergent GPU execution. We evaluate our method across multiple texture classes, demonstrating consistent improvement over analytic upscaling methods in perceptual quality.

Operating Systems.title: BunshinRL: Whole-Workspace Forking for Agentic Reinforcement Learning Rollouts
Operating Systems.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.

Operating Systems.title: Towards Runtime-Aware Observability for Java Virtual Threads
Operating Systems.summary: OS-level observability tools join application requests to kernel events through the OS thread ID, assuming that a unit of work occupies one OS thread until it completes. Java virtual threads break this assumption: many virtual threads are multiplexed onto a few carrier threads, so a stable thread ID hides a changing unit of work, and the join fails silently. Existing virtual-thread-aware channels republish context or identity on every mount and unmount, and the JVMTI-based one pays this cost for the lifetime of the JVM, whether or not an observer is attached. We bind a 64-byte off-heap trace buffer to each virtual thread, at a fixed address for its lifetime, and publish the address to eBPF consumers through four USDT probes in a patched OpenJDK; a re-implemented JVMTI channel over the same buffer serves as a controlled comparison. The four-probe design attributed all 768 test markers correctly on both the content and the identity plane, while the naive two-probe design silently misattributes trace context. With no consumer attached, publication costs at most about 33 ns per transition; the remaining dormant cost is buffer allocation, about 0.37 microseconds per virtual thread, which is negligible on transition-heavy workloads but nearly doubles the cost of a creation-only microbenchmark. The JVMTI channel costs about 20% on transition-heavy workloads and about 1.8 microseconds per virtual thread on the creation-only one. We also show that, of the two update strategies OTEP 4947 permits, only in-place rewriting guarded by the record's valid flag is sound for readers that cache the record's address, as lifecycle-event readers do.
Operating Systems.comment: 19 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables. Based on the author's MSc dissertation, School of Computing, Newcastle University, 2026. Code and data: https://github.com/Neltharion1127/ebpf-vthread-correlate

Operating Systems.title: GPUOS: A GPU Operating System Primitive for Transparent Operation Fusion
Operating Systems.summary:
Modern deep learning workloads often consist of many small tensor operations, especially in inference, attention, and micro-batched training. In these settings, kernel launch overhead can become a major bottleneck, sometimes exceeding the actual computation time.
  We present GPUOS, a GPU runtime JIT system that reduces launch overhead using a persistent kernel architecture with runtime operator injection. GPUOS runs a single long-lived GPU kernel that continuously processes tasks from a host-managed work queue, eliminating repeated kernel launches. To support diverse operations, GPUOS uses NVIDIA NVRTC to just-in-time compile operators at runtime and inject them into the running kernel through device function pointer tables. This design enables operator updates without restarting the kernel or recompiling the system.
  GPUOS introduces four key ideas: (1) a persistent worker kernel with atomic task queues, (2) a runtime operator injection mechanism based on NVRTC and relocatable device code, (3) a dual-slot aliasing scheme for safe concurrent operator updates, and (4) transparent PyTorch integration through TorchDispatch that batches micro-operations into unified submissions. The system supports arbitrary tensor shapes, strides, data types, and broadcasting through a generic tensor abstraction.
  Experiments show that GPUOS achieves up to 15.3x speedup over standard PyTorch on workloads dominated by small operations, including micro-batched inference and attention patterns. GPUOS improves utilization while remaining compatible with the PyTorch ecosystem.

Operating Systems.title: Idleness is Relative: Exploiting Tool-Call Idle Windows for Offloading in Agentic Systems with MORI
Operating Systems.summary: Agentic programs alternate between LLM inference and tool calls, each request extending the previous one's context. Program-aware schedulers pin a program's KV cache in GPU HBM across tool calls to avoid re-prefilling it at every step, but as contexts grow, pinned KV cache exceeds HBM, raising program eviction: deciding when a program releases GPU memory and when it returns. Offloading to CPU DRAM lets an evicted program wait out a tool call instead of recomputing its context, but existing schedulers leave DRAM to LRU, so offloaded programs thrash. Making these decisions is hard: tool-call durations vary by orders of magnitude and are unknown in advance. We observe that programs nevertheless stay busy (short tool calls) or idle (long ones) for extended periods, and use a program's idleness, its recent fraction of time in tool calls, as a continuous, relative metric. MORI ranks programs by idleness, keeps the least idle in HBM and the next in DRAM, and drops the rest, enforcing admission control at both tiers under any GPU-to-CPU capacity ratio; it also proactively demotes idle programs to make room for ready ones. On real coding-agent traces, MORI achieves on average 64% higher throughput and 72% lower p90 TTFT than the best offloading baseline under high load.

Hardware Architecture.title: VISTA: View-Independent micro-Doppler Reconstruction with Multistatic ISAC
Hardware Architecture.summary: The micro-Doppler (uD) spectrum provides detailed characteristics of target movement, making it highly valuable for applications such as target classification and human activity recognition. However, traditional Integrated Sensing And Communication (ISAC) systems are highly view-dependent and limited by blind spots and angle dependencies. Existing approaches rely on either configuration-specific solutions or data-driven models. The former results in poor generalization when device deployments or target orientations change, while the latter requires acquiring extensive multi-view datasets, which is time-consuming and not always feasible. To address these limitations, in this work we propose VISTA, a novel method for reconstructing the uD spectrogram in an absolute coordinate frame, yielding view-independent Doppler features that are invariant to the spatial distribution of ISAC nodes. We formulate the uD estimation as a sparse reconstruction problem that jointly leverages measurements from all ISAC receivers. This is solved using a modified Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) algorithm, which iteratively alternates between jointly selecting candidate velocity vectors across all receivers (RXs) and independently estimating the complex channel gain amplitudes for each RX. Our results show that, provided sufficient spatial diversity, VISTA successfully reconstructs the targets' absolute uD spectrograms with a median error \leq 0.69 m/s for speeds \leq 15 m/s.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Accepted to be presented in the IEEE ISAC 2026 conference

Hardware Architecture.title: From Grid to Chip: Power Architecture, Stability, and Flexibility of AI Data Centers
Hardware Architecture.summary: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) computing is transforming data centers into large, dynamic electrical loads. Their deployment is primarily constrained by energy availability and grid-connection capacity, which is further aggravated by the ability of power-delivery architectures, control systems, and computing workloads to operate reliably during fast grid disturbances. This article provides a comprehensive overview of forefront challenges and trends in the grid-to-chip framework, and presents a technological perspective on AI data centers as grid-interactive computing systems. First, it reviews grid-integration bottlenecks, evolving connection policies, grid-code requirements, which has fostered new technological trends via spatio-temporal flexibility available through workload orchestration, cooling systems, on-site resources, and energy storage. Second, it maps the evolution of power-delivery architectures from medium-voltage grid interfaces to chip-level, discussing higher-voltage DC distribution, solid-state transformers, wide-bandgap devices, advanced chip-level power delivery, and liquid cooling. Third, it establishes a three-level stability framework spanning rack-level DC-bus dynamics, facility-level converter interactions, and system-level grid-coupled behavior. The framework connects dominant instability mechanisms, including constant power load effects, impedance interactions, forced oscillations, and operating-mode transitions, with suitable modeling, assessment, and mitigation approaches. Synthesizing these topics, this article highlights grid-to-chip co-design as a central requirement for scalable AI infrastructure, linking computing workloads, power-delivery systems, energy buffers, and grid operation.
Hardware Architecture.comment: The manuscript has been accepted for publication in IEEE Open Journal of Power Electronics

Hardware Architecture.title: Starscream: Reimagining LLM Sharding on AMD Instinct GPUs with GPU Partitioning
Hardware Architecture.summary: As GPU accelerators grow larger to meet rising compute demands, they exhibit increasingly pronounced non-uniform memory access (NUMA) characteristics that challenge existing LLM frameworks. Chiplet-based architectures provide a practical path to larger GPUs while mitigating manufacturing yield constraints. Modern GPUs such as AMD Instinct MI300X employs such a multi-die design, and further offer GPU partitioning capabilities, partitioning a single physical GPU into multiple logical devices with NUMA-aware memory domains, promising faster kernel launches, and reduced memory access latencies with improved locality. However, current parallelization strategies, designed for homogeneous GPU topologies, when applied under partitioning, extend its unidimensional sharding causing significant performance degradation. Three bottlenecks emerge: (1) memory redundancy; (2) arithmetic intensity collapse; (3) communication overhead from flat collectives. We present Starscream, a rethinking of LLM sharding for the chiplet era. Rather than stretching inter-GPU sharding thinner, Starscream adds intra-GPU sharding along an orthogonal dimension, grounded in three foundational principles: kernel shape preservation, memory redundancy elimination, and communication overhead minimization. These principles form the basis for extending any sharding strategy into the partitioning regime. We demonstrate their effectiveness using tensor parallelism as a case study. On AMD MI300X and MI355X, exploiting partitioning capabilities yields up to 4x speedup for attention and 1.43x for fused GEMMs compared to chiplet-oblivious baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of chiplet-aware designs. Starscream's principles generalize across sharding strategies and future architectures.

Hardware Architecture.title: NVIDIA Vera: A Microarchitecture-Level Comparison with Grace, Turin, and Granite Rapids
Hardware Architecture.summary:
The majority of new HPC systems are centered around NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel CPUs. Vera is NVIDIA's latest data-center CPU, including its first custom data-center core design, Olympus. This paper investigates Vera in comparison to AMD Turin and Intel Granite Rapids, using NVIDIA Grace as a baseline. We navigate up the performance ladder, from microbenchmarks that isolate performance metrics, through NAS kernels and miniapps, to single-socket performance of a range of scientific codes.
  We find that Vera achieves the best performance of the architectures evaluated in most codes tested, and that this gain is primarily attributed to its high memory bandwidth, effective Spatial Multithreading implementation, and low-latency memory subsystem aided by the architecture's predictive structures. While Vera represents a major leap over its predecessor, we show that its comparatively modest floating-point performance trails Intel and AMD in a small number of compute-bound workloads reflecting NVIDIA's GPU focus for such workloads.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Accepted at PMBS26 (SC26 Workshops). 9 pages + 3-page artifact description, 11 figures, 1 table. Corrects a typo in Sec. IV-B relative to the proceedings version

Hardware Architecture.title: HARE: Fast Read Disturbance Threshold Profiling in Modern DRAM Chips via Reduced Timing Constraints
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Modern DRAM chips are vulnerable to read disturbance, which manifests as bitflips in a victim row physically near an aggressor row that is repeatedly activated. State-of-the-art mitigations rely on accurate and exhaustive profiling of the read disturbance threshold (RDT), i.e., the minimum number of aggressor row activations needed to induce the first bitflip. However, RDT changes significantly and unpredictably over time, motivating online profilers that dynamically adjust a mitigation's RDT configuration. RDT profiling is costly for online profilers (e.g., hundreds of seconds for a 16-bank DDR4 module) because 1) measuring a single DRAM row's RDT requires many activations and 2) each DRAM row can have a different RDT, requiring many rows to be profiled.
  We introduce HARE, an online RDT profiling technique that intentionally exacerbates read disturbance to quickly profile a DRAM module. HARE's key idea is to reduce the timing constraints between consecutive DRAM commands during profiling. Doing so significantly reduces profiling time by 1) directly reducing the execution time of the profiling command sequence and 2) exacerbating read disturbance such that the first bitflip occurs at a smaller activation count than with the conventional RowHammer sequence.
  From our characterization of 180 real DDR4 DRAM chips from four major DRAM manufacturers, we make three observations. First, HARE measures a DRAM row's RDT 31.2% faster than the RowHammer profiler and a DRAM module's minimum RDT with an average reduction of 21.7%. Second, HARE flips more than 95% of the cells that the RowHammer pattern flips. Third, HARE preserves the RDT ranking of rows well enough such that it can exhaustively reprofile a small set of rows to improve its minimum RDT estimation. Our end-to-end evaluations show that HARE enables significant system performance improvements and outperforms the RowHammer profiler.

Hardware Architecture.title: Sub-100KB On-Device CNN Training via Dynamic Sparse Updates and Hardware--Software Co-Design
Hardware Architecture.summary: The increasing demand for real-time processing and personalized deep learning has made edge-device training essential but challenging due to high memory and computational costs. To address this, we propose a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) training accelerator with a dynamic sparse update mechanism that selectively updates important parameters using a random channel strategy, avoiding costly evaluations. Combined with activation pruning, our approach reduces activation storage to just 3.4\% of the original. Our hardware features a fused forward dataflow that concurrently processes group normalization and convolution, reducing training time by 45\% through computation reordering and efficient zero-skipping. Implemented in TSMC 28nm at FP8 precision, the design operates at 800 MHz, achieving 8 TOPS peak throughput, 31.13 TOPS/W energy efficiency, and 14.8 TOPS/mm$^2$ area efficiency, with power consumption ranging from 257 to 272 mW. The design enables on-device training within a sub-100KB on-chip SRAM budget (95KB in silicon).

Hardware Architecture.title: TQIR: Trellis Quantization with Integer Reconstruction for Bandwidth-Efficient Edge LLM Acceleration
Hardware Architecture.summary: Autoregressive large language model (LLM) inference is often limited by external-memory bandwidth, while existing ultra-low-bit trellis quantization reconstructs floating-point weights and leaves runtime Hadamard-transform and decoder costs unresolved. This paper presents TQIR, an algorithm--hardware co-design that decouples storage precision ($S$) from decoded-weight ($W$) and activation ($A$) compute precisions, enabling a better accuracy--hardware trade-off. TQIR performs trellis matching with floating-point candidates offline while constraining each candidate to an INT8 or INT4 codeword that can be reproduced exactly for integer GEMM at runtime. To reduce transform cost while preserving the integer weight path, TQIR relocates the reverse Hadamard transform to the activation side and employs an $H_{128}$ Subspace Hadamard Transform, together with a subspace-aligned $128\times2$ trellis tile that preserves the original 256-weight sequence length. The configurable decoder, synthesized in a TSMC 16-nm process, delivers 307.2~Gweights/s in 0.0509~mm$^2$ and achieves 13.93$\times$ and 1.52$\times$ the normalized decoder-area efficiency of Ecco and Codeword Decomposition, respectively. These results show that fixed-rate trellis compression can reduce weight traffic while sustaining an integer-GEMM datapath matched to the evaluated memory and PE rates.
Hardware Architecture.comment: submitted to IEEE transactions on circuits and systems for AI

Hardware Architecture.title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms.
  In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.

Hardware Architecture.title: AMARA: Compiler-Driven Accelerator Architecture Design for Graphical Probabilistic Sampling
Hardware Architecture.summary: Sampling methods are fundamental primitives for training and inference on probabilistic models. However, practical deployment of sampling algorithms such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) remains difficult on general-purpose processors. Existing hardware accelerators improve sampling efficiency, but they are typically specialized for a narrow class of models, graph topologies, or update schedules, making it difficult to support the diverse workloads used in real applications. This paper presents AMARA, an end-to-end compiler-driven accelerator framework for probabilistic sampling on arbitrary probabilistic graphical models. AMARA introduces MCMC-IR, a domain-specific intermediate representation that separates local factorized computation from global update dependencies. Based on this representation, the compiler performs architecture-aware partitioning, scheduling, and memory-access optimization to expose parallelism and reduce irregular graph communication. The optimized program is lowered to a compact ISA and executed on a programmable ASIC accelerator with specialized compute, sampling, and memory support. By co-designing the compiler and the architecture, AMARA bridges the gap between model generality and accelerator efficiency for practical MCMC-based probabilistic computing. We evaluate AMARA across representative workloads with different structures, including grid-structured and irregular energy-based models, and causal inference networks. The results show that AMARA supports a broad spectrum of discrete probabilistic models while achieving high sampling throughput and efficient hardware utilization. AMARA achieves an average of 6.1$\times$ (up to 16.3$\times$) higher sampling throughput than a JAX-GPU baseline on irregular workloads, and offers broader programmability than state-of-the-art accelerators.

Hardware Architecture.title: Bit-Sparsity Aware Acceleration with Compact CSD Code on Generic Matrix Multiplication
Hardware Architecture.summary: The ever-increasing demand for matrix multiplication in artificial intelligence (AI) and generic computing emphasizes the necessity of efficient computing power accommodating both floating-point (FP) and quantized integer (QINT). While state-of-the-art bit-sparsity-aware acceleration techniques have demonstrated impressive performance and efficiency in neural networks through software-driven methods such as pruning and quantization, these approaches are not always feasible in typical generic computing scenarios. In this paper, we propose Bit-Cigma, a hardware-centric architecture that leverages bit-sparsity to accelerate generic matrix multiplication. Bit-Cigma features (1) CCSD encoding, an optimized on-chip sparsification technique based on canonical signed digit (CSD) representation; (2) segmented dot product, a multi-stage exponent matching technique for long FP vectors; and (3) the versatility to efficiently process both FP and QINT data types. CCSD encoding halves the cost of CSD encoding while achieving optimal bit-sparsity, and segmented dot product improves both accuracy and throughput. Bit-Cigma cores are implemented using 65 nm technology at 1 GHz, demonstrating substantial gains in performance and efficiency for both FP and QINT configurations. Compared to state-of-the-art Bitlet, Bit-Cigma achieves 3.2\texttimes{} performance, 6.1\texttimes{} area efficiency, and 15.3\texttimes{} energy efficiency when processing FP32 data while ensuring zero computing error.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Computers (TC)

Programming Languages.title: A Simplified Layout Algebra for GPU Kernels
Programming Languages.summary:
The layout algebra behind NVIDIA's CuTe library describes how tensor tiles map onto threads and memory. A layout is a shape with a stride for each entry, so a coordinate's address is the sum of its indices times their strides. As formalized by Shah and by Cecka, its central operations (e.g., composition, complement, division, product) are guarded by at least six interacting admissibility conditions. We show that this complexity is an artifact of a representational choice, not of the domain.
  We present a layout algebra in which every layout names the space its inputs and outputs live in: logical, physical, or thread-value indices. A layout into logical or thread-value space must be a bijection from its $N$ coordinates onto $[0,N)$. A layout into physical space must be alias-free: distinct coordinates land on distinct addresses, except under broadcast, where many threads read one value on purpose and the layout must mark where. Nothing maps out of a physical index.
  Composing $f$ with $g$ requires only that $f$'s range be exactly $g$'s flattened coordinate set. The index arithmetic can always be emitted naively: compute $f$, split the result by division and remainder into $g$'s coordinates, and apply $g$. Often the composite simplifies to a layout; we show that when it does, there is a coarsest such form, whose digits every other one refines, and we emit that.
  A warp's or thread's slice is a \emph{restriction}. A restricted layout is no longer composable, which forces the user to settle the whole view of a tile before taking slices.
  We validate the algebra by reproducing within it CuTe's operations, such as composition, complement, and division. We implement it in OCaml and use the implementation to rederive CuTe's atoms and usage patterns. The decision procedure is proved correct in Rocq.
Programming Languages.comment: Withdrawn by the authors due to intellectual property and confidentiality obligations to an affiliated company.

Programming Languages.title: Prophecy Variables, Program Analysis, Binding Times, and Staged Compilation in the BuildIt System
Programming Languages.summary:
BuildIt is a lightweight C++ library system for implementing domain specific languages (DSLs) and compilers through multi-stage execution. It uses partial evaluation to generate optimized code without requiring parsers, explicit intermediate representations (IRs), or custom code generators. History variables and forward execution support analyses of past computation, but optimizations such as data movement, operator fusion, and binding-time analysis also require information about future execution.
  We introduce prophecy variables into BuildIt to predict future program behavior and guide code generation. Repeated first-stage execution refines predictions until they satisfy the program's checks, extending BuildIt's existing reexecution machinery with little additional complexity. This approach obtains information typically computed by backwards dataflow analyses over an explicit IR while preserving BuildIt's lightweight implementation model. The cost of first-stage reexecution can be amortized over repeated executions of the generated code.
  We formalize the mechanism and mechanize its guarantees in Lean 4. We demonstrate prophecy variables in three applications: selective CPU-GPU data movement, neural-network operator fusion, and automatic binding-time analysis. These applications achieve performance improvements of up to 5.5x while simplifying the programming interface.

Programming Languages.title: DAISY: Fault-Guided Assertion Inference for Dafny
Programming Languages.summary:
Formal verification with Dafny provides strong correctness guarantees, but verification failures often require users to determine where helper assertions are needed and to manually write the assertions necessary for verification to succeed. This proof-engineering burden is difficult, time-consuming, and a barrier to the adoption of verification-aware languages.
  We present DAISY (Dafny Assertion Inference SYstem), a tool for fault-guided assertion inference in Dafny.
  Given a Dafny program and a target method, DAISY localizes likely assertion sites using verifier diagnostics, LLM-based localization, or their combination. It then annotates the program with assertion placeholders, retrieves relevant in-context examples, generates candidate assertions with an LLM, and validates candidates by running the Dafny verifier.
  To evaluate DAISY, we extend DafnyBench with verification-failing variants created by removing helper assertions from verified programs. The resulting benchmark distinguishes between programs with one missing assertion, two missing assertions, and all assertions removed, allowing us to evaluate DAISY on increasingly difficult proof failures. On this benchmark, DAISY verifies 86\% of programs with a single missing assertion and 36\% of programs with two missing assertions. These results show that fault-guided LLM assertion inference can repair many Dafny verification failures. They also show that successful repairs often differ from the original assertions, reducing proof-engineering effort without reconstructing the original proof.

Programming Languages.title: Coinduction in Grounded Arithmetic
Programming Languages.summary: A grounded arithmetic counts a sentence true only when a terminating process establishes it; a sentence no such process settles has no value. Such a logic can state that an event happens, but not that it never happens under unbounded choice. This paper extends such a logic so that it can. The base is Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) with Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA)'s least-fixed-point reading and ground induction. It adds a separate greatest-fixed-point former $ν$ with Park's coinduction rule, proves that one former cannot carry both ground induction and coinduction, and adds a dichotomy rule: the classical disjunction between a least-fixed-point atom and the greatest-fixed-point atom of its dual, under a derivable premise that the body's leaves are decided. The systems are sound for an explicit model reading every $ν$-body at its greatest fixed point, hence consistent; they agree with the least model where it has a value and prove sentences it leaves without one. The dichotomy trades the underivable hypothesis that an order is well-founded for the derivable one that its steps are decided, at the price of a change of model. With ground induction the dichotomy derives the omniscience rule of the sibling system OGA, so the system has no semantics whose certificates for universals are its own proofs; without the dichotomy it has one, though unsound for the least model. The systems prove, as single sentences, that every decided tree is well-founded or has an infinite branch given by a term, total in the new model; that random assignment terminates while its divergent twin runs forever; that a fair loop terminates and the alternating-bit protocol delivers every message; that open games are determined; that the termination gap in Nakata and Uustalu's trace semantics closes; and that Cinderella wins the bucket game at capacity three. Isabelle/HOL checks every result.

Programming Languages.title: Internal Reasoning and Consistency in Reflective Grounded Arithmetic
Programming Languages.summary:
Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) is a paracomplete arithmetic allowing direct expression of any general-recursive computation. Every RGA term is a program and truth is grounded evaluation, with a proof certificate at each universal quantifier. This paper shows, in a machine-checked Isabelle/HOL development, that such a system is powerful enough to carry out its own metamathematics. A fuel-indexed decider of RGA's grounded semantics and checkers for RGA's proofs are compiled primitive-recursive RGA terms. RGA proves internally that its decider never affirms 0 = 1, and that every well-formed term it affirms has an RGA proof accepted by a transparent test. RGA proves that, for each valid RGA proof, its conclusion is true. RGA proves that each grounded-true well-formed term is provable. RGA proves that no proof in either of two decided classes of RGA proofs derives 0 = 1.
  RGA's truth predicate also serves as a medium for proof by reflection, of the kind that adds nothing to the system. RGA derives disquotation for quantifier-free formulas as rules in every context, at a free variable, and proves, as one sentence, that whenever its normalizer for polynomials in one variable gives two terms the same normal form, the equation between them is true at every value of the variable. Each such polynomial identity then follows from that sentence by closed evaluation and disquotation, with no reflection rule. A companion paper proves Gödel's incompleteness theorems for RGA and its extensions.

Programming Languages.title: MLIRBench - A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning
Programming Languages.summary: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular in software engineering and have performed well on different programming tasks. However, it is still difficult to know whether these models truly understand program behavior or whether they mainly rely on patterns learned from their training data. This distinction is particularly important for intermediate representations (IRs), where operations, dataflow, and execution semantics are explicitly represented. In this paper, we introduce MLIRBench, a benchmark for evaluating how LLMs reason about MLIR programs. MLIRBench uses a multi-agent pipeline to generate program mutations, validate their behavior through execution, and construct reasoning tasks from torch and linalg program pairs. The dataset contains 1,768 validated pairs, including 888 linalg pairs and 880 torch pairs, labeled as EQUIV, DIVERGE, or ERROR. We evaluated nine models, including five open-weight and four proprietary models. Gemini 3.1 Pro achieved the highest hard-label accuracy of 92.65% across all 1,768 pairs, counting unsuccessful predictions as incorrect. Across its 1,768 scored predictions, it achieved an aggregate score of 74.18 and a judge-assigned result-behavior score of 5.04/10. These results show that strong semantic classification does not necessarily imply accurate prediction of detailed execution behavior, highlighting a gap in current LLM reasoning over compiler IRs. By exposing this gap through execution-validated program pairs, MLIRBench provides a reproducible foundation for studying semantic reasoning over compiler IRs and related tasks such as program repair and semantic classification.
Programming Languages.comment: Accepted at the 2027 IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO 2027)

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Exact Distances for Parameterized String Matching with Mismatches
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Two strings are considered to have parameterized matching when there exists a bijection of the parameterized alphabet onto itself such that it transforms one string to another. Parameterized matching has application in software duplication detection, image processing, and computational biology. We consider the problem for which a pattern $p$, a text $t$ and a mismatch tolerance limit $k$ are given and the goal is to find all positions in text $t$ for which pattern $p$ parameterized matches with $|p|$-length substrings of $t$ with at most $k$ mismatches. The number of mismatches is the Hamming distance under the best bijection, which we call the parameterized distance. Our main result is an algorithm that computes the parameterized distance at every position of the text, and hence solves this problem for every $k$ at once. Its running time is $O((σ_p^2+σ_s)\, n\log m + n\,T_M)$, where $n = |t|$, $m=|p|$, $σ_p$ and $σ_s$ are the numbers of parameterized and static characters, and $T_M$ is the time to compute one maximum weight matching in a bipartite graph with $2σ_p$ vertices. With the algorithm of Gabow and Tarjan, $T_M=O(σ_p^{2.5}\log(σ_p m))$. Since this bound does not depend on $k$, our algorithm improves the algorithm by Hazay, Lewenstein and Sokol for $k=\tildeΩ(σ_p^{5/3}+σ_s^{2/3})$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An EPTAS for Max-Cut on Interval Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Max-Cut was shown NP-hard on interval graphs by Adhikary, Bose, Mukherjee, and Roy (SoCG 2021). The best previously known approximation ratio for this class, due to Ahn, DeHaan, Kim, and Lee (APPROX 2025), exceeded the Goemans--Williamson ratio of about $0.878$ by only $10^{-34}$. We give a deterministic efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTAS): for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate cut of an unweighted $n$-vertex interval graph can be found in time $2^{O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^3(2/\varepsilon))}n^2$. The same guarantee and running time hold for Max-Bisection. An FPTAS is impossible unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$.
  Our algorithm rests on a structural theorem: every interval graph with $m$ edges can be turned into an interval graph of clique-width $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(2/\varepsilon))$ by deleting at most $\varepsilon m$ edges. The construction combines endpoint-rank coordinates, length-dependent rounding, and a shifted dyadic hierarchy. Intervals intersecting cell boundaries at their own scales are isolated at small total edge cost; the interactions of remaining long intervals with smaller subproblems can be summarized by counts. The structural theorem also yields a randomized EPTAS via Lampis's scheme for bounded clique-width; our direct dynamic program is deterministic and handles Max-Bisection.
  Finally, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is NP-hard to approximate Max-Cut within $84/85+\varepsilon$ on unweighted chordal graphs, which contain interval graphs. Thus an approximation scheme for Max-Cut on chordal graphs would imply $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Asymptotically Tight Bound on the Number of Distinct Squares in Circular Words
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A square is a word $xx$ with $x$ nonempty. We study the maximum number of distinct squares occurring in the rotations of a word of length $n$. Amit and Gawrychowski (SPIRE 2017) obtained an upper bound of $3.14n$. Charalampopoulos et al. (CPM 2026) improved the upper bound to $\lceil9n/5\rceil$ and gave a binary construction with at least $3n/2-O(\sqrt n)$ distinct squares for infinitely many $n$. They conjectured an upper bound of $3n/2$. Li and Song subsequently reported an improved upper bound of $5n/3$. We prove that a circular word of length $n$ containing $σ$ distinct letters has at most $\lfloor3(n-σ)/2\rfloor$ distinct squares. This settles the conjecture and establishes that the leading coefficient $3/2$ is optimal even for binary words. Our proof groups squares by their Lyndon roots and, for primitive words, uses a weighted count of circuits in the Rauzy graphs of the bi-infinite repetition of the word.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. Revised title and exposition, clarified proofs, and updated references. The main theorem gives the alphabet-sensitive upper bound $\lfloor 3(n-σ)/2\rfloor$, where $σ$ is the number of distinct letters

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Plurality Consensus for $h$-Majority via First-Repetition Rules
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In the h-Majority dynamics, each of n agents holds one of k opinions and, in every synchronous round, observes the opinions of h agents chosen independently and uniformly at random and adopts a most frequent one among them, breaking ties uniformly at random. Let M_0 be the initial number of agents holding the most frequent opinion, and Delta_0 its bias, its lead over the second most frequent opinion. We show that, for every sample size h >= 3, if Delta_0 >= L sqrt(M_0 log n) max{1, n/(h^2 M_0)} for a sufficiently large constant L, then h-Majority reaches consensus on the initially most frequent opinion within O((1 + n/(h^2 M_0)) log n) rounds with high probability. This is the time bound proved for the DejaVu dynamics with h samples (arXiv:2604.03648); our bias condition is that of DejaVu when h >= sqrt(n/M_0), and larger by a factor sqrt(n/(h^2 M_0)) otherwise. Our main contribution, the analysis of one round, rests on a comparison principle: among all rules that read the same observations and treat opinions symmetrically, plurality maximizes the difference between the probability of outputting the most frequent opinion and that of outputting any fixed competitor. We apply it to the rule that adopts the first opinion repeated among h-1 observations, and otherwise the h-th observation: its output law is the law of the new opinion of a random agent after one round of DejaVu with h-1 samples. Hence, in expectation, one round of h-Majority widens the gap between the most frequent opinion and each competitor at least as much as that round of DejaVu, whose analysis we use as a black box. Independently and concurrently, d'Amore, Rybicki, Shimizu, Shiraga and Vacus (arXiv:2610.40562) obtained, among other results, the same time bound under the weaker bias condition of DejaVu, with a different analysis of one round and a martingale analysis over many rounds.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Near-Optimal Consistency-Robustness Bounds for Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the problem of characterizing the optimal consistency--robustness tradeoff for single-machine non-clairvoyant scheduling with predicted processing times. For a fixed number of jobs $n$, Wei and Zhang (2020) established a lower bound on the achievable consistency--robustness tradeoff which is known to be tight only in a few restrictive cases, leaving the optimal tradeoff for general $n$ unresolved. A different worst-case-$n$ regime was introduced by Benomar et al. (2025), who applied the former work's construction to show that for $λ\in (0, 1)$, any $(1+λ)$-consistent algorithm must be $1 + Ω(\sqrt{1/λ})$-robust. On the other hand, the best known upper bound gives $(1+λ)$-consistency and $1+O(1/λ)$-robustness, leaving a polynomial gap. In this work, we develop a new lower bound using a multi-stage adversarial construction and a new algorithm that together give a near-optimal characterization of the consistency--robustness tradeoff: for every $n$, our upper bound is within a multiplicative factor $3/2$ of our lower bound, and thus our algorithm is within a multiplicative factor $3/2$ of the online optimal. In particular, our lower bound shows that any $(1+λ)$-consistent algorithm must have robustness at least $1/\sqrtλ$ as $n \to \infty$, while our algorithm achieves robustness at most $\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}+1/λ}$ for any $n$, matching the lower bound in the leading term as $λ\downarrow 0$; our upper bound also closes the polynomial gap in the worst-case-$n$ regime. We additionally show how our algorithm can be made error-tolerant, preserving the near-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff while incurring only slightly degraded performance under bounded prediction errors.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Efficient Influence Minimization via Source-Integrated Sampling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Influence minimization by node blocking is a fundamental problem in graph data management that seeks a small set of vertices whose removal minimizes the expected spread from a fixed source set. It supports decisions about where to intervene in large interaction networks to control harmful propagation, such as the spread of rumors and infectious diseases. Under the Independent Cascade (IC) model, selecting blockers requires comparing a large number of candidate sets, and estimating their effects on propagation can be costly. We propose SIG (Source-Integrated Greedy), a sampling framework for efficiently finding high-quality approximate solutions. Our key idea is to group the possible sets of neighbors directly activated by the sources according to their effects on blocker selection. SIG represents these groups in a compact weighted tree and computes their probabilities directly, allowing each sample to account for all source outcomes without enumerating them. We prove that SIG produces unbiased estimates of the lower-bound objective without increasing variance for fixed blocking plans, and establish a high-probability quality guarantee through independent validation. Extensive experiments on real-world networks show that SIG has the lowest mean total running time in all main comparisons, with speedups of up to 583x over the fastest baseline. SIG produces solutions competitive with those of prior methods and achieves the highest influence reduction in multiple settings, including on many of the largest networks, where several baselines exceed the runtime limit. Additional experiments show that SIG maintains consistently low running times as graph size and the blocking budget increase, while delivering stronger blocking solutions at larger budgets.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Sharp Lower Bounds for Parallel Log-Concave Sampling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
How many rounds of parallel queries are needed to sample from a smooth, strongly log-concave distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$? For every fixed condition number $κ\in (1, \infty)$, we prove that any sampler making polynomially many queries per round requires $Ω_κ(\log d)$ rounds to achieve constant total variation error in the worst case. The lower bound holds even if queries return derivatives of all orders. Together with the first-order parallel Picard algorithm of \cite{zhou2025parallel}, this establishes a depth complexity of $Θ_κ(\log d)$ for parallel log-concave sampling with $\operatorname{poly}(d)$ width.
  We then study centered Gaussian targets to understand how much width is needed at a given depth. From \cite{chewi2023query,zhou2026complexitygaussiansampling}, it is known that either one round of width $d$ or $\mathcal{O}(\sqrtκ \log d)$ rounds of constant width suffice for first-order Gaussian sampling. At fixed $κ$ we characterize the depth-width tradeoff interpolating between these regimes: when using $ \lceil c \log d\rceil$ rounds, if $0 < c < c_\star(κ)$ then the optimal width at constant TV error is $\widetildeΘ(d^{1-c/c_\star(κ)})$, while if $c \geq c_\star(κ)$ then it is $Θ_κ(1)$. Here, $c_\star(κ)$ is an explicit constant with $c_\star(κ) \sim \sqrtκ / 8$ as $κ\to \infty$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Conflict-Free Cuts: Exploring the Boundaries of Tractability
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A conflict-free cut of a host graph $G$ is an edge cut containing no conflicting pair of edges. The conflicts are specified by a conflict graph $\widehat G$ whose vertex set is $E(G)$. The conflict-free cut problem asks if the given instance $(G, \widehat G)$ has a conflict-free cut. When restricted to planar $G$ and 1-regular $\widehat G$, the problem is polynomial time solvable when $G$ has maximum degree 4, but NP-complete already at maximum degree 5. We study the complexity of conflict-free cut problem under restrictions on the degrees of $G$, the components of $\widehat G$, and the locality of the conflicts. A conflict is local if its two edges share an endpoint in $G$.
  We prove the following results.
  * For $Δ(\widehat G)\le1$, a directed-cycle formulation gives a polynomial-time algorithm when $|E(G)|\le2|V(G)|$, hence for maximum degree four. The problem is NP-complete on $5$-regular hosts with exactly $1$-regular conflicts.
  * For $Δ(\widehat G)\le1$, we give a constructive FPT algorithm in $s_4(G)=\sum_v\max\{0,d_G(v)-4\}$, single-exponential for planar hosts. For arbitrary conflicts, we give an XP algorithm in $η=\max\{0,|E(\widehat G)|-|V(G)|\}$.
  * On $4$-regular hosts, local exactly $2$-regular conflicts with components $C_3,C_4$ give NP-completeness. For local conflicts at maximum degree four, pair or triangle components separately permit polynomial algorithms, but mixing them gives NP-completeness. We classify cases where $\widehat G$ is a union of cliques.
  * An $a$-COC is a vertex set whose deletion leaves components of order at most $a$. For local conflicts, the problem is FPT in the minimum $2$-COC size, but NP-complete with a supplied $3$-COC of size six. Without locality, hardness holds with a supplied $2$-COC of size six. Both hardness results use exactly $1$-regular conflicts.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Faster Scaling Algorithm for Maximum Weight Matroid Intersection
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We consider the maximum weight matroid intersection problem. In this problem, we are given two matroids $M_{1}=(E,\mathcal{I}_{1})$ and $M_{2}=(E,\mathcal{I}_{2})$ and integer weights $w(e)$ on the elements $e\in E$, and the goal is to find a maximum-weight common independent set. We give a randomized algorithm that constructs an optimal solution using $\widetilde{O}(nr\log W)$ queries to the independence oracles of the matroids, where $n$ is the size of the ground set $E$, $r$ is the minimum rank of the two matroids, and $W$ is the maximum weight.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Faster Strongly Polynomial Time Algorithm for Submodular Function Minimization
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a strongly polynomial time algorithm for submodular function minimization with overall running time $\widetilde{O}(n^{2}\mathsf{EO}+n^{3})$, where $\mathsf{EO}$ is the running time of a single evaluation of the function. Our algorithm improves upon the previously fastest strongly polynomial algorithms of Lee, Sidford, and Wong (FOCS 2015), Dadush, Végh, and Zambelli (SODA 2018), and Jiang, Lee, Song, and Zhang (SODA 2024) that run in time $\widetilde{O}(n^{3}\mathsf{EO}+n^{4})$. Similarly to prior works, our work combines a cutting plane algorithm with the combinatorial arc-finding framework of Iwata, Fleischer, and Fujishige (JACM 2001). We achieve our faster running time by developing an algorithm that runs the cutting plane method end to end, without restarting after discovering arcs and contracting strongly connected components.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tree Decomposition of Product and Nest Graphs for Assortment Optimization under the Generalized Nested Logit Model
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The generalized nested logit model extends the nested logit model by allowing each product to belong to multiple nests. The overlapping nests in the generalized nested logit model can capture complex substitution patterns, and the model has found applications in many areas. We study the assortment optimization problem under the generalized nested logit model and prove that it is NP-hard when there are only two nests or when any two distinct nests have at most one product in common. Motivated by these complexity results, we introduce novel concepts of product and nest graphs that capture which products are included in which nests. We use the tree decompositions of the graphs to characterize when the assortment optimization problem admits efficient solution methods. When the treewidth of a product graph is bounded, the assortment optimization problem can be solved in polynomial time. If the treewidth of the product graph is unbounded but the treewidth of the nest graph is bounded, then there exists a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. These results represent the first polynomial-time algorithms for assortment optimization under the generalized nested logit model. Our numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the generalized nested logit model provides a better fit to the data than many existing models in the literature.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 32 pages in main text, 18 pages in appendices

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Improved Subquadratic Bound for Online Bisection
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The online bisection problem is a natural dynamic variant of the classic bisection problem, where one has to dynamically maintain a partition of $n$ elements into two clusters of cardinality $n/2$. During runtime, an online algorithm is given a sequence of requests, each being a pair of elements: an inter-cluster request costs one unit while an intra-cluster one is free. The algorithm may change the partition, paying a unit cost for each element that changes its cluster. This natural problem admits a simple deterministic $O(n^2)$-competitive algorithm [Avin et al., DISC 2016]. While several significant improvements over this result have been obtained since the original work, all of them either limit the generality of the input or assume some form of resource augmentation (e.g., larger clusters). Moreover, the algorithm of Avin et al. achieves the best known competitive ratio even if randomization is allowed. In this paper, we present the first randomized online algorithm that breaks this natural quadratic barrier and achieves a competitive ratio of $\tilde{O}(n^{7/4})$ without resource augmentation and for an arbitrary sequence of requests.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Full version of the paper published in STACS 2024, with competitive ratio improved to $O(n^{7/4} \log^{1/4} n)$

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Bounded Knapsack in Truly Subquadratic Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Bounded Knapsack asks how many copies of each item to take to maximize profit under a capacity constraint. Given $n$ records with binary-encoded multiplicities, we return optimal counts in randomized time with a fixed power saving in the maximum item weight $w_{\max}$ or maximum item profit $p_{\max}$.
  Fix $1<ρ<2$ and suppose integer $(\min,+)$-convolution on length-$m$ arrays can be computed with failure probability at most $η$ in $\widetilde O(m^ρ)$ time, up to polynomial factors in the entry bit length and $\log(1/η)$. Put $f(ρ)=4(3-ρ)/(8-3ρ).$ For any fixed $ε>0$, on inputs whose integers have magnitude polynomial in $n+\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})$, our algorithm runs in time $$\widetilde O\bigl(n\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})^{f(ρ)+ε}\bigr).$$ It returns optimal counts with high probability. If convolution saves $δ=2-ρ$ in its exponent, knapsack retains $δ/(1+3δ/2)$. With the integer convolution exponent $1.9601397040925$, a separate parameter choice gives $\widetilde O(n+\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})^{1.961})$, including for 0-1 Knapsack.
  We keep the copies compressed. Witnessed convolutions generate residual queries, and local linear programs filter them by cost. Resilient lattice cores allow recursive states to coalesce. Progression reserves support rounding, and a thin affordable fiber yields a lift that reduces the normalized column volume. This volume bounds the number of LP regions a grid lookup examines.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Small Maximum Likelihood on Fixed Cavender-Farris-Neyman Trees: An Approximation Scheme and Limits to Fully Polynomial Approximation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Small Maximum Likelihood fits the edge substitution probabilities of a given phylogenetic tree to an observed alignment, summing over the unobserved ancestral states. For the binary Cavender--Farris--Neyman model, we assume a uniform root and an edge-specific substitution probability $p_e\in[0,\tfrac12]$ for each edge $e$, shared across all alignment sites. We give a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme. The algorithm achieves a factor of $1+\varepsilon$ for both the negative log likelihood and the loss after subtracting the uniform-root contribution. Its main step fixes ancestral sequences at one periodically spaced class of depths while summing over all remaining ancestors. A posterior entropy bound controls the cost of this restriction, and dynamic programming optimizes the resulting components over a finite parameter grid. We also give a randomized reduction from Clique showing that an FPTAS returning feasible rational edge probabilities would imply $RP=NP$. These results separate fixed-accuracy approximation from fully polynomial approximation for the same fixed-tree model.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Multiple-Choice Knapsack with Small Items
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Multiple-Choice Knapsack problem is a generalization of the Knapsack problem in which items are partitioned into disjoint classes and exactly one item must be selected from each class. Besides the standard dynamic program running in time $\mathcal{O}(nc)$, where $n$ is the total number of items and $c$ is the knapsack capacity, no other pseudopolynomial-time algorithm is currently known. We present an $\mathcal{O}(n+w_{\max}^4)$-time algorithm, where $w_{\max}=\max_i (w_{in_i}-w_{i1})$ is the maximum weight range within a class.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Geometric Interpretation of 3-SAT and Phase Transition
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Interpretation of 3-SAT as a volume filling problem, and its use to explore the SAT/UNSAT phase transition.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Minimizing Monotone Norms in Fractional Load Balancing
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We devise a fully polynomial time approximation scheme for minimizing a monotone norm $\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert$ over a convex set $X\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d_{\geq 0}$. We study the multi-customer setting, where $X=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ and the solution set $X_i\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d_{\geq 0}$ is given by a linear minimization oracle for each customer $i$. Our algorithm computes, for any given $\varepsilon>0$, a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate solution. With high probability, it uses $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( \varepsilon^{-2}(n+d) \right)$ single-customer linear minimization oracle calls and the same number of generalized KL projections to the dual space $Y=\{y\in \mathbb{R}^d_{\geq 0}: \left\lVert y \right\rVert^* \le 1\}$. We assume no prior knowledge on $X$, and our running time depends only on $n$, $d$, and $\varepsilon$. Our result is robust in the sense that it allows for approximate linear minimization oracles and approximate KL projections. We show that the (approximate) KL projection can be performed efficiently for large classes of monotone norms, demonstrating the applicability of our approach.
  While such a result (with exact projection) is well-known for the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm via multiplicative weight updates and was recently obtained for ordered norms via a smooth norm approximation and a novel randomization, existing techniques do not extend to general monotone norms. In particular, a key feature used in previous proofs was dual price stability, which was derived from a global contraction property of the KL projection to the dual space $Y$. We show that this property does not extend to general monotone norms. Therefore, we use a different price mechanism, based on the well-known mirror descent paradigm, for which a local contraction property holds and guarantees stability.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Beyond Worst-Case Online Algorithms via Input Subsampling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study whether classical competitive ratios survive input subsampling, when both the online algorithm and the offline optimum are evaluated on the same subsampled input. We consider the canonical problems of prophet inequalities and ski-rental. In these settings, for any single subsampling rate, the classical worst-case ratios remain unchanged. We ask a stronger question: can one adversarial input remain worst-case at two distinct rates $p>q$?
  For prophet inequalities, in the model where the policy knows the sampling rate and learns item survival online, every instance has competitive ratio strictly below $2$ at one of the two rates, and we determine the tight simultaneous guarantee. For ski rental, in the fluid model where sampling scales the horizon, the answer depends on $q/p$. Against adversarial distributions over horizons, one unrestricted randomized algorithm achieves a strict simultaneous improvement over $e/(e-1)$ for every distribution exactly when $q/p$ is below approximately $0.34$. Requiring the algorithm to buy by the breakeven time lowers this threshold to approximately $0.31$, showing that unlike classical ski-rental algorithms, buying later can provably help in this setting.
  Our results therefore reveal a new form of beyond-worst-case fragility under input subsampling: instances that are worst-case at one rate need not remain hard at two rates simultaneously.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal-Time Independent Subset Sampling over Acyclic Joins
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Join results can greatly exceed their inputs even when applications need only a small random subset. We study sampling that includes each result independently with a prescribed probability given by the product of its input-tuple weights (PRODUCT). For fixed full acyclic joins with static weights, we achieve input-linear preprocessing and index space together with output-linear expected sampling work, eliminating logarithmic factors from previous bounds. A shared join-tree index supports weighted draws over the entire join and locates high-probability results. Direct Bernoulli trials handle high-probability results, allowing Poisson thinning to generate the remaining independent inclusion decisions with bounded overhead. Our exact sampler uses expected $O(N)$ preprocessing, $O(N)$ index space, and expected $O(1+mμ)$ time per call including output construction. Here $N$ is the input size, $m$ counts relation occurrences, and $μ$ is the expected sample size. The guarantees hold on a real random-access machine with unit-cost exact arithmetic and logarithms, continuous uniform randomness, and expected-time hashing. The time bounds are optimal, matching input reading and explicit output writing. Our floating-point prototype has lower sampling latency than the fastest applicable baseline in 17 of 18 PRODUCT settings on three queries over the STATS benchmark. Construction savings on large joins can offset indexed materialization's faster sampling over a limited number of calls. On a real-data path at $μ=100$, our sampler achieves a $20.5\times$ speedup over indexed materialization for construction plus 300 calls, measured after common data preparation and loading.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Online Vertex Connectivity Augmentation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Network design problems form a classic subfield of online algorithms, but almost nothing is known about their more challenging vertex-connectivity variants. We initiate the study of online vertex-connectivity network design for arbitrary demand pairs by considering the fundamental problem of connectivity augmentation.
