For Online Metric Matching, Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs (1993) and Khuller, Mitchell, and Vazirani (1994) established an optimal deterministic competitive ratio of $2m-1$, attained by the Retrospective (Permutation) algorithm. Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs (1998) conjectured that the same ratio is achievable for online transportation. Recently, Seth, Das, and Raghvendra (2026) obtained a competitive ratio of approximately $6.66m-2.89$ using their Robustified Greedy algorithm. We give an algorithm with competitive ratio $ρ(m-1)+1$, where $ρ\approx5.64$. Our algorithm builds on minimum-spanning-tree search techniques developed by Harada and Itoh (2025) and Arndt, Moseley, Pruhs, and Uetz (2026), using priority-based virtual depth-first searches over the known facilities. However our algorithm uses a phase to shift the geometric search scales, to decide when to skip certain searches and optimize the thresholds that define what edges to include in a given search.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: The majority of this work was generated and edited by iteratively prompting ChatGPT-6 Astra. After review, we believe the results to be correct and want to post the work for the community to view, but we are actively working on simplifying the prose and proof to more clearly highlight the technical insights and contributions

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: List Update with Time Windows and Delays without Batch-Serving
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study list update with time windows and delays when every request requires a separate access. Unlike batch-serving models, serving several requests to one element still incurs one access per request, and each access may change the list for subsequent requests. For time windows of overlap at most $k\ge2$, our deterministic First-Element Removal algorithm is $(3-2/k)$-competitive, hence $3$-competitive in general. Against an oblivious adversary, a randomized adaptation of BIT is $7/4$-competitive on arbitrary $2$-overlap inputs. More generally, on inputs without self-overlap, it is $\left(13/4-9/[2(k+1)]\right)$-competitive for every $k\ge2$. For delays, we give a deterministic $5$-competitive algorithm and a lower bound of $2+\sqrt3$ for deterministic delay-unaware algorithms. Our analyses extend inversion potentials with per-request credits that reconcile different service times and orders.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Finding the Farthest in High Dimensions: Dynamic Diameter and Farthest-Neighbor Search
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give faster algorithms for diameter and farthest-neighbor search in high-dimensional Euclidean space. For every fixed $1<c<\sqrt2$, we maintain an actual factor-$c$ diameter pair under arbitrary point insertions and deletions, with worst-case update time $n^{2/c^2-1}\poly(d,\log n)$ and space $n^{2/c^2}\poly(d,\log n)$, suppressing logarithmic dependence on the execution length and failure probability. Here $n$ bounds the number of active points. The update exponent improves Indyk's algorithm~\cite{indyk} (SODA'03) bound from $1/c^2$ to $2/c^2-1$, while the space exponent improves from $1+1/c^2$ to $2/c^2$. At $c=\sqrt{3/2}$, the update exponent decreases from $2/3$ to $1/3$. A separate construction achieves approximation exactly $\sqrt2$ with update time polynomial in $d$ and $\log n$. All these guarantees hold against adaptive updates, even when every previous random choice is exposed.
  We also improve the time--space tradeoff near linear space. This construction has an always-correct variant with expected amortized update bounds and requires no advance bound on the number of updates. The dynamic structures store a current answer, so reporting its two point identifiers takes constant time.
  The geometric method also gives static diameter algorithms and a farthest-neighbor structure for a fixed set that answers arbitrary adaptive queries. At approximation $\sqrt2-\varepsilon$, the diameter time is $n^{1+O(\varepsilon)}$, and the query time is $n^{O(\varepsilon)+o(1)}$ with near-linear preprocessing and space, up to polynomial input-parameter factors. On binary points, this improves the $n^{O(\sqrtθ)}$ overhead of the algorithm that Andoni, Jiang, and Zharkov~\cite{ajz2026} (STOC'26) for Hamming approximation $2-θ$ to $n^{O(θ)+o(1)}$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A PTAS for Constraint Satisfaction Problems on Interval Graphs and Bounded Rank-Width Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We present a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for all Boolean arity-two maximum constraint satisfaction problems (Boolean Max-2-CSP) where the constraint graph is either interval or has bounded rank-width. This class of problems includes, for example, Max-Cut, Max-DiCut, Max-2-Lin(2), and Max-2-SAT. In particular, this settles the approximability of Max-Cut on interval graphs. To achieve these results, we show the following.
  1. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, there is an $n^{\mathcal O(r \varepsilon^{-2})}$-time $(1 - \varepsilon$)-approximation for Boolean Max-2-CSP on graphs of rank-width at most $r$.
  2. There is a polynomial-time algorithm that, for any interval graph $G = (V, E)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, finds a subgraph $H = (V, F)$ of $G$ such that $|F| \geq (1 - \varepsilon) |E|$ and $H$ has rank-width at most $\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon^{-1})$.
  Our techniques additionally extend to all bounded-alphabet arity-two max CSPs.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximation Algorithms for Matroid-Intersection Coloring with Applications to Rota's Basis Conjecture
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study algorithmic matroid intersection coloring. Given $k$ matroids on a common ground set $U$ of $n$ elements, the goal is to partition $U$ into the fewest number of color classes, where each color class is independent in all matroids. It is known that $2χ_{\max}$ colors suffice to color the intersection of two matroids, $(2k-1)χ_{\max}$ colors suffice for general $k$, where $χ_{\max}$ is the maximum chromatic number of the individual matroids. However, these results are non-constructive, leveraging techniques such as topological Hall's theorem and Sperner's Lemma.
  We provide the first polynomial-time algorithms to color two or more general matroids where the approximation ratio depends only on $k$ and, in particular, is independent of $n$. For two matroids, we constructively match the $2χ_{\max}$ existential bound, yielding a 2-approximation for the Matroid Intersection Coloring problem. For $k$ matroids we achieve a $(k^2-k)χ_{\max}$ coloring, which is the first $O(1)$-approximation for constant $k$. Our approach introduces a novel matroidal structure we call a \emph{flexible decomposition}. We use this to formally reduce general matroid intersection coloring to graph coloring while avoiding the limitations of partition reduction techniques, and without relying on non-constructive topological machinery.
  Furthermore, we give a \emph{fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme} (FPRAS) for coloring the intersection of two matroids when $χ_{\max}$ is large. This yields the first polynomial-time constructive algorithm for an asymptotic variant of Rota's Basis Conjecture. This constructivizes Montgomery and Sauermann's recent asymptotic breakthrough and generalizes it to arbitrary matroids.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Intermittent Cauchy walks enable optimal 3D search across target shapes and sizes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Efficiently locating rare targets requires balancing the exploration of novel space with the exploitation of local vicinities. While this tradeoff is well-documented in simplified environments, its behavior in realistic three-dimensional environments remains unclear. Here we analyze intermittent Lévy walks in three dimensions and show that search efficiency becomes strongly dependent on target geometry, with volume, surface area, and elongation governing performance across the Lévy spectrum. Against this geometric complexity, the Cauchy walk ($μ= 2$) emerges as a robust, near-optimal solution across a wide range of target geometries. Specifically, we prove that for convex targets of surface area $Δ$ in a domain of volume $n$, the optimal expected detection time scales as $n/Δ$, and that the Cauchy walk achieves this scaling up to polylogarithmic factors, while other Lévy strategies are suboptimal in different geometric regimes. Our findings provide a theoretical framework for biological movement patterns, including marine predator foraging and immune surveillance, and inform the design of efficient search algorithms for engineered systems such as autonomous nanoscale explorers.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). Published version: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2614625123

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Edge-wise Graph Alignments
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Pairwise graph ``alignments'', usually defined as maximum common subgraphs, have been considered in many application domains, including the comparison of molecular structures. Most commonly, the problem is formulated as maximum common induced subgraph (MCIS) or maximum common edge subgraph (MCES) problems. Sometimes these formulations are restricted to connected common subgraphs. Common subgraph problems readily generalize to more than two input graphs. However, this concept is fundamentally distinct from the notion of multiple sequence alignments. Abstractly, alignments are defined as super-structures from which the individual input objects are recovered via structure-preserving projections. While the mathematical construction readily applies to common induced subgraphs, it does not fully encompass the common edge subgraph problem, which is the variant more commonly employed in cheminformatics applications.
  In order to consistently define multiple edge-based alignments of graphs we represent a graph $G$ as E-graph $(E,\mathscr{V})$, where $E$ is the edge set of $G$ and $\mathscr{V}$ is the set of sets of incident edges. This representation implicitly encodes the vertices in terms of edge data. Alignments of E-graphs are themselves E-graphs that contain the input (E-)graphs as subgraphs. Maximum edge subgraphs correspond to maximum induced sub-E-graphs, and they can thus be computed using a slightly modified version of the VF2 algorithm without the need to switch from graphs to line graphs. Furthermore, multiple alignments of (E-)graphs yield a natural definition of a consensus graph that is ``on average'' present in the input without having to be a subgraph of every (and in fact of any) input graph.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Bounds for Downward-Closed Prophet and Secretary Problems
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study online selection problems subject to arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints, under different arrival orders, with different distributional assumptions. We establish the following bounds: (1) $Θ(\log^2 n / \log \log n)$ for the standard (adversarial-order) prophet problem, (2) $Ω(\log n)$ for the (Bayesian, random-order) prophet secretary problem, and by extension, for the standard (prior-free, random-order) secretary problem, and (3) $O(\log n / \log \log n)$ for the free-order prophet problem. Together with complementary bounds established in prior work, these results pin down the asymptotically tight competitive ratios for all these variants of prophet and secretary problems subject to downward-closed constraints. Our results refine and reinforce the big-decisions-first principle by Rubinstein and Singla [2026], establishing a superconstant separation between the random-order and free-order models.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Locality Meets Interference: Structure and Scheduling in Radio Multicasting
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study multipoint-to-multipoint multicasting in synchronous radio networks with unknown participant locations and unrestricted message aggregation. Let $n$ be the network size, $k$ the number of participants, and $d$ their hop diameter. A supplied distance-two coloring with $C$ colors yields completion within $(C-1)d+1$ slots and at most $nk$ transmissions. In unit disk graphs, coordinates, one-hop neighbor data, and a common degree bound $Δ_0$ suffice for a $15(Δ_0+1)$-color schedule. A known fixed separation bound permits optimal deterministic $Θ(d)$ completion from coordinates alone. Without geometric data, strong selectivity gives $O(d\min\{n,(Δ_0+1)^2\log n\})$ slots when $n$ is known. Independent random transmission gives $O((Δ_0+1)(d+\log(k/η)))$ slots with failure probability at most $η$; for fixed $Δ_0$, this simplifies to $O(d+\log(1/η))$. A star construction shows that the logarithmic term is necessary for this random rule when the degree grows. We extend color schedules to fixed deletions and subgraphs connected over bounded windows of cycles. Separate conditional reductions preserve additive costs under diameter guessing and control parameter-table and cluster preprocessing. Finally, a counterexample shows that pruning and reranking a breadth-first tree can destroy interference-free delivery. For one-hop designated delivery with receiver degree at most $b$, we prove that the optimal schedule length equals the chromatic number of an associated conflict graph and is at most $2b-1$, with matching examples.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Explicit Edit Codes via Multicoloring
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: For any fixed integers $q\ge2$ and $t\ge1$, we construct explicit $q$-ary codes of length $n$ that correct any combination of at most $t$ insertions, deletions, and substitutions, with redundancy at most $2t\log_q n+O_{q,t}(\log\log n)$ $q$-ary symbols. This matches the leading redundancy term of Levenshtein's classical existential bound. Building on the standard graph-coloring approach, we use a prime-based multicoloring of the edit-confusion graph to assign multiple colors to each $q$-ary word of length $m<n$. Appending a short, edit-protected representation of an assigned color to the length-$m$ word yields a length-$n$ codeword. The choice among the assigned colors carries additional message information, thereby reducing the redundancy. The construction admits deterministic encoding and decoding in $\widetilde O_{q,t}(n^{6t+2})$ and $\widetilde O_{q,t}(n^{7t+2})$ time, respectively.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Canonical Truncation for Mixed-Integer and Combinatorial n-Fold Optimization
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We consider a special block-structured integer program with $n$ blocks. Every block has a prescribed number of vectors that need to be selected while minimizing the objective $c^{\intercal}x + g(Ax)$, where $c$ is a rational cost vector, $A$ is an integral matrix with $d$ rows, and $g \colon \mathbb{Z}^d \to \mathbb{Q}\cup \{+\infty\}$ is an arbitrary function. We access $g$ via an oracle that minimizes $c^{\intercal}x + g(Ax)$ when all but $O(d)$ variables are fixed. Our algorithm runs in time $(ndΔ)^{O(d)}(Q + \text{poly}(|I|))$ where $Δ$ is the largest absolute value of an entry in $A$, $Q$ is the necessary time to evaluate the oracle for $g$ and $|I|$ is the size of the input. This model is a variation of the model studied by Dadush et al.~[IPCO 23]. Their model has only a single block but individual upper and lower bounds on the variables instead of prescribed block sums. For their model they present an algorithm with running time $t^d(dΔ)^{O(d^2)}Q$ where $t$ is the number of variables.
  We use our algorithm to solve mixed-integer linear programs with no upper bounds on the variables, a linear objective, and arbitrarily many constraints involving only fractional variables in time $(mΔ)^{O(m)}\text{poly}(|I|)$, where $m$ is the number of constraints involving integral variables and $Δ$ is the largest absolute value of coefficients of integral variables. This improves the dependence on $m$ in the exponent to asymptotically match the dependency in the integer setting. Further, we use our algorithm to generalize the parameterized algorithm for scheduling on uniformly related machines by Rohwedder~[ICALP 25] to obtain an algorithm for multiple knapsack with running time $w_{\max}^{O(d)}\text{poly}(|I|)$ where $w_{\max}$ is the maximum weight of an item and $d$ the number of different weights.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Deterministic Algorithms for $k$-SAT: Generalization of Chains and Recurrence Proof
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We present a deterministic algorithm for 3-SAT running in $1.32736^n$ time. The algorithm is built on a branching-and-chain framework augmented with a polynomial-time expansion procedure that joins short chains through additional clauses to form bounded-size blocks, which impose stronger constraints on the assignment space. After branching, the algorithm chooses between derandomized local search guided by the block structure and enumeration of block assignments together with selected port variables, reducing the remaining formula to 2-SAT. A weighted analysis of branching, partial-assignment, and local-search costs, together with inductive bounds for chains and block interactions, establishes the running-time guarantee. The framework is self-contained and also offers guidance for practical SAT solver design by identifying useful clause-overlap structures and suggesting when to switch between local-search and reduction-based strategies.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Polynomial-Time Sixth-Power Excluded Grid Theorem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a polynomial-time construction for a sixth-power excluded-grid theorem. Every graph whose treewidth is at least $g^6$ times a fixed polylogarithmic factor contains a $g\times g$ grid minor that our randomized algorithm finds with constant probability. The algorithm outputs an explicit minor model, and the exponent in its running time is independent of $g$. This improves the ninth-power existence bound of Chuzhoy and Tan~\cite{CT21} and the $g^{98}$ threshold in the polynomial-time construction of Chekuri and Chuzhoy~\cite{CC16}. Quantitative bounds relating treewidth to grid size are central to bidimensionality, developed by Demaine, Hajiaghayi, and collaborators~\cite{DH05,DH08}.
  The main ingredient is an asymmetric local routing theorem that uses substantially fewer attachment paths than backbone paths. A balanced recursion preserves connectivity by charging deletions to the boundary of a fixed reference cluster. We construct the smaller attachment sets through a routing hierarchy: either it exposes an accessible well-linked boundary, or its quotient graphs contain the desired grid. These arguments implement cluster splitting using approximate cuts and flow computations. An explicit cut-matching construction and a constructive grid-extraction procedure complete the algorithm.
  We also give a general packing--covering hypothesis for trees meeting three prescribed terminal sets under which the exponent can be reduced below six. A companion Lean development verifies the new construction, its success guarantee, and the composition of its polynomial running time, using explicit interfaces for the published algorithms and standard finite-data operations.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Algorithms for Conservative Finite-Valued CSPs Parameterized by Treewidth
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We consider valued constraint satisfaction problems (VCSPs) with a fixed finite domain $D$ and a fixed finite constraint language $Γ$, in the setting where $Γ$ contains all crisp unary constraints (called hard lists) and the remaining cost functions are finite-valued. We call such a language a finite-valued hard-list language. Let $c_Γ$ be the size of the largest set $S\subseteq D$ such that $Γ$ can express (using the usual VCSP closure operations) a binary disequality function on elements of $S$. Our main result tightly connects the complexity of the problem parameterized by treewidth to this value $c_Γ$.
  (1) The problem can be solved in time $(c_Γ)^{\mathsf{tw}} \cdot (|I| + |\mathcal{T}|)^{O(1)}$ when given an instance $I$ with a tree decomposition $\mathcal{T}$ of width $\mathsf{tw}$ of the primal graph of $I$.
  (2) If $c_Γ\geq 2$, there is no such algorithm solving the problem in time $(c_Γ- \varepsilon)^{\mathsf{tw}} \cdot (|I| + |\mathcal{T}|)^{O(1)}$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$, unless the Primal Treewidth SETH (and hence CNF-SETH) fails.
  In particular, this gives a far-reaching generalization of a similar result of Esmer et al. [ESA 2024] on the optimization version of list homomorphism for graphs.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: The abstract has been truncated for arXiv

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Scheduling with Mandatory Breaks: NP-Hardness and an Additive-One Approximation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In classical fixed-interval scheduling, each job of a given set must be processed during a prescribed time interval. The goal is to assign each job to exactly one machine such that no two jobs assigned to the same machine overlap in their interiors, and the number of machines used is minimized. Without further constraints this is interval graph coloring and is solvable in polynomial time through greedy approaches. We study a variant in which every used machine must remain idle during a contiguous break of prescribed length $x$ somewhere in the scheduling horizon. We show that this additional constraint makes the problem hard, except when $x\le1$. First, for every fixed $x\ge2$, deciding whether $k$ machines suffice for the assignment of a given set of jobs is NP-complete, even when all coordinates are bounded linearly in the number of jobs, so machine minimization is strongly NP-hard. Second, for $x=1$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that solves the problem exactly. Finally, we give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on every feasible instance, outputs a schedule using at most $\mathrm{OPT}+1$ machines, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the true minimum. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no polynomial-time algorithm guarantees $\mathrm{OPT}$ machines for any fixed $x\ge2$, so the additive guarantee of one is best possible.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Classes Testable with $O(1/ε)$ Queries for $ε$ Below an $n$-Independent Threshold
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In this paper, we study classes of Boolean functions that are testable with $O(ψ+1/ε)$ queries, where $ψ$ depends on the parameters of the class (e.g., the number of terms, the number of relevant variables, etc.), is independent of (or sublinear in) $1/ε$, and is independent of the total number of variables $n$. In particular, when $ε$ is sufficiently small so that $ε=O(1/ψ)$, the query complexity is $O(1/ε)$, matching the known tight lower bound $Ω(1/ε)$. In particular, if the structural parameters of the class are fixed and $ε=1/ω_n(1)$ (e.g., $1/\log n$), then the asymptotic query complexity is $O(1/ε)$.
  This result was previously known for classes of terms of size at most $k$ and exclusive OR functions of at most $k$ variables. In this paper, we extend this list to include the classes: $k$-junta, functions with Fourier degree at most $d$, $s$-sparse polynomials of degree at most $d$, and $s$-sparse polynomials.
  Additionally, we show that for any class $C$ of Boolean functions that depend on at most $k$ variables, if $C$ is properly exactly learnable, then it is testable with $O(1/ε)$ queries for $ε<1/ψ$, where $ψ$ depends on $k$ and independent of the total number of variables $n$.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Cycle-Cover Inequalities and Improved Approximation for Shortest Common Superstring with Reverse Complements
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Shortest Common Superstring (SCS) problem is a classical idealized model of genome assembly. However, SCS does not account for the double-stranded nature of DNA: sequencing reads may originate from either strand without a known orientation. This motivates a natural variant, Shortest Common Superstring with Reverse Complements (SCS-RC), which asks for a shortest string containing each input string or its reverse complement as a substring. For SCS, the MGREEDY algorithm constructs an optimal cycle cover of the overlap graph and concatenates the strings obtained by breaking each cycle at its minimum-overlap edge. This algorithm was recently shown to achieve a tight $3$-approximation. Its reverse-complement extension, MGREEDY-RC, also constructs an optimal cycle cover of the overlap graph augmented with reverse complements, but its best known approximation guarantee was $3.75$ (CPM 2026). We extend this cycle-cover inequality to SCS-RC and show that MGREEDY-RC achieves a $3$-approximation, which is tight even over the DNA alphabet. The $3$-approximation guarantee for MGREEDY-RC yields a $2.5$-approximation for TGREEDY-RC, which greedily merges the strings derived from the cycle cover. By replacing this greedy merging step with an algorithm based on a reduction to a maximum-weight Hamiltonian path problem constrained to contain a given perfect matching, we obtain a $(22/9+\varepsilon)$-approximation for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. This improves upon the previous best ratio of $8/3$ (WABI 2026), establishing the best known polynomial-time approximation guarantee for SCS-RC.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Hardness, Approximation, and Parameterized Algorithms for Asynchronous Border Minimization
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In the Asynchronous Border Minimization Problem (BMP), a set of DNA probe strings is placed on a grid and synthesized using a common sequence of nucleotide-deposition steps. At each step, every cell may accept or skip the offered nucleotide. The cost is the total number of disagreements between neighboring cells over all steps. We study both free placement, where the probes may be rearranged, and fixed placement, where their positions are given. We show that free-placement BMP on a square grid is NP-complete over three symbols. For one-dimensional BMP, we prove APX-hardness over a binary alphabet, and NP-completeness even when every probe has length two. We also obtain an $8/7$-approximation for the latter restriction. For square grids, we give a randomized $O(n^{1/4}\log n)$-approximation, improving the earlier $O(n^{1/4}\log^2 n)$ guarantee. Both free- and fixed-placement BMP on rectangular grids are fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized only by the allowed border cost.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Online Survivable Network Design with Arbitrarily Small Connectivity Loss
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the online survivable network design problem, a graph with edge costs is known in advance, and requests arrive one at a time. Each request is a pair of vertices $(s,t)$ with a connectivity requirement $k$, and the algorithm must irrevocably buy edges so that $s$ and $t$ are joined by $k$ edge-disjoint paths. The goal is to keep the total cost close to that of an optimal offline solution.
  Gupta, Krishnaswamy, and Ravi~\cite{GKR12} obtain an $O(k\log^3 n)$-competitive algorithm, where $k$ is the maximum requirement, without relaxing the connectivity requirement. Dehghani, Ehsani, Hajiaghayi, Liaghat, and Seddighin~\cite{DEHLS18} obtain a polylogarithmic competitive ratio when the connectivity requirement is allowed to be relaxed by a factor of $2+\varepsilon$. We show that relaxing the connectivity requirement by a factor of only $1+\varepsilon$ suffices to obtain a polylogarithmic competitive ratio.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: 2-Layer Fan-Planarity in Polynomial Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In this paper, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding whether a bipartite graph admits a 2-layer fan-planar drawing. This resolves an open problem posed in several papers since 2015. We also obtain a linear-time algorithm for the one-sided case.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: A preliminary version appeared in the proceedings of GD 2026

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: When Elements Fail: Weighted Fault-Tolerant Matroid Bases
Optimal-Size Strong Connectivity Preservers under Two Edge Failures in Subcubic Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A $k$-edge-failure strong connectivity preserver of a directed graph on $N$ vertices is a spanning subgraph that has the same strongly connected components as the input after each set of at most $k$ edge deletions. The lower-bound construction of Baswana, Choudhary, and Roditty [BCR18], adapted to strong connectivity in [CC20], gives the previous best bound of $Ω(2^kN)$ necessary edges. Hoppenworth, Saranurak, and Wang [HSW25] prove an $O(k4^kN\log N)$ upper bound, leaving a logarithmic gap for fixed $k$. We close this gap by giving an explicit strongly connected graph on $N=2^d$ vertices with $N-1+(N/2)\log_2N$ edges, every one of which is necessary in a two-failure preserver. Together with the upper bound of [HSW25], this proves that the optimal size in the worst case is $Θ_k(N\log N)$ for every fixed $k\geq2$, whereas it is $Θ(N)$ for $k=1$ [GIP20]. The same graph has a one-failure preserver with at most $3(N-1)$ edges. We also give a randomized algorithm that either returns a spanning subgraph or reports failure. For every fixed $c,\varepsilon>0$, with probability at least $1-N^{-c}$ it returns a correct preserver for $k=2$ with $O(N\log N)$ edges, in $\widetilde O(N^{(ω+3)/2+\varepsilon})$ time and $\widetilde O(N^2)$ space. Here $ω$ is the matrix multiplication exponent over a fixed finite field.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Binary Search Tree with the Unified Bound
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a deterministic online binary search tree (BST) that satisfies the unified bound of Iacono [SODA 2001], which subsumes the working-set and dynamic-finger bounds: it serves every sequence $X$ of $m$ searches on $n$ keys at total cost $O(m+\mathrm{UB}(X))$, and every single search at cost $O(\log n)$. Previously, no BST was known to satisfy the unified bound, even offline. As a consequence, the dynamic optimality conjecture implies Iacono's conjecture that splay trees satisfy the unified bound. We also show that the unified bound is $O((m+n)(1+\log c_σ))$ on every sequence of searches that avoids a fixed permutation $σ$, where $c_σ$ is the Füredi-Hajnal limit of $σ$. Hence every BST that satisfies the unified bound, including ours, serves such sequences at this cost. For permutations this bound is tight, and it improves the previous upper bound $O(nc_σ^2)$ on the optimal cost, due to Berendsohn, Kozma and Opler [STOC 2024]. Finally, we extend the tree to support insertions and deletions: a sequence $X$ of $m$ operations, starting from $n_0$ keys, costs $O(n_0+m+\mathrm{UB}(X))$ in total, where $\mathrm{UB}$ is now the extension of the unified bound to insertions and deletions by Bădoiu, Cole, Demaine and Iacono [TCS 2007]. Hence, if splay trees are dynamically optimal for searches, insertions and deletions, then they serve every such sequence at this total cost as well.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Lower Bounds for Testing Directed Acyclicity in the Unidirectional Bounded-Degree Model
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study property testing of directed acyclicity in the unidirectional bounded-degree oracle model, where a query to a vertex reveals its outgoing neighbors. We prove that there exist absolute constants $d_0\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that for every constant $d\ge d_0$, any one-sided $\varepsilon$-tester for acyclicity on $n$-vertex digraphs of maximum outdegree at most $d$ requires $\widetildeΩ(n^{2/3})$ queries. This improves the previous $\widetildeΩ(n^{5/9})$ lower bound for one-sided testing of acyclicity in the same model. We also prove that, under the same degree assumption, any two-sided $\varepsilon$-tester requires $Ω(\sqrt n)$ queries, improving the previous $Ω(n^{1/3})$ lower bound. We further prove an $Ω(n)$ lower bound for tolerant testing for some absolute constant outdegree bound $d$ by reduction from bounded-degree $3$-colorability.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: The author has withdrawn this paper due to an error in the proof of the one-sided lower bound. In particular, the bound on the probability of a long blue path in Lemma 4.3 does not hold for adaptive exploration.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A One-Sided Sublinear-Query Tester for Bounded-Degree 2SAT
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a one-sided tester for satisfiability of 2CNF formulas in the bounded-degree model. For every degree bound $Δ$, distance parameter $\varepsilon>0$, and $ν\in(0,1/2)$, its query complexity on $n$-variable formulas is $\widetilde O_{\varepsilon,Δ,ν}(n^{1/2+ν})$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Exact and Approximation Algorithms for Computing Smallest SESs and BMSs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Compression schemes represent repetitive strings compactly by using repeated substrings. Computing the minimum size of a representation of a given input string is important for compression and for understanding relationships between compression schemes, although this task is NP-hard for several schemes. In this paper, we introduce exact and approximation algorithms for finding smallest substring equation systems (SESs) and bidirectional macro schemes (BMSs). Specifically, for an input string of length $n$, we give deterministic and randomized algorithms for computing a smallest SES using $O^*(4^n)$ and $O^*(2^n)$ time and space, respectively. We also give a deterministic algorithm for computing a smallest BMS using $O^*(2^n)$ time and space. We further give deterministic and randomized $(1+α)$-approximation algorithms for smallest SESs using $O^*(4^{e^{-α}n})$ and $O^*(2^{e^{-α}n})$ time and space, respectively, for every $α\ge 0$. A conversion from SESs to BMSs gives $4(1+α)$-approximation algorithms for smallest BMSs with the same time and space bounds. All time bounds hold in the worst case, and the randomized algorithms return correct answers with high probability. Our algorithms adapt several approaches to exact and approximation algorithms for combinatorial problems, such as dynamic programming over determinant expansions and a greedy algorithm for monotone submodular functions.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Individually Fair Facility Location
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study individually fair facility location, where each client must connect to an open facility within a prescribed radius and the objective is to minimize total opening and connection cost. We show that preserving the radii changes the approximability of metric facility location fundamentally. For every fixed radius violation below three, no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm achieves a sublogarithmic cost factor unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. The hardness holds with uniform opening costs and uniform radii. It contradicts the strict-fairness constant-factor guarantee recently claimed by Liu, Xu, and Zhang [Theory of Computing Systems, Vol. 70 (2026)].
  We then establish a positive result for arbitrary client radii. We give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that has cost at most $1.725$ times the strictly fair optimum and serves every client within three times its fair radius (in the Appendix we show how this can be de-randomized). We use the approach of Byrka, Srinivasan and Swamy [IPCO 2010]. The facility-location radius factor three is therefore optimal among deterministic polynomial-time algorithms with constant cost factor, unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. Experiments on real-world data indicate that the worst case radius bound is rarely realized in practice: the algorithm serves over 99.8% of clients within their stated radius, and never beyond 1.5 times it. Our code is available at https://github.com/milindmaiti/IFFL_Implementation.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Unified Algorithmic Framework for Dynamic Assortment Optimization under MNL Choice
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We consider assortment and inventory planning problems with dynamic stockout-based substitution effects, and without replenishment, in two different settings: (1) Customers can see all available products when they arrive, a typical scenario in physical stores. (2) The seller can choose to offer a subset of available products to each customer, which is more common on online platforms. Both settings are known to be computationally challenging, and the current approximation algorithms for the two settings are quite different. We develop a unified algorithm framework under the MNL choice model for both settings. Our algorithms improve on the state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of approximation guarantee and runtime, and the ability to manage uncertainty in the total number of customers and handle more complex constraints. In the process, we establish various novel properties of dynamic assortment planning (for the MNL choice model) that may be useful more broadly.

Graphics.title: BrickFlow: Connectivity-Guided Brick Reconstruction
Graphics.summary: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/

Graphics.title: Consistent Video-to-Video Translation via Explicit Correspondences
Graphics.summary: Interactive video-to-video applications require real-time generation while maintaining long-range temporal consistency. However, recent methods achieve speed by restricting attention to a fixed-length causal window. This limits long-range consistency whenever relevant history falls outside the context window. To address this limitation, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based approach grounded in a simple observation. Video-to-video translation provides an explicit cross-frame reference: the regions that match in the input video should match in the output video too. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input, guiding retrieval of previously generated outputs in the corresponding regions, and condition the model on these patches through correspondence cross-attention. Our experiments demonstrate that vid2vid-long consistently improves long-range temporal consistency across recent video models while preserving generation quality and real-time performance.

Graphics.title: Neural Render Proxies for Interactive and Differentiable Lighting
Graphics.summary: Within the CG animation production pipeline, the challenges artists tackle in Lighting can be immense. Even minor adjustments require re-rendering massive scenes with slow offline renderers; global illumination has to be sampled and complex shaders have to be evaluated, leading to iteration times of minutes to hours per frame. To accelerate this process, we introduce a novel neural render proxy (NRP) that enables differentiable relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials at interactive rates. Our main insight is the decoupling of traditional rendering into path sampling and emission computation. From a single, light-agnostic render pass, we collect light transport data in the form of path samples. This enables rapidly sampling lighting conditions on the fly, and training a scene-specific lightweight neural network that learns how light is transported from any scene location to any image pixel. This approach is compatible with non-differentiable production renderers, induces minimal memory requirements during inference, and scales only with resolution and the number of light sources and parameters, but independently of scene and appearance complexity. Our evaluation demonstrates interactive frame rates for relighting (~30-60 Hz) while closely approximating the visual fidelity of ground-truth path tracing. In addition, the differentiable NRP enables fast, gradient-based inverse workflows, allowing artists to efficiently solve for lighting parameters from intuitive image-space edits or generative targets.
Graphics.comment: Accepted at Computer Graphics Forum (Proc. EGSR 2026)

Graphics.title: Sprint3D: Accelerating End-to-End 3D Asset Generation through Pipeline Optimization
Graphics.summary: Image-to-3D generative models now produce asset-quality textured meshes, but at minutes per asset they remain slow to iterate with and costly to deploy. Prior work has mostly accelerated the sampling of the networks, and where it also optimizes the mesh processing, it trains its own generators. We instead start from a publicly released pipeline and ask how much of its end-to-end time can be saved. Profiling the public Pixal3D pipeline shows that its latency is dominated by what happens after the networks: the four rectified flows take 14% of the wall-clock time and mesh post-processing takes 85%, most of it in CPU-based UV unwrapping. We therefore first rebuild the mesh post-processing on the GPU and take it off the critical path, then cut the per-evaluation overhead of the flows and distill them from 76 to 8 network evaluations. The resulting pipeline, Sprint3D, reduces the median time per asset from 133 s to 4.05 s on one H200 GPU at the same export settings (33$\times$). At the same time, on 2,653 held-out Toys4K objects it improves every input-view normal metric of the Pixal3D protocol, with a slightly lower mean silhouette IoU, lower point-cloud alignment scores and less fine texture detail. The rebuilt post-processing alone also speeds up TRELLIS.2, which uses the same export code, by 6.7$\times$ without a detectable change in the evaluated metrics.

Graphics.title: PIM: A Physical Intuition Model for Low-Latency Prediction of Object Interaction Outcomes
Graphics.summary: Predicting object interaction outcomes from initial conditions is a central problem in data-driven physical reasoning. Existing methods often use rigid-body-level states or predict the evolution through autoregressive rollouts. Coarse representations cannot represent local deformation, while rollout errors may compound over long prediction horizons. Instead, we introduce PIM, a Physical Intuition Model that directly predicts a physical system's equilibrium state from its initial mesh geometry, kinematics, and physical attributes. PIM combines local k-nearest-neighbor (KNN) attention to encode intra-object geometry, anchor-based cross-object attention to model interactions, and a dual-branch decoder that predicts object-level translations and per-vertex residual displacements. Across MuJoCo scenarios involving both rigid and deformable interactions, PIM achieves lower vertex and centroid errors than the evaluated baselines. By predicting complete equilibrium states in a single forward pass, PIM substantially reduces latency relative to autoregressive learned models and MuJoCo rollouts under the evaluated protocols, enabling low-latency inference when only the final outcome is required.
